item.title: Grants for Minority Owned Businesses 2026: 5 Federal Options
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Grants for minority owned businesses 2026: compare 5 federal options (8(a), WOSB, microloans, MBDA, grants.gov) with eligibility, deadlines and steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Federal grants for minority-owned businesses are rare in 2026. SBA states plainly that it "does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business," so the federal options that actually work for a minority-owned firm are five programs that pay through contracts, loans or free help, not cash gifts. They are the SBA 8(a) Business Development Program, the WOSB/EDWOSB contracting program, SBA microloans, MBDA Business Centers, and project grants on grants.gov (mainly SBIR/STTR). Since September 10, 2026, being a member of a racial or ethnic group no longer counts as automatic proof of "social disadvantage" for new 8(a) applicants (Federal Register, Aug 11, 2026). Plan for that before you apply.

Which option is right for you?

Pick based on what your business needs in the next 6–12 months, not on which program has "minority" in its name.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, pre-revenue or under 2 years oldFree counseling at an SBDC or Women's Business Center, then a microloansba.gov/local-assistance/find
You need $5,000–$50,000 for equipment or inventorySBA microloan through a local intermediarySBA Microloans
You already sell to businesses or government (daily work use)WOSB/EDWOSB if woman-owned, and/or 8(a)SBA Certifications
You have 2+ years in business and documented evidence of discrimination8(a) Business Development ProgramSBA 8(a) program page
You run R&D or a tech productSBIR/STTR (actual non-repayable awards)/sbir-grants-how-to-apply-in-6-steps-2026/
Nonprofit, university or minority-serving institutionMBDA or SBA cooperative agreements on grants.govgrants.gov Search Grants
Tight budget, no money for consultantsSBDC + APEX Accelerator, both freeSBA counseling

Why these picks: microloans and counseling have no certification gate. WOSB is the easiest certification to qualify for. 8(a) is the most valuable, but it now has the strictest proof requirement. SBIR is the only option here that hands for-profit firms money they don't repay.

Are there federal grants for Black-owned businesses in 2026?

No federal grant program is written only for Black-owned businesses, and as of 2026 the federal minority programs no longer presume that Black owners qualify.

Two legal changes explain it:

  • MBDA (Commerce Department). In Nuziard v. MBDA (N.D. Tex., March 5, 2024), the court ordered MBDA to "immediately stop considering a business owner's race or ethnicity" when deciding who gets its business services. MBDA Business Centers must serve all owners. MBDA's own future is also uncertain: a March 2025 executive order directed eliminating MBDA "to the maximum extent consistent with applicable law" (Wikipedia summary). Courts then ordered it restored, with a preliminary injunction in May 2025 and a permanent injunction in November 2025, which the government appealed in January 2026 (Senate Small Business Committee; case docket).
  • SBA 8(a). SBA's final rule, published August 11, 2026 and effective September 10, 2026, removes the rebuttable presumption of social disadvantage for Black Americans, Hispanic Americans, Native Americans, Asian Pacific Americans and Subcontinent Asian Americans (Federal Register; Holland & Knight summary).

What this means in practice: a Black business owner can still enter 8(a). They just have to show evidence instead of checking a box. Firms already in 8(a) do not have to re-prove social disadvantage (Inside Government Contracts).

Admissions have also slowed sharply. SBA itself reports about 2,100 new 8(a) firms approved in 2021–2024 versus 65 under the current administration (SBA, June 11, 2026).

Pitfall: Many websites still list "federal grants for Black-owned businesses" pages written before 2024. If a page says you "automatically qualify" for 8(a) because of race, it is out of date. Fix: check any source against the SBA rule date (September 10, 2026).

Example (illustrative): a Black-owned IT services firm with three years of revenue might skip 8(a) for now. It could register in SAM.gov, bid on general small-business set-asides, and build its evidence file for 8(a) in parallel.

What federal grants exist for minority women-owned businesses in 2026?

Minority women can stack two SBA contracting certifications, 8(a) and WOSB/EDWOSB. Neither is a cash grant, but both limit who can compete for certain federal contracts. The WOSB side does not depend on race at all, which makes it the more predictable path in 2026.

The federal government's goal is to award 5% of prime and subcontracting dollars to women-owned small businesses each year. Contracting officers can set aside or sole-source contracts to WOSBs and EDWOSBs only when the procurement's NAICS code is authorized for the program (SBA guidance for contracting officials).

Requirement (as of October 2026)WOSBEDWOSB8(a)
Ownership51%+ owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizensSame as WOSB51%+ owned and controlled by socially and economically disadvantaged U.S. citizens
Personal net worthNo capUnder $850,000 (retirement accounts excluded)$850,000 or less
Adjusted gross incomeNo cap$400,000 or less (3-year average)$400,000 or less
Total assetsNo cap$6.5 million or less$6.5 million or less
Race/ethnicity evidenceNot requiredNot requiredEvidence of discrimination against your group + material harm (new rule)
Decision time target90 days after complete package90 days90 days after complete
UpkeepProgram exam every 3 years; annual attestation currently in abeyanceSameMax 9 years in program

Sources: SBA WOSB page, SBA 8(a) page.

Steps to stack both:

  1. Confirm your NAICS code and size at the SBA Size Standards Tool.
  2. Register or renew your entity in SAM.gov (order explained here).
  3. Apply for WOSB (or EDWOSB if you meet the financial caps) at certifications.sba.gov.
  4. Apply for 8(a) separately in the same portal once you have your discrimination evidence assembled (see the 8(a) section below).
  5. Update your SAM.gov profile so contracting officers can find your certifications.

For the women-specific angle alone, see /small-business-grants-for-women-federal-options-2026/.

Is there such a thing as 'free grants' for Black-owned businesses from the federal government?

No. No federal agency hands out unrestricted "free grants" to individual businesses, and the FTC treats offers like that as a classic scam pattern. Real federal grants are competitive, tied to a specific project, and listed for free on grants.gov.

The FTC's Government Grant Scams page says "the government won't get in touch out of the blue about grants" and "real government grants require an application." Its March 2026 alert adds that government grants are not awarded for personal needs and that agencies will not demand a fee to release a grant.

Red flags to act on immediately:

  • A text, DM or call says you "qualify" for a Black-business or minority grant you never applied for.
  • Someone asks for a "processing fee," gift cards, wire transfer or crypto.
  • Someone asks for your SSN or bank login "to verify eligibility."
  • The money is described as usable for rent, personal debt or bills.

Fix: don't reply. Search the program name on grants.gov. If it isn't there, it isn't a federal grant. Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Where the "free money" idea comes from: some federal money really is non-repayable, but it goes to organizations running projects. MBDA's Business Center awards go to the centers, not to business owners, and SBIR funds R&D projects. If you own a small business, what reaches you is free advising from those centers, or a loan or contract.

Example (illustrative): a bakery owner who sees an Instagram ad for a "$10,000 federal minority grant, $99 fee to apply" is looking at a scam. A legitimate next step would be an SBDC appointment and a microloan application through a local intermediary.

What federal programs specifically help Black women-owned businesses in 2026?

Black women-owned businesses can use WOSB/EDWOSB (based on sex and finances), MBDA Business Centers (open to all owners since 2024), and 8(a) (based on evidence). None sets aside money by race, so plan around the parts you can document.

In practice, the strongest 2026 route for many Black women owners is EDWOSB first, then 8(a) if the evidence is strong. The 8(a) final rule says acceptable discrimination evidence can include sex-based discrimination, not only racial prejudice (Inside Government Contracts). A Black woman applicant may therefore be able to document more than one basis.

Steps:

  1. Book a free session at a Women's Business Center. SBA funds more than 100 WBCs that offer free or low-cost counseling.
  2. Check your finances against the EDWOSB caps in the comparison table above.
  3. Apply for EDWOSB at certifications.sba.gov.
  4. Start an evidence folder for 8(a): dated documents showing a government or private entity disfavored your group, proof you were a member of that group at the time, and records of how it harmed you economically (for example, a denied loan or a lost bid).
  5. Ask a local MBDA Business Center, if one still operates in your area, for help with access to capital or contracts.

Pitfall: relying on MBDA while its status is still in litigation (see the Black-owned businesses section above). Fix: call your nearest center before you build a plan around it, and keep SBDC/WBC as your backup.

What federal options exist for small/micro Black-owned businesses with limited revenue?

SBA microloans of up to $50,000 are the most realistic federal entry point for very small minority-owned businesses. Certification programs come later, because 8(a) expects about two years in business.

SBA microloan facts, as of October 2026 (SBA Microloans):

  • Maximum loan: $50,000; average about $13,000
  • Longest repayment term: 7 years
  • Interest: typically 8%–13%, set by the intermediary (rates change; check the official page)
  • Allowed uses: working capital, inventory, supplies, furniture, fixtures, machinery, equipment
  • Not allowed: paying off existing debt or buying real estate
  • Who decides: an SBA-approved nonprofit intermediary in your area, not SBA
OptionRevenue floorSize capBest forLimitation
SBA microloanNone stated; must be operating, for-profitSBA size standardsEquipment, inventory, first working capitalIt's debt; intermediaries may require collateral or training
SBDC / WBC counselingNoneNonePre-revenue planning, loan packagesAdvice only, no money
WOSB/EDWOSBNoneSize standard by NAICSWomen owners ready to bid on contractsOnly helps if you sell to federal agencies
8(a)None, but "potential for success such as having been in business for two years"Size standard by NAICSEstablished firms with federal capacityStrict evidence test; very few admissions recently

Sources: SBA 8(a), SBA counseling.

On size: SBA says "most manufacturing companies with 500 employees or fewer, and most non-manufacturing businesses with average annual receipts under $7.5 million, will qualify as a small business." Receipts are averaged over the latest five complete fiscal years, and affiliates count (SBA size standards). Micro businesses rarely fail the size test. They usually fail the track-record test.

Pitfall: applying for a microloan to refinance a credit card. That is a prohibited use. Fix: spell out uses such as "commercial oven, $8,400" in your request.

Example (illustrative): a one-person landscaping company with $40,000 in annual revenue might request a $15,000 microloan for a trailer and mower. It would work with an SBDC adviser on the cash-flow projection the intermediary asks for.

There are 63 lead SBDCs with more than 900 service centers, so most owners have one within driving distance.

How do you apply for SBA's 8(a) Business Development Program in 2026?

Apply through certifications.sba.gov. You'll need to meet the ownership and financial requirements in the comparison table above and upload evidence of social disadvantage under the September 10, 2026 rule.

Additional eligibility points, as of October 2026 (SBA 8(a) page):

  • Small under your NAICS size standard
  • Good character; no prior 8(a) participation (it's one-time only)
  • Potential for success, "such as having been in business for two years"
  • The 9-year term is split into a 4-year developmental stage and a 5-year transitional stage

Under the new rule, social disadvantage has three parts (SmallGovCon, Sept 2026):

  1. An identifiable racial, ethnic or cultural group suffered discrimination from a governmental or private entity.
  2. You were a member of that group when the action happened.
  3. You suffered material harm, defined as "loss of access to or diminished opportunities related to economic advancement" (Inside Government Contracts).

The portal now asks you to upload evidence and select the type of governmental or private entity involved, rather than write a long narrative.

Steps:

  1. Confirm your SAM.gov registration is active (check it here).
  2. Pull 3 years of personal and business tax returns, a personal financial statement, ownership documents and bylaws/operating agreement.
  3. Assemble your discrimination evidence, with dates, the entity involved and the harm.
  4. Sign in at certifications.sba.gov, choose the 8(a) program, and complete the eligibility questions and uploads.
  5. Submit and watch your email. SBA targets a decision within 90 days once the file is complete.

Pitfall 1: If your application was pending before September 10, 2026, SBA may send it back through "Return to Business." You then have 45 calendar days to update it, or the system closes it automatically. Your original submission date is kept in the queue (SmallGovCon). Fix: set a calendar reminder for day 30, not day 45.

Pitfall 2: Expecting a fast decision in a non-defense industry. SBA says it will prioritize reviews for defense-critical firms, such as ammunition and guided missile manufacturing (same source). Fix: bid on general small-business set-asides while you wait.

Note: firms owned by Alaska Native Corporations, Indian Tribes, Native Hawaiian Organizations or Community Development Corporations are not covered by the new individual-owner test (Federal Register).

Who 8(a) is not for: startups under two years old, firms that don't want to sell to the government, and owners without documentation. Its main limitation is that it's a contracting program. Nobody receives a check for getting certified.

How does grants.gov differ from SBA contracting programs for minority businesses?

Grants.gov lists competitive, project-specific grants, mostly for governments, nonprofits, universities and R&D. SBA's minority-focused programs are certifications and loans for for-profit firms. Knowing which side you're on prevents wasted applications.

Grants.govSBA programs (8(a), WOSB, microloans)
What you getAward for a defined project; must follow federal cost rulesContract eligibility or a loan
Typical applicantsNonprofits, institutions, states; small businesses mainly via SBIR/STTRFor-profit small businesses
DeadlinesFixed close date per NOFORolling applications
Repay?No (but strict reporting)Loans: yes; contracts: you deliver work
PrerequisiteSAM.gov UEI + Grants.gov accountSAM.gov for contracting; none for microloans

How to search grants.gov correctly:

  1. Go to grants.gov and open Search Grants.
  2. Under Opportunity Status, keep Posted and add Forecasted.
  3. Under Eligibility, choose Small businesses (or your nonprofit type).
  4. Under Agency, try Department of Commerce, or the agencies that run SBIR.
  5. Open each listing and read the NOFO's eligibility section before anything else.

Pitfall: applying as a for-profit to a grant restricted to nonprofits or institutions. Fix: read the "Eligible Applicants" line first. If you're a nonprofit, the proposal guide at /how-to-write-grants-for-nonprofits-federal-proposal-guide/ covers the next stage.

The big exception for for-profits is SBIR/STTR, which was reauthorized on April 13, 2026 through September 30, 2031, after a lapse that began October 1, 2025 (Crowell & Moring). SBIR is not minority-specific, but it is one of the few federal sources of non-repayable money for small firms. For the full process, see /how-to-apply-for-grants-for-small-business-2026-guide/.

What are the 2026 deadlines for MBDA and SBA minority business programs?

There's no single annual deadline. SBA certifications and microloans accept applications on a rolling basis, while MBDA and SBIR money follows dated NOFOs that open and close each cycle.

Program2026 deadline status (as of October 2026)Where to check
8(a)Rolling; returned applications due 45 days after returncertifications.sba.gov
WOSB/EDWOSBRolling; 90-day decision targetSBA WOSB
MicroloansRolling, set by each intermediarySBA Microloans
MBDA Rural Business Center Program (MBDA-OBC-2026-00003)Posted May 29, 2026; closed June 29, 2026; archived July 29, 2026Simpler.Grants.gov listing
SBIR/STTRAgency-specific solicitationsEach agency's solicitation and grants.gov

The FY2026 MBDA Rural Business Center NOFO was limited to institutions of higher education described in the Higher Education Act and required cost sharing (listing; NOFO PDF). Individual businesses could not apply. It is listed under Assistance Listing 11.805, the MBDA Business Center Program.

Steps to catch the next cycle:

  1. On grants.gov, use Search Grants and type "11.805" or "MBDA" in the keyword box.
  2. Include Forecasted under Opportunity Status to see what's coming before it posts.
  3. Open the SAM.gov assistance listing for 11.805 for program-level details.
  4. Keep SAM.gov active year-round. Registration lapses can block a submission days before a deadline. See /sam-gov-registration-renewal-5-steps-before-it-expires/.

Pitfall: treating third-party "2026 MBDA grant" pages as open calls. Several aggregator sites list MBDA programs with no close date. Fix: trust only the close date on grants.gov or Simpler.Grants.gov.

Next steps

Start with the free, rolling options today, and only pay for outside help once you know which program fits.

Do today (DIY):

  1. Run your NAICS code through the SBA Size Standards Tool and write down your size standard.
  2. If you're woman-owned, compare your net worth, AGI and assets with the EDWOSB caps and start the WOSB/EDWOSB application at certifications.sba.gov.
  3. Use SBA's local assistance finder to book a free SBDC or Women's Business Center appointment. Ask them to name the microloan intermediaries near you.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • Free, federally funded help: APEX Accelerators (formerly Procurement Technical Assistance Centers, PTACs) are run with Defense Logistics Agency funding and give free government-contracting help, including SAM.gov and certification files (GovCon Chamber explainer). They suit firms getting ready to bid. They don't write your bids for you, and wait times vary by office.
  • Paid 8(a)/WOSB consultants or grant writers: fees vary widely and are quoted case by case (as of October 2026; get a written quote). They can help a firm with complex ownership or a thin evidence file. They're not worth it for a micro business that only needs a microloan, and nobody can guarantee SBA approval. Be wary of anyone who claims they can.

FAQ

Are there grants for minority women owned businesses in 2026?

There's no federal cash grant reserved for minority women. The practical federal tools are WOSB/EDWOSB contract set-asides and 8(a) certification, which can be held at the same time. Women's Business Centers offer free counseling, and SBIR is open if you do R&D.

Are there free grants for black owned businesses in 2026?

Not from the federal government. SBA says it doesn't fund business startup or expansion with grants, and the FTC warns that unsolicited "free grant" offers are scams. Legitimate federal grants are listed free on grants.gov and require an application.

What grants exist for black women owned businesses in 2026?

Federally, Black women owners usually do best with EDWOSB (no race evidence needed), plus 8(a) if they can document discrimination and material harm under the September 10, 2026 rule. Sex-based discrimination can count as evidence for 8(a). Private and state grants exist too, but they fall outside this federal-only guide.

What federal help exists for small black owned businesses in 2026?

For micro businesses, SBA microloans (up to $50,000, terms up to 7 years) and free SBDC counseling are the most accessible. 8(a) expects roughly two years in business. Size standards rarely block small firms, but missing SAM.gov registration often does.

item.title: SBIR Grants: How to Apply in 6 Steps (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SBIR grants for 2026: registration order (SAM.gov, SBA Company Registry, agency portals), Phase I and II amounts, and how to write and submit a proposal.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

SBIR (Small Business Innovation Research) is a federal program that gives U.S. small businesses non-dilutive money to research and commercialize new technology. The government takes no equity and you repay nothing. To apply, register in SAM.gov, then the SBA Company Registry on SBIR.gov, then the portal of the agency that posted your topic. After that you submit a Phase I proposal. As of October 2026, SBA's no-waiver ceilings are $335,937 for Phase I and $2,239,578 for Phase II (SBIR.gov). The program is running again: Congress reauthorized it on April 13, 2026, after a six-month lapse, and it now runs through September 30, 2031 (Crowell).

Which option is right for you?

Your first move depends on your situation. A for-profit startup with no federal registrations should open SAM.gov today. A nonprofit or university usually joins as an STTR research partner and does not apply as the lead.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, for-profit, no registrations yetStart the SAM.gov entity registration. Every later step needs the UEI it issuesSAM.gov
Beginner with a deep-tech idea and no topic matchNSF SBIR/STTR. NSF takes unsolicited ideas, and it starts with a short Project Pitch rather than a full proposalNSF Seed Fund: Get Started
Health, biotech or medical device companyNIH/CDC/FDA parent announcements, which have three standard due dates a yearNIH SBIR/STTR funding opportunities
Defense or dual-use technology (daily work with DoD needs)DoD topics in DSIP. Releases are frequent and each topic is narrowDSIP
Nonprofit or university researcherPartner with a small business on an STTR. Nonprofits can't be the SBIR applicantSBIR.gov eligibility FAQ
Tight budget, can't pay a grant writerFree help from state SBIR support or federally funded advisors (see Next steps)SBIR.gov Apply

Here is the reasoning behind each row. SAM.gov comes first because the SBA registry asks for your UEI. NSF suits beginners because a short pitch tells you whether you fit before you spend weeks writing. NIH's cycle repeats every year, so you can plan around it. DoD pays for very specific problems. Nonprofits are excluded because SBIR requires a for-profit applicant.

What Is SBIR (and STTR)?

SBIR and STTR are federal programs that fund small businesses doing R&D aimed at commercial products. STTR also requires a formal partnership with a nonprofit research institution. SBA coordinates both programs, and 11 federal agencies fund awards through them (SBIR.gov). Each agency writes its own topics, runs its own review and pays its own awards. That is why the process feels different at NSF, NIH and DoD.

SBIR vs. STTR at a glance

FeatureSBIRSTTR
Who appliesA for-profit small businessA for-profit small business, with a research institution partner
Research partner requiredNoYes: a university, nonprofit research institution or qualifying FFRDC
Work splitMostly done by the companyCompany does at least 40%, research institution at least 30% (SBIR.gov)
Where the PI worksThe company must be the PI's primary employer (SBIR.gov)Set by agency rules. NSF STTR also requires a co-PI from the partner institution (NSF 26-510)
Phase I ceiling without a waiver$335,937Same SBA guideline
Phase II ceiling without a waiver$2,239,578Same SBA guideline

The ceilings come from SBIR.gov as of October 16, 2026. Check the official page, because SBA adjusts these guidelines.

Who is eligible

Per SBIR.gov's eligibility FAQ, the company must:

  • be organized for profit
  • have a place of business in the United States, with the work also done in the U.S.
  • be more than 50% directly owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (the FAQ also lists other allowed ownership structures)
  • have no more than 500 employees, counting affiliates

The three phases

Phase I tests feasibility. Phase II funds full R&D, and only Phase I awardees or Direct-to-Phase-II applicants can get it. Phase III is commercialization paid for with non-SBIR money, such as a government production contract or private sales. SBIR.gov describes Phase I as typically lasting 6–12 months and Phase II as about 24 months (SBIR.gov Apply).

The 2026 reauthorization (S. 3971) added a new Phase II "strategic breakthrough" award worth up to $30 million. It also expanded foreign-risk screening and set up future caps on how many proposals one company can submit (Wisconsin CTC). If you have ties to foreign investors, foreign partners or foreign-funded research, expect more disclosure forms than older guides describe.

How to Pronounce SBIR

Most people in the field say SBIR as one word, "ess-bur" (rhymes with "fur"). Some spell it out as "S-B-I-R." SBA doesn't publish an official pronunciation, so either is fine on a call with a program officer.

For example, an applicant might say, "We're applying for an ess-bur Phase I at NSF and an ess-tee-tee-are with a university partner." STTR is almost always spelled out letter by letter. Don't mix SBIR up with SBIRT, a healthcare term covered in its own section below.

How to Find SBIR Grants

You find SBIR grants by searching open topics on SBIR.gov, then confirming the details on the agency's own solicitation page. The agency version is the one that counts. The 11 agencies publish on different schedules, so a topic that closed last month may come back next cycle under a new number.

Steps to find a matching topic

  1. Go to SBIR.gov and open the topics and solicitations search.
  2. Filter by agency, and by status (open or pre-release). Pre-release topics are worth watching. At DoD, the pre-release window is when you can email the topic author with technical questions (DoD SBIR).
  3. Search keywords from your technology: the material, the sensor type, the disease area. Avoid generic words like "innovation."
  4. Open the full solicitation on the agency site and write down the closing date, the time zone, the award ceiling and the submission portal.
  5. Check fit. Does the topic ask for your exact capability, or something next to it? Topic-driven agencies such as DoD tend to reject "close enough" proposals.

Agency cycles you can plan around (as of October 2026)

AgencyHow topics workKnown dates
NSFBroad technology areas. Project Pitch first, then an invited full proposalFull proposals due November 4, 2026 and March 4, 2027 (NSF 26-510)
NIH / CDC / FDAInvestigator-initiated parent announcements, e.g., PA-27-100 for SBIR (NIH)Standard due dates fall around September 5, January 5 and April 5
DoDNarrow topics in numbered releases in DSIPFY2026 Releases 1–4 opened between May and July 2026, each closing about four weeks after opening (DoD SBIR)

A common mistake is relying on a third-party deadline calendar. After the 2025–2026 lapse, many calendars were out of date. Treat the agency's solicitation PDF as the only source for the deadline.

How to Get SBIR Funding (Step-by-Step)

To get SBIR funding, register in a fixed order, match one agency topic, then win Phase I before you compete for Phase II. Registrations can take weeks, so start them before you write anything.

The 6 steps

  1. Confirm eligibility. Check the for-profit, ownership, 500-employee and U.S. location rules against SBIR.gov's FAQ. SBIR.gov's registry also has an optional eligibility check as its first step (SBIR.gov Company Registration).
  2. Register in SAM.gov. On SAM.gov, choose Get Started under entity registration and pick Register Entity, not "Get a Unique Entity ID Only." Under purpose of registration, pick All Awards if any target agency awards SBIR as a contract (DoD often does). "Financial Assistance Awards Only" covers grants only. You need the UEI from SAM.gov before you can finish the SBA registration (SBIR.gov Apply). The full sequence is in our guide to Grants.gov vs SAM.gov registration order.
  3. Register in the SBA Company Registry on SBIR.gov. It takes four steps: an optional eligibility check, sign-in or account creation, company information (including your UEI), then ownership and contact details. When you finish, you get an SBC Control ID that works at all 11 agencies (SBIR.gov Company Registration). Save the registration PDF, because some agencies ask you to attach it.
  4. Register in the agency portal. NSF needs a Research.gov account with Login.gov (NSF 26-510). NIH needs eRA Commons accounts for the organization and the PI, plus Grants.gov. DoD needs a DSIP account.
  5. Pick one topic and win Phase I. Write to the solicitation, which the next section covers, and submit before the deadline.
  6. Plan Phase II and Phase III early. Phase II generally goes to Phase I awardees. Your Phase I final results become the evidence for Phase II, and real customer interest supports your Phase III case.

How much each phase pays (as of October 2026; check each solicitation)

PhaseSBA no-waiver ceilingNSF (NSF 26-510)Typical length
Phase I$335,937Up to $305,0006–18 months at NSF
Phase II$2,239,578Up to $1,250,000About 24 months
Fast-Track (Phase I + II together)n/aUp to $1,555,555Combined
Strategic BreakthroughUp to $30M (new in 2026)Phase II awardees, by invitationVaries
Phase IIINo SBIR funds; other federal or private moneyn/aVaries

Sources: SBIR.gov and NSF 26-510.

SBIR.gov's Apply page gives typical ranges of $50,000–$323,000 for Phase I and $650,000–$2.2 million for Phase II (SBIR.gov Apply). Inside those ranges, each agency and NIH institute sets its own caps. Some NIH institutes allow more for approved topics. The budget limit in your specific announcement is the number to use.

Common registration mistakes and fixes

  • Company name or address doesn't match. SAM.gov, the SBA registry and the agency portal must show the same legal name and address. Fix SAM.gov first, then update the others.
  • Expired SAM.gov registration. SAM.gov registrations must be renewed every year (SAM.gov: Entity Registration). A lapse can block an award even after you're selected. See SAM.gov registration renewal.
  • Not sure whether you already have a UEI. Look it up before creating a duplicate entity (UEI lookup guide).

How to Write an SBIR Grant Proposal

A competitive SBIR proposal follows the agency's template exactly. It answers the topic's technical objectives directly and pairs them with a believable commercialization plan. Reviewers score against the solicitation's criteria, so write to those criteria, not to a general pitch deck.

Writing steps

  1. Download the current solicitation and its instructions. For NSF that is NSF 26-510. For NIH it is the parent announcement plus the SBIR/STTR instructions. For DoD it is the release instructions and the component instructions. Old templates carry old page limits.
  2. Build an outline from the review criteria. Make each criterion a heading so reviewers can find your answer quickly.
  3. State the technical risk plainly. Phase I pays to answer "can this work?" Name the hypothesis, the specific objectives and the measurable go/no-go results.
  4. Write the commercialization plan. Cover customers, the market, competitors, the revenue model and the path to Phase III. NSF's Project Pitch asks about technical innovation, commercial potential and broader impacts before you're invited to write a full proposal (NSF Seed Fund).
  5. Build the budget and justification. Stay under the cap, which includes direct costs, indirect costs and fee. For STTR, show the 40%/30% work split clearly. NSF does not allow cost sharing (NSF 26-510).
  6. Gather the required attachments. Typical ones are biosketches, letters of support, the SBA registry PDF and foreign-disclosure forms.
  7. Do a compliance pass. Check page limits, font rules, file names and that every required section is present.

Example: matching a topic objective

Say a DoD topic asks for "a sensor that operates at -40°C with under 5 W power draw." A weak objective reads "develop an innovative low-power sensor." A strong one reads "demonstrate a prototype maintaining ±2% accuracy at -40°C at ≤5 W, measured in an environmental chamber by month 5." The second version quotes the topic's own numbers and makes them testable. (These values are illustrative only, not from a real topic.)

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Writing one proposal and sending it everywhere. Each agency weighs commercialization, mission fit and format differently. Rewrite for each one.
  • A thin commercialization section. Fix it with named customer conversations, letters of support and a pricing assumption you can defend.
  • Ignoring submission limits. NSF allows two Project Pitches per company per year and limits each organization to one PI at a time (NSF 26-510). DoD allows one proposal per topic per company (DoD SBIR).
  • Writing as a nonprofit. Nonprofit and academic proposal habits (broad aims, heavy literature reviews) don't fit SBIR's product focus. Our nonprofit proposal guide covers federal formats where nonprofits are the applicant.

How to Submit an SBIR Proposal

You submit through the sponsoring agency's own portal, not through SBIR.gov. SBIR.gov only issues your SBC Control ID and lists topics. Submit at least two business days early, because validation errors usually show up at the end.

Portal by agency

AgencySubmission systemKey requirement
NSFResearch.govAn invited Project Pitch first. Login.gov sign-in. Decisions come about 6 months after submission (NSF Seed Fund)
NIH / CDC / FDAGrants.gov (often through NIH ASSIST)eRA Commons accounts for the organization and the PI (NIH R43)
DoDDSIPProposals sent any other way are disregarded. Must be certified in DSIP by 12:00 p.m. ET on the close date (DoD SBIR)
Other agencies (DOE, NASA, USDA, EPA, etc.)Named in each solicitationCheck the solicitation's "how to apply" section

Submission steps

  1. Confirm that SAM.gov is Active and that the details match your SBA registry record (how to check SAM status).
  2. Log in to the agency portal and start the proposal under the exact solicitation or topic number.
  3. Enter your UEI and SBC Control ID, then upload each section in the required format.
  4. Run the portal's validation check. NIH ASSIST, Research.gov and DSIP all flag missing items before final submission. If you file through Grants.gov directly, see our Grants.gov Workspace guide.
  5. Have the authorized company official certify and submit. At DoD, a proposal that was started but never certified is not submitted.
  6. Save the confirmation and tracking number, and check for any error emails over the next 48 hours.

Submission pitfalls and fixes

  • Deadline in the wrong time zone. DoD closes at noon ET, not midnight. Put the exact time in your calendar.
  • The PI has no portal account. At NIH, the PI's eRA Commons ID must be linked to your organization. Set this up weeks ahead.
  • Wrong SAM.gov purpose for a contract. DoD SBIR awards are often contracts. Change the SAM.gov purpose to "All Awards" before you're selected, not after.

SBIR vs. SBIRT: Don't Confuse These Two

SBIRT is not a grant program. It stands for Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment, a public-health approach to substance use (SAMHSA). If you searched "how to do SBIRT" or "how to score SBIRT," you want SAMHSA's clinical guidance, not SBA.

SBIRSBIRT
Full nameSmall Business Innovation ResearchScreening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment
FieldFederal R&D fundingHealthcare, substance use
Run bySBA plus 11 agenciesPromoted by SAMHSA (HHS)
Who uses itSmall businessesClinicians, clinics, schools, hospitals
Common pronunciation"ess-bur""ess-bert"

There's one place the two terms meet: SAMHSA itself funds SBIRT grants. Its FY 2026 notice is TI-26-005. Those are SAMHSA grants for health providers, not SBIR awards. A clinic searching for "SBIRT funding" should read that notice, not SBIR.gov.

Next steps

You can finish the first registration today and have a target topic picked by the end of the week.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Start or verify your SAM.gov entity registration and write down your UEI. Choose "All Awards" if DoD is a possible target.
  2. Create your SBA Company Registry record on SBIR.gov and save the SBC Control ID PDF.
  3. Pick one cycle. If NSF fits, submit a Project Pitch now. Pitches get a response in about 1–2 months (NSF Seed Fund), so the November 4, 2026 deadline is likely too close and March 4, 2027 is the realistic target.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • State SBIR support programs and Phase 0 matching programs. SBIR.gov notes that some states run Phase 0 programs that help pay for proposal preparation (SBIR.gov Apply). Cost: often free or subsidized (as of October 2026; check your state's official page). They suit first-time applicants who need feedback on fit and format. Limitation: what's offered and who can get it varies by state, and advisors review your draft but won't write it for you.
  • APEX Accelerators. These DoD-funded centers give free help with federal contracting registrations such as SAM.gov (APEX Accelerators). Free (as of October 2026; check the official page). They suit companies targeting DoD contracts. They are not for science writing, since their focus is procurement readiness, not technical narratives.
  • Private SBIR consultants and grant writers. Fees vary widely, from flat-fee reviews to full writing packages (as of October 2026; ask for a written quote). They suit funded teams with no time to write. They're a poor fit if your budget is tight or you haven't confirmed a topic match. No consultant can guarantee an award.

FAQ

What is SBIRT screening?

SBIRT screening is the first step of Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment. A clinician uses a short validated questionnaire to estimate how risky a person's alcohol or drug use is (SAMHSA). The result decides whether the person needs no action, a brief conversation, or a referral to specialty care. It has nothing to do with SBIR funding.

How do you score SBIRT?

You score the screening tool, not SBIRT itself. With the AUDIT alcohol screen, the commonly cited positive cutoff for adults is 8 or higher. Lower cutoffs apply to some groups, such as 5 or higher for adolescent girls and older adults and above 0 during pregnancy (NIAAA, Alcohol Research: Current Reviews). Follow your clinic's protocol and SAMHSA guidance for the tool you use.

How do you use SBIRT?

Screen everyone in the setting with a validated tool. Then give a brief, motivational conversation to people at moderate or high risk, and refer people at severe risk to specialty treatment (NIAAA). Primary care, emergency departments and schools commonly use it. SAMHSA's materials cover how to set it up.

How do you pronounce SBIRT?

Most clinicians say "ess-bert," as one word. SBIR, the grant program, is usually said "ess-bur." The extra "T" is the quick way to tell which one someone means.

item.title: Grants for Veterans to Start a Business: 5 Options (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Grants for veterans to start a business are rare. Compare 5 real options (federal grants, VA VR&E, state grants, SBA loans) with Grants.gov steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

There are almost no federal cash grants for veterans to start a business. The SBA says so directly: "The federal government does not provide grants to start a business" (SBA, Veteran-owned businesses). Five real options are open to veterans: research grants (SBIR/STTR) listed on Grants.gov, the VA's Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E) self-employment track for service-connected disabilities, small state or university veteran grants, private grants such as the Amber Grant for women, and SBA-backed loans plus VetCert contracting status. Most "veteran business grant" lists blend these together. This guide sorts out which ones are grants, which are loans, and which only give you a contracting advantage.

Which option is right for you?

The right first step depends on your disability rating, your stage, and whether you are building a technology product. Find your row, then open the page listed.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner with an idea, no business yetFree VBOC counseling plus Boots to Business Reboot (you need a plan before anyone funds you)SBA VBOC program
Service-connected disability ratingVR&E self-employment track (the closest thing to VA-paid startup costs)VA VR&E self-employment
Building tech or R&D (software, medical device, energy)SBIR/STTR Phase I (real federal grants for small businesses)SBA grants page
Need working capital fast, limited budget for feesSBA Express loan with the veteran fee waiver ($0 upfront guaranty fee)SBA veteran fee notice
Want steady revenue from government work (daily work use)VetCert VOSB/SDVOSB certificationSBA veteran contracting programs
Woman veteranWVETP training plus private grants (Amber Grant) plus WOSB certificationSBA VETP programs
Texas or California residentState-specific programs (TVC Veteran Entrepreneur Program, CalVet DVBE)CalVet DVBE

Why these picks: counseling is free and makes every later application stronger. VR&E is the only VA program that can pay for startup items. SBIR is the only large pool of federal grant money that for-profit startups can actually win.

Are There Grants for Veterans to Start a Business? (The Honest Answer)

No federal grant program gives veterans no-strings cash to open a for-profit business. On its grants page the SBA writes, "SBA does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business" (SBA, Grants). Most money labeled "veteran business grant" turns out to be a loan, a loan guarantee, a contracting preference, or a small private or state award.

The SBA does run grants. They just go to other places (SBA, Grants):

  • SBIR and STTR fund research and development that could be commercialized. These are the federal grants a veteran-owned startup can realistically win.
  • STEP goes through state agencies to help established small businesses export.
  • Community organization grants fund the nonprofits that run Boots to Business, Veterans Business Outreach Centers (VBOCs), and the Women Veteran Entrepreneurship Training Program (WVETP). The money pays for training you can use for free. It never reaches your business directly.

Here's how the common "veteran grants" break down by type:

ProgramWhat it really isRepay?Who runs it
SBIR/STTRFederal R&D grant or contractNo11 federal agencies via SBIR.gov / Grants.gov
VA VR&E self-employmentBenefit that can cover tools, licenses, supplies, trainingNoVA
SBA Express / 7(a) Veterans AdvantageBank loan with SBA guarantee; fee waiver for veteransYesYour lender + SBA
VetCert (VOSB/SDVOSB)Certification for set-aside contractsN/A (you earn revenue)SBA
State/university veteran grantsSmall one-time awardsNoStates, universities, foundations
Amber Grant and similarPrivate competition prizeNoPrivate foundation

Pitfall: Some websites promise "free government grants for veterans" if you pay a processing fee. Federal agencies don't charge a fee to apply on Grants.gov, and the SBA's own pages say startup grants don't exist. A paid "grant list" is a red flag. Fix: Apply only through .gov sites or organizations named on SBA.gov or VA.gov.

Government Grants for Veterans to Start a Business: What's Actually on Grants.gov

If you search Grants.gov for "veteran," you'll mostly find VA research, veteran health, and nonprofit service grants, not startup capital. Those grants go to organizations that serve veterans. The useful search for a founder is a filter by applicant type, not by the word "veteran."

Grants.gov eligibility categories include Small businesses, For profit organizations other than small businesses, and Individuals. Each one works as a search filter. "Small businesses" means firms that meet SBA size standards (Grants.gov, Grant Eligibility). Simpler.Grants.gov, the newer search tool, shows how few opportunities individuals can apply for. At the time of the search used for this guide, it listed only a few dozen individual-eligible opportunities, against hundreds for for-profit organizations (Simpler.Grants.gov Search).

How to search Grants.gov for grants your business can actually apply for

  1. Go to Grants.gov Search Grants.
  2. Under Opportunity Status, check Posted and Forecasted. Forecasted listings give you a head start of several months.
  3. Under Eligibility, check Small businesses. Leave "Individuals" unchecked unless you'll apply as a person rather than as a company.
  4. Under Category, try Science and Technology and other Research and Development, which is where most SBIR/STTR listings sit.
  5. In Keyword(s), enter terms tied to your product, such as "SBIR," "STTR," or your technology area. "Veteran" works poorly here.
  6. Open a listing and read the eligibility section of the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) before you do anything else.

Example (illustrative): Say a veteran is building a wearable sensor for workplace safety. Filtering by Small businesses plus a keyword like "SBIR sensor" would find relevant SBIR solicitations. A search for "veteran grant" would mostly turn up VA medical research awards that a startup can't apply for.

Pitfall: You find a grant you qualify for but can't submit. Applying as a business requires SAM.gov registration and a UEI, which can take weeks. Fix: Register first. The order is explained in Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: Registration Order in 4 Steps. Once you're registered, the full application walkthrough is in our Federal Grant Application Guide for Small Business.

VA Grants for Veterans to Start a Business: What the VA Actually Offers

The VA doesn't run a startup grant program for veteran-owned businesses. Its main business benefit is the VR&E self-employment track, which is limited to veterans with service-connected disabilities. The VA also used to verify veteran-owned firms, but that job moved to the SBA.

Facts that matter for your plan:

  • Certification moved to SBA. On January 1, 2023, the VA transferred VOSB and SDVOSB verification from its Center for Verification and Evaluation to the SBA's Veteran Small Business Certification program (VetCert). The SBA began taking applications on January 9, 2023 (IVMF, Syracuse University). Apply at certifications.sba.gov (SBA, Veteran contracting assistance programs).
  • Eligibility for certification: The business must be at least 51% owned and controlled by eligible veterans. For SDVOSB status, those owners must be rated as service-disabled by the VA (SBA).
  • The contracting goal: The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act (P.L. 118-31, Sec. 863) raised the government-wide SDVOSB goal from 3% to "not less than 5 percent" of prime contract and subcontract dollars (Congressional Research Service, R47226).
VA / VA-linked optionCash to you?Who qualifiesWhere to start
VR&E self-employment trackIndirectly (VA pays for approved items)Service-connected disability + employment barrierVA.gov self-employment
VOSB/SDVOSB status (now SBA VetCert)No, but it opens set-aside contracts51% veteran-owned and controlledcertifications.sba.gov
VBOC counseling (SBA-funded)No, free counselingVeterans, service members, Guard/Reserve, spousesSBA VBOC

Limitation: VetCert isn't funding. It helps you compete for government contracts. If you sell only to consumers, it does little for you.

Funding for Veterans to Start a Business: Loans, Grants, and Other Real Options

For most veterans, startup money will come from an SBA-backed loan, with grants as a small extra if anything. Pick the type of funding before you look at specific programs, because each type has a different cost and a different way to apply.

OptionTypeKey numbers (as of October 2026; check the official page)Best forNot for
SBA Express (veteran fee waiver)Loan, 50% SBA guarantyUp to $500,000; $0 upfront guaranty fee for businesses owned by veterans or military spouses (SBA notice)Working capital, equipment, quick approval through your bankFounders without credit history or collateral; the waiver doesn't cover lender fees
Standard SBA 7(a)LoanLarger amounts; SBA has published no veteran discount for standard 7(a) loans approved October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2027 (SBA FY2027 7(a) fees)Buying a business or real estateAnyone expecting the veteran fee waiver on a non-Express loan
MREIDLDisaster loanCovers losses when an essential employee is called to active duty (SBA)Existing businesses hit by a Reserve/Guard call-upBrand-new startups
SBIR/STTRFederal grant or contractAmounts set per agency solicitation (SBA Grants)R&D-heavy productsRetail, food service, most service firms
State/university grantsGrantFor example, TWU awards 5 grants of $5,000 to Texas veterans (TWU)Small gaps such as equipment or licensesCovering full startup costs
Hivers & StriversAngel equityPre-seed to Series A; checks typically $250,000–$1 million (Talk Business & Politics)Scalable startups led by service academy graduates (Hivers & Strivers)Lifestyle businesses; anyone who wants to keep full ownership

Older lists often name StreetShares as a veteran lender. Its current status couldn't be confirmed from a primary source for this guide, so check it directly before you count on it.

Steps to use the SBA Express veteran fee waiver

  1. Confirm the business is at least 51% owned and controlled by one or more veterans (or eligible spouses), as the SBA notice requires (SBA notice).
  2. Collect your DD-214 and a short business plan. A VBOC can review the plan for free.
  3. Use SBA's Lender Match tool on SBA.gov to find lenders that make SBA Express loans.
  4. Ask the lender in writing: "Will this be an SBA Express loan with the veteran upfront guaranty fee waived?"
  5. Compare the lender's own fees and interest rate. The waiver covers only SBA's upfront guaranty fee.

Pitfall: The lender books a standard 7(a) loan instead of an Express loan, and you lose the waiver. Fix: Ask for the program name in writing on the term sheet.

Grants for Disabled Veterans to Start a Business: Specific Programs to Check

Service-disabled veterans have two real options: the VA's VR&E self-employment track and SDVOSB set-aside contracts. Neither one deposits startup cash in your account. VR&E, though, can pay for specific approved startup items.

Under federal regulation, VR&E self-employment comes in two categories (38 CFR § 21.257, via Cornell LII):

  • Category I: For any veteran whose evaluation shows self-employment is "a suitable vocational goal." VA may provide vocational training, incidental business management training, licenses and fees, and "necessary tools and supplies for the occupation."
  • Category II: For veterans "with the most severe service-connected disability(ies)," where self-employment is the only reasonably feasible goal. These veterans get everything in Category I plus extended services.

Before approving either category, VA must conduct "a comprehensive review and analysis of the feasibility" of your business plan. That review covers market conditions, costs, financing, and coordination with the SBA (38 CFR § 21.257). VA.gov lists the requirements: a service-connected disability, an employment barrier, and enrollment in VR&E. Service members without a rating can still apply (VA.gov).

Steps to apply for the VR&E self-employment track

  1. Go to VA.gov Veteran Readiness and Employment and choose Apply for VR&E benefits (VA Form 28-1900). If you already have a rating, you can apply online.
  2. Go to the orientation and meet your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC). Say early that you want the self-employment track.
  3. Write your business plan. The VA offers help with plan development and concept analysis (VA.gov). A VBOC can help too.
  4. Submit the plan for VA's feasibility review.
  5. If VA approves it, the items VA will provide (tools, licenses, supplies, training) are written into your rehabilitation plan.

Example (illustrative): Picture a veteran with a service-connected back injury who wants to start a home-based bookkeeping business. Under Category I, an approved plan might include accounting training, software, and a business license. VA would pay for those items under the plan. It would not hand over a lump-sum grant.

Pitfall: Buying equipment before the plan is approved and expecting VA to pay you back. Fix: Wait until the item appears in your signed rehabilitation plan.

Grants for Female Veterans to Start a Business: Where to Look

Women veterans have three places to look: SBA-funded training aimed at them, private grants open to all women-owned businesses, and contracting certifications they can hold alongside veteran status. None of these is a federal startup grant. Together they cover training, some cash, and access to government work.

OptionTypeNumbers (as of October 2026; check the official page)Limitation
WVETP (e.g., V-WISE at Syracuse IVMF)SBA-funded trainingV-WISE has a 15-day online course, a 3-day residency, and post-training support (SBA VETP)Training only, no cash
Amber GrantPrivate grantThree $15,000 monthly awards; three $75,000 year-end grants for monthly winners (Amber Grant)Highly competitive; check the site for any application fee
WOSB certificationFederal contractingGovernment goal: 5% of federal contracting dollars; certification is free at SBA Certifications (SBA WOSB)Set-asides apply only in specific NAICS industries
TWU Veteran Grant (Texas)University grant5 × $5,000; the 2026 window ran January 27–February 27, 2026 (TWU)Texas veterans who have already formed a business

WOSB eligibility requires the business to be small under SBA size standards and at least 51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizens, with women running daily operations (SBA WOSB). A business owned by a woman service-disabled veteran can hold both WOSB and SDVOSB status, which opens two kinds of set-aside contracts.

Example (illustrative): A woman veteran starting an IT services firm could take V-WISE first, then apply for VetCert and WOSB at certifications.sba.gov. Meanwhile she could apply for the monthly Amber Grant as a separate, non-government source of cash.

For federal grant options aimed at women more broadly, see Small Business Grants for Women: Federal Options (2026).

Grants for Veterans to Start a Business in Texas, California, and Other States

State and local programs are where veterans are most likely to find actual small grants. Many state "veteran grants," though, go to organizations rather than to individual business owners. Check who the eligible applicant is before you spend time on an application.

Texas. The Texas Veterans Commission's Veteran Entrepreneur Program offers consulting on business plans, financing, market research, and government contracting. It also refers veterans to lenders and partners such as the SBA, SCORE, SBDCs, and VBOCs (TexVet). The TVC's Fund for Veterans' Assistance gives reimbursement grants to charities, local governments, and veterans service organizations, not to individual entrepreneurs. It has awarded over $359 million across more than 1,600 grants since 2009 (TVC Grants). For individuals, the TWU Veteran Grant listed above is a real cash option.

California. The Disabled Veteran Business Enterprise (DVBE) program, created in 1989 under Public Contract Code 10115, sets a goal of awarding 3% of state contracts to certified DVBEs. Certification requires an honorable discharge, a service-connected disability of at least 10%, and California residency (CalVet DVBE). The Department of General Services and CalVet run it together. As with VetCert, this is access to contracts, not a grant.

StateMain veteran business programGrant to individuals?Contact
TexasTVC Veteran Entrepreneur ProgramNo (consulting); FVA funds organizationstvc.texas.gov
TexasTWU Veteran GrantYes, $5,000 × 5twu.edu
CaliforniaDVBE (DGS + CalVet)No (3% state contracting goal)DVBE@calvet.ca.gov, (916) 651-3054 (CalVet)

Steps to check any state's program

  1. Search your state's veterans affairs agency site for "entrepreneur" or "business enterprise."
  2. Look for the eligible applicants line. If it says "nonprofit," "local government," or "veterans service organization," you can't apply as a business owner.
  3. Check whether the program is a grant, a loan, or a certification, and whether it reimburses costs or pays upfront.
  4. Note the application window. Many small grants open once a year for a few weeks. The TWU window in 2026 was one month.
  5. Ask your regional VBOC which state programs are active right now.

Pitfall: Applying to a program that's already closed for the year. Fix: Put the next expected opening date on your calendar and use the gap to finish your registrations and business plan.

How to Find Grants for Veterans to Start a Business Near Me

The most reliable "near me" search runs through your regional Veterans Business Outreach Center. The SBA funds 31 VBOC organizations nationwide, and they know which local grants, competitions, and lenders are active (SBA VBOC). Generic web searches for "veteran grants near me" turn up mostly loan ads and fee-based lists.

VBOCs offer workshops, business plan review, mentorship, financial statement analysis, and specialized training in areas such as franchising and international trade. Service members, veterans, Guard and Reserve members, and military spouses can all use them (SBA VBOC).

Steps to find local help

  1. Open SBA's local assistance search at sba.gov/local-assistance and enter your ZIP code.
  2. Filter or scroll to Veterans Business Outreach Center, and note your regional center's phone number and website.
  3. Book an intake session and ask three questions: "Which grants or pitch competitions are open locally?", "Which lenders here do SBA Express veteran loans?", and "When is the next Boots to Business Reboot?"
  4. Ask for an introduction to your SBA district office's Veterans Business Development Officer (SBA).
  5. If you plan to sell to the government, ask the VBOC to walk you through VetCert.

Example (illustrative): A veteran in San Antonio who enters a ZIP code would get the South Central region's VBOC. That center could point to the TVC consulting team and to the TWU grant window. Either is more useful than a nationwide grant list.

SBA's general help line is 866-SBA-HELP (866-722-4357), Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–8:00 p.m. ET (SBA).

Next steps

Start with free registrations and counseling today. Funding decisions come later, once you know which of the five options fits.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Book a free VBOC intake through the SBA local assistance search (about 10 minutes).
  2. If you have a service-connected rating, start the VR&E application on VA.gov.
  3. If SBIR or federal contracting fits your plan, look up whether your business already has a UEI with UEI Number Lookup: Free SAM.gov Search in 3 Steps, then register in SAM.gov.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: Free help comes first. VBOCs, SCORE, and SBDCs cost nothing and suit most first-time founders. If you're going after an SBIR award and want someone to write it, a private proposal consultant is the paid option. Fees are set by each consultant (as of October 2026; get a written quote). A consultant makes sense if you have a strong technology and no time to write, and doesn't make sense for a non-R&D business, where SBIR isn't a fit anyway. Be aware that no consultant can guarantee an award, and that a fee paid to a grant consultant won't buy you the "free startup grant" the SBA says doesn't exist.

Related guides on this site:

FAQ

Are there any grants for veterans to start a business?

Not from the federal government as direct startup cash. The SBA states that "the federal government does not provide grants to start a business." Real grant-type options are SBIR/STTR research awards, items paid for through VA VR&E, and small state, university, or private awards such as the $5,000 TWU Veteran Grant in Texas.

Are there grants available for veterans to start a business?

Small ones, usually through states, universities, and private foundations, often with short yearly windows. Check the eligible-applicant rules, because many state veteran funds, like the Texas Fund for Veterans' Assistance, pay organizations rather than individuals. Your regional VBOC can tell you which programs are open now.

Are there business grants for veterans?

Yes, but most are aimed at specific groups or purposes rather than general startup costs. SBIR/STTR fund R&D, VR&E covers approved items for veterans with service-connected disabilities, and the Amber Grant awards $15,000 monthly grants to women-owned businesses, including those owned by veterans. For everything else, veterans typically use SBA Express loans, which carry a $0 upfront guaranty fee for veteran-owned businesses.

Free grants for veterans to start a business — do they really exist?

Free money with no strings and no competition doesn't exist. Every legitimate grant has eligibility rules, an application, and reporting requirements. Avoid any site that charges a fee to "unlock" veteran grants, and apply only through .gov sites or organizations listed by the SBA or VA.
