item.title: SAM.gov Registration Renewal: 5 Steps Before It Expires
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SAM.gov registration renewal is free and due every 365 days. Learn the 60/30/15-day timeline, the 5 renewal steps, how to check status and what a lapse does.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To renew your SAM.gov registration, sign in to SAM.gov through Login.gov, open your Entity Workspace, choose Update from the entity's Actions menu, review every section, re-certify, and submit. It costs nothing and must happen every 365 days (SAM.gov). Start when the first reminder email arrives, 60 days before expiration, because IRS and CAGE validation alone can take up to 10 business days (DOJ JustGrants).

Which option is right for you?

Most readers should renew it themselves on SAM.gov, and the table below shows where each situation should start.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, first renewal, still have the Entity Administrator loginRenew it yourself, following the 5 steps belowSAM.gov Entity Registration
The person who registered left and nobody can log inRequest the Entity Administrator role. You may need a notarized letterFederal Service Desk (FSD.gov)
Daily grant work, with active awards and applications in progressRenew at the 60-day email and calendar next year's dateYour SAM.gov Entity Workspace
Tight budget, want a person to walk you through itFree APEX Accelerator counselingAPEX Accelerators
Not sure if you're active, expired or pendingCheck status before doing anything elseOur status check guide
Got a letter asking you to pay to renewIgnore it and renew on SAM.gov directlySAM.gov

Here's why. If you still have access, doing it yourself is fastest. If the admin left, you have to fix access before anything else, and FSD handles that. Free counseling suits owners who don't want to read every certification alone. A paid notice is never needed, because renewal is free (SAM.gov).

What Is the SAM.gov Registration Renewal Timeline?

Your SAM.gov registration has to be renewed every 365 days, and you should start about 60 days before the expiration date shown in your entity record. SAM.gov states that "you must renew your registration every 365 days to keep it active" (SAM.gov). The federal grants rule says the same thing in legal terms: recipients must "review and update" their SAM.gov information "annually from the date of initial registration or subsequent updates" (2 CFR 25.200).

Your date is the expiration date shown in your entity record, not the calendar year or your fiscal year end. The Department of Justice tells applicants to "renew your registration prior to its expiration date, which is listed in the entity record on SAM.gov" (DOJ JustGrants).

The reminder schedule (as of October 2026)

Days before expirationWhat happensWhat you should do
60SAM.gov emails the Entity Administrator (FSD Quick Start Guide)Start the renewal. Gather your banking, address and POC details
30Second reminder emailYou should have submitted by now. DOJ advises starting at least 30 days before any deadline (DOJ JustGrants)
15Third reminder emailIf you haven't submitted, do it today. Validation can take up to 10 business days
0Registration becomes InactiveRenew right away. New awards and payments may be held

Third-party guides say there is no grace period and no auto-renewal (FedReady). That fits SAM.gov's own wording: if you don't renew, the registration expires.

Timeline pitfalls and fixes

  • The reminders go to a dead inbox. The emails go to the Entity Administrator's address. If that person left, nobody sees them. Fix: log in now and check who holds the Entity Administrator role. Add a second admin you trust.
  • You renew the week a grant is due. Grants.gov checks SAM status when you submit. A renewal that is still "Submitted" is not "Active." Fix: put your expiration date minus 60 days on a shared calendar.
  • You assume a mid-year update reset the clock. 2 CFR 25.200 counts the annual review "from the date of initial registration or subsequent updates." Don't guess, though. Read the expiration date in your Entity Workspace after every submission.

How to Renew Your SAM.gov Registration (Step-by-Step)

You renew by signing in, opening the entity's Update option in Entity Workspace, reviewing each section, re-certifying and submitting for validation. The labels below come from the Federal Service Desk's Quick Start Guide for Updating Entity Registrations (FSD). SAM.gov sometimes renames buttons, so if a label looks a little different, use the closest match.

Before you start: have these ready

  • Login.gov access for a user who holds the Entity Administrator role (or another role that can register)
  • Your UEI (12 characters). If you don't know it, use our UEI lookup guide
  • Legal business name and physical address exactly as the IRS has them for your EIN/TIN
  • Current bank routing and account numbers for EFT
  • Names, emails and phone numbers for your points of contact (POCs)

The 5 renewal steps

  1. Sign in. Go to SAM.gov and select Sign In in the upper right. Select Accept on the notice. You'll be sent to Login.gov to enter your credentials and complete multi-factor authentication.
  2. Open Entity Workspace. You land in your SAM.gov Workspace. In the Entities widget, select the Entities title to open the Entity Workspace.
  3. Choose Update. Find the entity record, then select the three-dot Actions menu next to its expiration date and choose Update. You'll get two choices: update only the points of contact, or update/renew the entire registration. Pick the full update/renew. Per FSD, only that option makes the registration active for another year. A POC-only edit doesn't renew it.
  4. Review every section and re-certify. Work through core data (name, address, TIN, banking/EFT), assertions, representations and certifications, and points of contact. For grant-only entities, check that your purpose of registration is still right. Read the financial assistance certifications in full, because their text can change between years (see the nonprofit section below).
  5. Submit and wait for validation. Submit the registration. It goes to IRS TIN and CAGE validation, which can take up to 10 business days (DOJ JustGrants). You can't edit a submitted registration until processing finishes (FSD), so check everything before you click.

When the notarized letter comes in

A routine renewal by an existing Entity Administrator usually needs no notarized letter. The letter is for giving "access to new Entity Administrators on existing registrations where there is no existing administrator to approve your role request" (Virginia APEX Accelerator). It is signed by someone with signing authority, notarized, and uploaded through a ticket at FSD.gov. Some third-party guides say a letter is needed for every renewal. If you're unsure, ask FSD before you pay a notary.

Example renewal (illustration only)

For example, picture a nonprofit whose record shows an expiration date of March 14. The 60-day email arrives around January 13. The finance director logs in that week and notices the bank changed after a merger. She updates the EFT details and submits on January 16. That leaves several weeks of buffer even if validation takes the full 10 business days.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeWhat happensFix
Choosing the POC-only updateThe record isn't renewed and still expiresUse the full update/renew path
Legal name doesn't match IRS records (e.g., "Inc." missing)TIN validation fails and the record stays "Submitted"Enter the name exactly as on your IRS letter (CP 575 or 147C)
Old bank account left in EFTPayments may go nowhere or be rejectedUpdate EFT during renewal
Submitting with an error, then trying to fix itThe record is locked until processing endsProofread every section before submitting
Waiting for the 15-day emailValidation may finish after expirationStart at the 60-day email

SAM.gov Registration Renewal Cost: Is It Free?

Yes. SAM.gov registration renewal is free on the official government site, and any charge comes from a private company, never from the government. DOJ says plainly: "There is no cost to register with SAM.gov" (DOJ JustGrants). That covers new registrations, renewals and updates, as well as getting a UEI.

The Better Business Bureau warns about third parties that offer SAM.gov registration and renewal help for a fee and sometimes don't deliver (BBB Scam Alert). The most common version is a fake renewal notice. It's a letter or email with your business name and real expiration date, which is public, plus a payment link.

How to tell a real notice from a sales pitch

  • Real SAM.gov emails remind you to renew and point you to SAM.gov. They don't ask for payment.
  • Sales notices use words like "mandatory," "final notice" or "registry," quote a fee, and link to a domain that isn't sam.gov. Some say in small print that they aren't a government agency.
  • Check the domain. Federal sites end in .gov. Renewal happens only at sam.gov, and support only at fsd.gov.

If you already paid, the payment didn't renew anything. Log in to SAM.gov and renew it yourself. Then contact your card issuer about the charge.

SAM.gov Registration Fee: What You're Actually Paying For (If Anything)

There's no government fee, so any SAM.gov registration fee pays a private company for help. That help is optional. Some organizations pay because they don't have staff time, or because a messy record (name mismatch, lost admin access) needs hands-on fixing. Before paying, compare it with the free options.

OptionCost (as of October 2026; check the official page)Good forNot forLimitation
Renew yourself on SAM.gov$0 (SAM.gov)Anyone with admin access and clean recordsEntities that have lost all login accessYou read and certify everything yourself
Federal Service Desk (FSD.gov)$0 (SAM.gov External Resources)Error messages, admin role problems, notarized letter ticketsPeople who want someone to do it for themHelp desk only. Staff explain but won't enter your data
APEX Accelerator counselor$0 (APEX Accelerators)Small businesses and nonprofits wanting one-on-one guidanceLast-minute same-day emergenciesAppointment wait times vary by office. Focus leans toward contracting
Private consultant or registration firmVaries, so get a written quoteOrganizations that want to hand off the workAnyone with clean data and an hour to spareYou still certify, so legal responsibility stays with you

Pitfalls with paid services

  • Your certifications are still yours. Whoever clicks through, your organization makes the representations. A consultant can't take on that liability.
  • Handing over Login.gov credentials to an outside firm puts your banking data at risk. If you hire help, add them through SAM.gov roles instead of sharing a password.
  • "Expedited processing" doesn't exist for a fee. IRS and CAGE validation runs on the government's timeline.

How to Check Your SAM.gov Registration Status

To check your SAM.gov registration status, search your UEI or CAGE code in SAM.gov's public entity status tracker, or open your Entity Workspace to see the status and expiration date. The status tracker is linked from the SAM.gov homepage and footer and needs no login.

Status meanings

GSA defines these registration statuses (GSA SAM.gov Entity Validation FAQ):

StatusWhat it meansCan you apply/receive awards?
Pending ID AssignmentEntity validation for a UEI is in progressNo
ID AssignedYou have a UEI only, no registrationNo direct awards (SAM.gov)
Work in Progress RegistrationStarted but not submittedNo
Submitted RegistrationSubmitted and waiting for TIN and CAGE validationNot yet
Active RegistrationValidated and registeredYes
Inactive RegistrationRegistration expired. The UEI stays the same and never expiresNo, until renewed

Steps

  1. Go to SAM.gov and open the Entity Status Tracker link (homepage or footer).
  2. Enter your 12-character UEI or your CAGE code and search.
  3. Read the status and the expiration date. For more detail, sign in and open Entity Workspace.

For example, if you submitted a renewal six business days ago and still see "Submitted," that's normal. If it's still "Submitted" after 10 business days, open an FSD ticket with your UEI. Our step-by-step status guide shows the screens in more detail.

SAM.gov Entity Registration Renewal for Nonprofits and Grant Recipients

Nonprofits, universities and researchers with active federal awards must keep SAM.gov active until the award fully closes out, not just until the money is spent. Federal rules require an active registration "at all times during which it has an active Federal award… or an application under consideration" (2 CFR 25.200). The standard award term in 2 CFR Part 25 extends that duty until you submit all final reports or receive the final payment, whichever is later (eCFR 2 CFR Part 25, Appendix A).

Grant-specific things to check during renewal

  • Purpose of registration. Entities that only take grants and cooperative agreements can register for financial assistance awards only (FSD Quick Start Guide for Grants Registrations). If you've started bidding on contracts, you need a full registration. SAM.gov notes that a UEI-only entity "cannot apply directly for federal awards" (SAM.gov).
  • Financial assistance certifications. On January 28, 2026, GSA proposed adding three certifications to the financial assistance reps and certs, covering "illegal DEI," immigration-related conduct and support for violence or terrorism. They would apply at registration and at each annual renewal (91 Fed. Reg. 3726; comments closed March 30, 2026) (Feldesman). GSA estimated about 222,760 financial assistance registrants could be affected (Inside Government Contracts). Read the exact text on screen when you renew, and talk to counsel if any line doesn't fit your programs.
  • Downstream systems pull from SAM. DOJ's JustGrants uses SAM.gov "as the primary source" of applicant information (DOJ JustGrants). A wrong address or POC in SAM carries over into your grant records.
  • Grants.gov roles depend on SAM POCs. Your E-Business POC in SAM controls Grants.gov roles. See Grants.gov vs SAM.gov registration order for how the two connect.

Example (illustration only)

For example, a university lab's three-year award ends June 30, but the final financial report is due 120 days later. The SAM record must stay active through that final report, and through the final drawdown if that comes later. Letting it lapse in August because "the grant is over" breaks the award term.

Pitfalls

  • Multiple UEIs. A department may hold its own UEI apart from the parent university. Each registration has its own expiration date, so track them separately.
  • Single Audit data. Renewal doesn't touch your audit filings, but agencies check both. If you spent $1,000,000 or more in federal awards, see our single audit threshold guide.

What Happens If Your SAM.gov Registration Expires?

If your SAM.gov registration expires, its status turns Inactive. You can't receive new federal awards, and payments on existing awards may be held until you renew and the record is Active again. Your UEI doesn't change and never expires (GSA), so you renew the existing record rather than starting over.

What an expiration can cost you

  • New awards. If your registration isn't active with current information when an agency is ready to award, "the Federal agency may make a Federal award to another applicant" (2 CFR Part 25, via Justice Grants; eCFR 2 CFR Part 25).
  • Applications in progress. Grants.gov and agency systems check SAM status when you submit, so an expired record can get the application rejected (GrantSights).
  • Active award payments. Agencies can hold drawdowns while the registration is inactive. Third-party guides report that a lapse "prevents receiving award payments" even on existing grants (GrantSights). How strict this is varies by agency and payment system.
  • Compliance record. A lapse during an award breaks the 2 CFR 25 award term, and the agency may raise it at monitoring or closeout.

Steps to recover from an expired registration

  1. Confirm the status is Inactive in the Entity Status Tracker.
  2. Sign in and use Update in Entity Workspace, the same path as a normal renewal. Review every section, because an expired record often has stale bank or POC data.
  3. Submit, then email your grants officer: "Our SAM.gov registration lapsed on [date]; renewal submitted [date]; UEI [xxxx]." Ask whether any payment requests are on hold.
  4. If validation stalls past 10 business days, open an FSD ticket and mention the award deadline.
  5. Once the record is Active, resubmit any held payment requests or rejected applications if the deadline allows.

If nobody can log in, start with the Entity Administrator role request at FSD. A notarized letter may be required when there's no existing admin to approve you (Virginia APEX Accelerator).

SAM.gov Registration Renewal vs. New Registration: Key Differences

A renewal keeps your existing UEI and profile and asks you to review, update and re-certify. A new registration starts with entity validation and gets a UEI assigned. Don't create a second registration because your old one expired. Renew the record tied to your existing UEI.

RenewalNew registration
UEIKeeps the existing UEI (never expires)UEI assigned after entity validation
Starting pointUpdate from the Actions menu in Entity WorkspaceGet Started / register entity from Workspace
Data entryPre-filled. Review and editEverything entered from scratch
Entity validationUsually not repeated unless legal name or address changesRequired before UEI assignment
IRS/CAGE validationYes, up to 10 business days (DOJ)Yes, plus validation time
Notarized admin letterOnly if no admin exists to approve a new oneDepends on admin setup. Ask FSD
Cost$0$0
FrequencyEvery 365 daysOnce per entity

Steps to decide which one you need

  1. Search your organization's name in the UEI lookup. If a UEI appears, even with an Inactive status, you renew.
  2. If no UEI appears and you're sure the organization never registered, start a new registration. Our federal grant application guide for small business covers the full order.
  3. If you changed legal structure (e.g., a sole proprietorship became an LLC with a new EIN), you probably have a new legal entity that needs its own registration. Ask FSD before creating one.

Next steps

Today you can look up your expiration date, confirm who gets the reminder emails, and put renewal on a calendar.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open the Entity Status Tracker on SAM.gov, enter your UEI and write down the expiration date.
  2. Sign in and confirm the Entity Administrator is a current employee with a working inbox. Add a backup admin if you can.
  3. Create a calendar event for 60 days before expiration, titled "SAM renewal – allow 10 business days," and invite your finance lead.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: use the comparison table in the fee section above to pick a free or paid option, and book it the same week the 60-day email arrives so appointment waits don't eat into your validation buffer.

Related guides on this site:

  • Check SAM Registration Status: SAM.gov Application Guide
  • Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: Registration Order in 4 Steps (2026)
  • UEI Number Lookup: Free SAM.gov Search in 3 Steps
  • Grants.gov Workspace: Create and Submit in 5 Steps (2026)

FAQ

Is there a SAM.gov registration renewal guide from the government?

Yes. The Federal Service Desk publishes a Quick Start Guide for Updating Entity Registrations that walks through Sign In, Entity Workspace and the Update action (FSD). SAM.gov's Entity Registration page links to a registration checklist and FAQs.

How much does SAM.gov registration renewal cost?

Nothing. SAM.gov doesn't charge for registration, renewal or updates (DOJ JustGrants). Fee requests come from private companies, and the BBB has warned about some of them (BBB).

Why did I get a SAM.gov registration fee notice?

Your business name and expiration date are public, so private firms send official-looking renewal notices. Paying them doesn't renew your record. Only submitting the update on sam.gov does.

How often is SAM gov entity registration renewal required?

Every 365 days (SAM.gov). For grant recipients, 2 CFR 25.200 requires an active registration for the whole time you have an active award or an application under review (2 CFR 25.200).

How do I check my SAM.gov registration status?

Enter your UEI or CAGE code in the public Entity Status Tracker on SAM.gov, or sign in and open Entity Workspace. "Active" means you're eligible. "Submitted" means validation is still running, and "Inactive" means the registration expired (GSA).

item.title: Grants for Nonprofits Without 501c3: 4 Paths Compared
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Grants for nonprofits without 501c3 status: compare fiscal sponsorship, government status, pending Form 1023 and partners, with IRS numbers and steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Yes, you can get grants for nonprofits without 501c3 status. Most groups do it in one of four ways: through a fiscal sponsor that already has 501(c)(3) status, by applying as a government or tribal entity, by applying while Form 1023 is pending, or by applying directly to federal programs that list "nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status" as eligible. Grants.gov really does treat nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status as their own eligibility category, separate from 501(c)(3) nonprofits. That means the deciding factor is each funding notice's eligibility list, not a general rule.

Which option is right for you?

Match your current legal setup to the row below and start there. Each row names the first page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to openWhy
Beginner: informal group, no EIN, no corporationFiscal sponsorshipYour sponsor's application page; directory at the National Network of Fiscal SponsorsYou can apply under the sponsor's status within weeks, without forming an entity
State nonprofit corporation, Form 1023 filed or about to bePending-status path + direct applicationsIRS "Where's my application"Exemption can date back to formation, and some notices accept non-501(c)(3) nonprofits
Daily work: city, county, tribe, school district, public universityApply as a government entityIRS Governmental Information LetterGovernments are eligible applicants on their own and never need 501(c)(3)
Daily work: a for-profit or a nonprofit without 501(c)(3) that wants federal moneyFilter notices by eligibilitySimpler.Grants.gov SearchSome notices list "Nonprofits non-higher education without 501(c)(3)" or "Unrestricted"
Tight budget, under $50,000 a year in receiptsForm 1023-EZ ($275) or a Model C sponsorIRS user fee pageThe cheapest route to your own status, or no filing fee at all
Bigger project with staff, wants independenceFull Form 1023 ($600)About Form 1023Over time, direct eligibility is cheaper than paying a sponsor a percentage

Can You Apply for Grants Without a 501(c)(3)?

Yes. Without your own 501(c)(3), you apply through someone who is eligible (a fiscal sponsor, a government body, a partner) or to programs that accept non-exempt nonprofits. The money has to go to a legal entity that the funder's rules allow.

Federal notices of funding opportunity (NOFOs) list eligible applicant types using Grants.gov categories. These categories include state, county, city or township, and special district governments; federally recognized and other Native American tribal governments; independent school districts; public and private institutions of higher education; public and Indian housing authorities; "Nonprofits having a 501(c)(3) status with the IRS, other than institutions of higher education"; nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status; and small businesses. Individuals appear too, but Grants.gov says most opportunities are for organizations, not individuals.

On the SF-424 application form, the "Type of Applicant" field includes the option "N: Nonprofit without 501C3 IRS Status (Other than Institution of Higher Education)". A non-exempt nonprofit selects that option when a NOFO allows it. Our SF-424 field-by-field guide explains the rest of the form.

Whatever your status, the applying entity has to be registered. Under 2 CFR 25.200, an applicant must be registered in SAM.gov before it submits, must include its Unique Entity ID (UEI) in the application, and must keep the registration active while an application or award is open. For a fiscally sponsored project, the sponsor registers, not you.

How to check eligibility for a specific notice

  1. Open Simpler.Grants.gov Search.
  2. Under Eligibility, check "Nonprofits non-higher education without 501(c)(3)" (or your government type), and also check "Unrestricted."
  3. Open a result and find the eligibility section of the NOFO itself. The search tag is a summary, and the NOFO text controls.
  4. Look for extra conditions such as "must be incorporated in the state," "must have audited financials," or "consortium lead must be a unit of local government."
  5. Before you write anything, confirm that the entity applying (you, your sponsor, or your partner) holds an active SAM.gov registration. Our SAM.gov status check guide shows where to look.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Mistake: Taking a "nonprofit" eligibility tag to mean 501(c)(3) only. Fix: Read both nonprofit categories. Some notices accept either kind.
  • Mistake: Starting SAM.gov registration a week before the deadline. Fix: Register first. SAM.gov's entity registration checklist lists the documents you'll need, including your legal name and physical address exactly as your EIN records show them. Our Grants.gov vs SAM.gov order guide gives the order of steps.

What Is Fiscal Sponsorship and How Does It Work for Grants?

A fiscal sponsor is an existing 501(c)(3) that legally receives and manages grant money for your project, for a fee. That lets you apply for grants before you incorporate.

Fiscal sponsorship is a set of contracts that let a person or group carry out charitable work using a sponsor's tax-exempt status. The field's standard reference, Fiscal Sponsorship: 6 Ways to Do It Right, names six models. In practice most projects end up in one of two:

Model A (comprehensive)Model C (pre-approved grant)
Legal status of your projectBecomes a program of the sponsorStays separate (it can be an informal group or its own entity)
Who employs staffThe sponsorYou
How money movesSponsor spends directly on project costsSponsor receives funds, then re-grants them to you after review
Typical fee (2023 field scan)8%–12% of revenue6%–8% of revenue
Best forProjects with employees and federal compliance needsVolunteer groups, artists, short-term projects

Those fee ranges come from the 2023 Fiscal Sponsor Field Scan by Social Impact Commons and the National Network of Fiscal Sponsors, as summarized here. Across all sponsors, fixed fees ranged from 5% to 12% of revenue (as of the 2023 scan; check each sponsor's current rate). Under both models the sponsor must keep discretion over how charitable funds are used. This is a legal requirement, not paperwork for its own sake.

Steps to apply for a grant through a fiscal sponsor

  1. Shortlist sponsors whose mission matches yours. Search the National Network of Fiscal Sponsors directory, or ask your local community foundation which sponsors it works with.
  2. Ask each sponsor four questions: Which model do you use? What is your fee, and does it apply to federal funds? Do you have an active SAM.gov registration and UEI? Have you managed federal awards under 2 CFR 200 before?
  3. Sign a written fiscal sponsorship agreement before you apply. It should spell out who owns intellectual property, how fast payments go out, and what happens if you leave.
  4. Confirm that the funder accepts sponsored projects. Many private foundations say so in their guidelines. For federal grants the sponsor is simply the applicant, so the sponsor's type has to match the NOFO's list.
  5. Prepare the application together. The sponsor's name, EIN, and UEI go in the applicant fields. Your project is described as the program, and the sponsor's authorized representative signs.
  6. Report through the sponsor. Federal financial reports and audits fall on the sponsor, which is one reason Model A sponsors charge more.

Example (illustration only): A neighborhood watershed group with no EIN finds an EPA environmental education notice open to 501(c)(3) nonprofits. A regional environmental nonprofit agrees to act as a Model A sponsor at a 10% fee. The sponsor submits through its own Grants.gov workspace, hires the group's coordinator as a part-time employee, and files the federal reports. The group gets no money directly. In return it gets a funded program and a track record.

Pitfalls

  • Your eligibility is the sponsor's eligibility. If the NOFO excludes the sponsor's entity type, you can't apply either, however well your project fits.
  • The fee counts against your budget. Ask whether the federal award can cover the fee as an indirect cost. Our de minimis indirect rate guide explains the 15% election a sponsor without a negotiated rate might use.
  • Using a sponsor in name only. If the sponsor doesn't actually oversee how the money is spent, it puts its own exemption at risk. Expect real review, not a rubber stamp.

Government Entity Status: Who Qualifies Without 501(c)(3)

Tribal governments, state and local agencies, and public schools or universities are eligible for most federal grants without ever filing for 501(c)(3) status. Their governmental status is what makes them eligible.

The IRS explains that "Governmental units, such as states and their political subdivisions, are not generally subject to federal income tax" because of their sovereign powers and public nature. A political subdivision gets its exemption from being governmental, not from being a charity.

EntityGrants.gov categoryNeeds 501(c)(3)?Proof that funders ask for
State agencyState governmentsNoStatute or agency charter; governmental information letter
County, city, townshipCounty / City or township governmentsNoGovernmental information letter
Special district (water, fire, library)Special district governmentsNoEnabling statute or formation order
Federally recognized tribeNative American tribal governments (federally recognized)NoListing as a federally recognized tribe
Public school districtIndependent school districtsNoState education agency records
Public universityPublic and state-controlled institutions of higher educationNoState charter; many also hold an IRS letter
Housing authorityPublic housing authorities / Indian housing authoritiesNoHUD records

Categories are from Grants.gov Eligibility (as of October 2026).

Steps for a government applicant

  1. Request a governmental information letter if a private funder or partner wants proof of tax status. Call the IRS at 877-829-5500. The letter is free.
  2. Register the exact legal entity in SAM.gov. For example, "City of X" or "X County Board of Commissioners," not the parks department's nickname. Use our UEI lookup guide to see whether your government already has a UEI. Many do, often under the finance office.
  3. Select the matching government type in the SF-424 "Type of Applicant" field.

Pitfall: Community groups sometimes ask a city to apply for them and pass the money through. This works, but the government becomes the recipient and must follow subaward rules. Settle in writing who does the work and who covers any match before anyone applies.

How to Start a Nonprofit Without a 501(c)(3)

You can incorporate as a nonprofit under state law, or run as an unincorporated association, while Form 1023 is pending. Until the IRS approves you, though, donations aren't tax-deductible.

Two separate systems are involved. Your state creates the legal entity. The IRS decides whether that entity is tax-exempt. The IRS accepts exemption applications from a corporation, an unincorporated association, or a trust, so incorporating isn't strictly required. Grant applications and SAM.gov registration go more smoothly for a corporation, however.

Steps

  1. Draft your organizing document. For a corporation, that's articles of incorporation, filed with your state's Secretary of State (or its equivalent office). For an unincorporated association, it's articles of association or a constitution. The IRS requires the document to include your name, your purposes, the date it was adopted, and the signatures of at least two individuals.
  2. Include the two clauses the IRS looks for. The first limits your purposes to 501(c)(3) purposes: charitable, religious, educational, scientific, literary, testing for public safety, fostering amateur sports competition, or preventing cruelty to children or animals. The second dedicates your assets to exempt purposes if you dissolve.
  3. Get an EIN from the IRS. It's required before any exemption application. The Form 1023-EZ instructions say plainly that "All organizations must have an EIN".
  4. Adopt bylaws and seat a board. Funders and SAM.gov both expect identifiable officers.
  5. Choose your IRS form. Form 1023-EZ is open if your annual gross receipts haven't gone over and won't go over $50,000 in any of the past or next three years, and your total assets are $250,000 or less. Otherwise, file Form 1023.
  6. File on Pay.gov. Both forms must be filed electronically. On Pay.gov, create an account, search for "1023," and select the form.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Missing dissolution clause. This is one of the most common reasons the IRS asks follow-up questions. Fix: Copy the required language from the Form 1023 instructions into your articles before you file them with the state.
  • Choosing 1023-EZ when you'll soon outgrow it. If you're expecting a $150,000 federal grant within three years, you don't meet the gross-receipts test. Fix: File the full Form 1023.

Can a Nonprofit Operate Without a 501(c)(3)?

Yes. State nonprofit incorporation and federal tax exemption are separate. You can operate legally as a state nonprofit corporation before or without 501(c)(3) status, but you give up deductible donations and many grant opportunities.

There's also a small-organization exception. A charity whose gross receipts are normally not more than $5,000 a year may be treated as 501(c)(3) without applying. That doesn't help much with grants, because it leaves you with no determination letter to show a funder.

What changes when you run without recognized 501(c)(3) status:

  • Donors: Gifts generally aren't deductible until the IRS recognizes you. If you file within 27 months, recognition can apply back to your formation date (see the pending section below).
  • Private foundations: Many grant only to organizations they can verify in the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search. If you aren't listed, you're often screened out automatically.
  • Federal grants: Not ruled out. Notices that list nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status remain open to you, provided you're registered in SAM.gov.
  • Taxes: Without exemption, a nonprofit corporation may owe federal income tax on net income. Talk to a tax professional if money is building up.

Example (illustration only): A state-incorporated food pantry with an EIN but no IRS letter yet could apply directly to a USDA notice that lists "Nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status." At the same time it could raise individual donations through a Model C sponsor, so donors get a deductible receipt.

Free Grants for Nonprofits Without 501(c)(3): What's Really Available

Most offers of "free grants" are scams. The real options are fiscally sponsored projects, small grants from local community foundations, and federal notices that accept non-exempt applicants, all of which take an actual application.

USAGov warns that "Promises of 'grants' or 'free money' from the government are often scams". The FTC adds that legitimate government assistance never charges an upfront or processing fee. Red flags include an unsolicited call, text, or social media message; a request for a "processing fee"; or payment by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. Report these offers at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

SourceOpen to groups without 501(c)(3)?Typical routeCost to apply
Federal NOFOs on Grants.govOnly when the notice lists that type or "Unrestricted"Direct, via SAM.gov + Grants.govFree registration and listing
Federal NOFOs (501(c)(3) only)Through a fiscal sponsorSponsor appliesSponsor fee, about 5%–12% (2023 scan)
Community foundation small grantsOften, with a sponsor or a local government partnerFoundation's own portalUsually free
State and city pass-through grantsVaries by programCity/state portalFree
"Guaranteed free grant" websitesNo legitimate version exists—Any fee is a warning sign

Example (illustration only): A volunteer mural group looks for "free grants." It skips the sites charging to "unlock" a grant list and instead asks its county community foundation whether small arts grants accept fiscally sponsored projects. Then it uses Simpler.Grants.gov to see whether any National Endowment for the Arts notice accepts its sponsor's entity type.

Pitfall: Paying for grant databases while you still lack an eligible legal entity. Fix: Settle the legal path first (sponsor, partner, or your own status), then search.

Pending 501(c)(3) Status: What Grants Can You Apply For While Waiting?

With a pending application, you can often apply using your EIN and state incorporation, because IRS approval usually dates back to your formation if you filed on time.

Here is the IRS rule. If you file Form 1023 or 1023-EZ within 27 months after the end of the month you were legally formed, and the application is approved, your exemption takes effect on your formation date. If you file later, the IRS asks extra questions, and the effective date may be your submission date instead.

Processing times listed on the IRS "Where's my application" page (updated June 28, 2026):

FormIRS benchmarkApplies to filings submitted by
Form 1023-EZ80% decided within 22 daysFeb 24, 2026
Form 102380% decided within 191 daysJan 12, 2026

Fees are $275 for 1023-EZ and $600 for 1023, paid on Pay.gov (as of October 2026; check the official page).

Steps while you wait

  1. Save your Pay.gov submission confirmation. Some private funders accept it as proof that your application is pending.
  2. Apply directly to federal notices that list "Nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status." On the SF-424, choose "N" because that is your status today, not the status you expect to get.
  3. For 501(c)(3)-only funders, use a short-term Model C sponsor and plan to move the grants to your own entity once you're approved.
  4. Check Tax Exempt Organization Search after the benchmark date passes. If your filing predates the IRS cutoff date and you still aren't listed, call 877-829-5500.

Pitfall: Choosing "M: Nonprofit with 501C3 IRS Status" on the SF-424 while you're still pending. That misstates your status on a federal form. Fix: Choose "N" and explain in the narrative that your application is pending.

Fiscal Sponsorship vs. 501(c)(3): Which Is Right for Your Project?

Fiscal sponsorship is faster and has no IRS fee, but you give up some control and a share of your funding. Your own 501(c)(3) gives you independence and direct eligibility, but costs more upfront and can take months.

FactorFiscal sponsorshipOwn 501(c)(3)
Time until you can applyAs soon as the agreement is signedCorporation + EIN now; IRS letter in ~22 days (EZ) or ~191 days (1023) for 80% of cases
Upfront government feesNone to the IRS$275 or $600 IRS fee, plus state filing fees
Ongoing cost5%–12% of revenue (2023 scan)Accounting, Form 990 filings, possibly an audit
ControlSponsor has legal discretion over fundsYour board decides
Federal compliance burdenMostly the sponsor'sEntirely yours
Track recordBelongs to the sponsor's entityBuilds under your own name and UEI
Easy to exit?Depends on the agreement's transfer clauseNot applicable

Sources: IRS processing times, IRS user fees, fee scan summary.

Decision rule: If your project is a pilot, will last less than two years, or has no one to handle bookkeeping, choose a sponsor. If you expect steady revenue for several years and can recruit an independent board, file Form 1023 now. Each year on a sponsor at a 10% fee hands over a share that, past a certain budget size, is more than a bookkeeper would cost.

Pitfalls:

  • A sponsor agreement with no clause for transferring assets and grants when you spin off. Fix: Negotiate the clause before you sign.
  • Assuming a funder will move an open federal award from your sponsor to your new 501(c)(3). Fix: Ask the program officer. Transfers of federal awards need agency approval and aren't automatic.

Next steps

Choose one legal path today and confirm it with a single eligibility check before you write any proposal.

Do it yourself today:

  1. On Simpler.Grants.gov, filter Eligibility to your entity type (or "Nonprofits non-higher education without 501(c)(3)" plus "Unrestricted"), and save two notices that fit your work.
  2. If you have no entity, email two sponsors from the National Network of Fiscal Sponsors directory with the four questions from the fiscal sponsorship section.
  3. If you're incorporated, confirm you have an EIN, then run the IRS 1023-EZ financial check to decide between the $275 and $600 forms.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • A comprehensive (Model A) fiscal sponsor takes on accounting, payroll, and federal reporting for about 8%–12% of revenue (2023 field scan; check each sponsor's current rate). It suits projects with staff and federal awards. It's a poor fit for groups that want full control, or that will spin off within months, because transferring awards takes time.
  • A nonprofit attorney or CPA can draft your articles and file Form 1023. Fees vary widely by region and complexity, so ask for a flat quote in writing. This suits organizations with complicated programs or more than $50,000 a year in revenue. It's usually unnecessary for small groups that clearly qualify for 1023-EZ.
  • Free official help: Grants.gov support answers questions about registration and submission, but it can't tell you whether your project is eligible. Ask the program contact listed in the NOFO about eligibility.

Related guides on this site:

FAQ

Can you be a nonprofit without being a 501(c)(3)?

Yes. A nonprofit is created under state law, and 501(c)(3) is a separate federal tax status from the IRS. Many nonprofits operate legally while their application is pending, and some never apply. Without recognition, though, donations generally aren't deductible and many foundations won't fund you.

Grants for nonprofits 501(c)(3): what do funders actually check?

Private funders usually look up your EIN in the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search to confirm your status. Federal agencies check that your entity type matches the NOFO and that your SAM.gov registration and UEI are active, as 2 CFR 25.200 requires.

How long does it take to get 501(c)(3) status approved?

According to the IRS, 80% of Form 1023-EZ applications are decided within 22 days, and 80% of full Form 1023 applications within 191 days. Those figures apply to filings submitted before early 2026 (IRS, updated June 28, 2026). Incomplete applications take longer.

Do fiscally sponsored projects need their own EIN?

Under Model A, usually not. The project is a program of the sponsor and uses the sponsor's EIN and UEI. Under Model C, the project receives re-granted funds as its own grantee, so it typically needs an EIN. Ask your sponsor which it requires before you sign.

item.title: Single Audit Threshold 2026: 3 Steps to Check Your Status
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Single audit threshold 2026: $1,000,000 in federal awards expended. Use this 3-step check, Type A table and FAC deadline to see if you owe one.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

For 2026, the single audit threshold is $1,000,000 in federal awards expended during your fiscal year. Under 2 CFR 200.501, a non-federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more must get a single audit, or in limited cases a program-specific audit. That figure has applied to fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024, when OMB's 2024 Uniform Guidance revision raised it from $750,000 (FAC submission guide). To check your own status, add up the federal money you actually spent in the year, compare the total to the threshold for the year your fiscal period began, and confirm that your entity type is covered.

Which option is right for you?

Your first move depends on how much federal money you spend and what kind of organization you are. Find your row below and open the page listed in it.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant, no federal awards yetSkip the audit for now and get registered. Audit questions only start once you spend federal money/grants-gov-vs-sam-gov-registration-order-in-4-steps-2026/
Nonprofit or local government spending well under $1M a yearKeep clean records. No single audit is required, but your records stay open to review2 CFR 200.501
Nonprofit, tribe, college or government spending close to or over $1MRun the 3-step check below, then start looking for a Yellow Book auditorFAC audit resources
For-profit small business (SBIR/STTR, other direct awards)Read your award terms. Subpart F doesn't apply to for-profits, but award terms or a pass-through entity can still require an auditYour Notice of Award / 2 CFR 200.501
Subrecipient getting federal money through a state agencyCount pass-through funds as federal, and check your state's own audit rulesYour subaward agreement and state grants office
Researcher at a universityYour institution's single audit usually covers your awards. Talk to the sponsored programs officeYour sponsored programs office
Tight budget, close to the lineHold off on hiring anyone until your expenditure total is confirmed. Audit costs for entities under the threshold can't be charged to federal awards2 CFR 200.425

What Is the Single Audit Threshold?

The single audit threshold is the amount of federal awards you can expend in one fiscal year before a single audit becomes mandatory. It is currently $1,000,000. The rule is in 2 CFR 200.501(a): "A non-Federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more during the non-Federal entity's fiscal year in Federal awards must have a single or program-specific audit conducted."

Three parts of that sentence decide most cases.

First, it says "expends." Receiving cash or signing an award doesn't count toward the threshold. Spending does. 2 CFR 200.502 bases the timing on "when the activity related to the Federal award occurs." That covers expenditure transactions, disbursements to subrecipients, loan proceeds, property received and program income.

Second, it covers all your federal awards combined. Direct grants, cooperative agreements, subawards from a state, federal loans and some non-cash assistance all go into one total. Non-cash assistance such as donated federal property is valued at fair market value at the time you receive it, or at the value the agency assigns (2 CFR 200.502).

Third, it is measured over your fiscal year, not the federal fiscal year, unless the two happen to match.

Here's an example. Say a community health nonprofit has a July–June fiscal year. In FY2026 it spends $640,000 from an HHS grant and $410,000 from a subaward passed through its state. Its federal awards expended total $1,050,000, so it needs a single audit, even though neither award reaches $1M by itself.

Entities below the line are not exempt from oversight. Under 2 CFR 200.501, their records "must be available for review or audit by appropriate officials of the Federal agency, pass-through entity, and the Government Accountability Office (GAO)."

What Is the Single Audit Threshold for 2026?

For fiscal years that begin in 2026, and for any fiscal year beginning on or after October 1, 2024, the threshold is $1,000,000. As of October 2026, no further increase has been adopted. OMB published a proposed rewrite of 2 CFR Part 200 on May 29, 2026 (document 2026-10817). Accounting firm commentary on that proposal reports that "the single audit threshold remains $1,000,000" (Pease Bell). The proposal targets grant administration and award terms. OMB aimed for an October 1, 2026 effective date, but as of the latest updates reviewed, a final rule had not been confirmed as published (CASRAI). Check eCFR 2 CFR 200.501 before you rely on any figure.

The date your fiscal year began is what matters. The Federal Audit Clearinghouse uses the same split in its eligibility screen: "$750,000 in federal awards for fiscal years beginning before October 1, 2024" and "$1,000,000 in federal awards for fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024" (FAC).

Fiscal year (example)BeganThreshold that applies
Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2024Before Oct 1, 2024$750,000
Jul 1, 2024 – Jun 30, 2025Before Oct 1, 2024$750,000
Oct 1, 2024 – Sep 30, 2025On Oct 1, 2024$1,000,000
Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2025After Oct 1, 2024$1,000,000
Jul 1, 2025 – Jun 30, 2026After Oct 1, 2024$1,000,000
Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2026After Oct 1, 2024$1,000,000

A few mistakes come up often:

  • Using the date your award was signed. Your audit year depends on your fiscal year, not on when the grant agreement was signed.
  • Assuming a year that ends in 2025 always gets $1M. A July 2024 – June 2025 year began before October 1, 2024, so the $750,000 threshold still applies to it.
  • Waiting for the 2026 Compliance Supplement before deciding. The Supplement tells auditors what to test. It doesn't set the threshold. The final 2026 Supplement was delayed, and a draft went to the AICPA's audit quality center for planning only (Baker Tilly; BPM). Your threshold test doesn't depend on it.

What Is the Audit Threshold (General, Non-Federal)?

"Audit threshold" can also mean a state law, funder or lender trigger for a financial statement audit. Those triggers are separate from the federal $1,000,000 single audit rule. A single audit tests how you spend federal money. Other audits come from other rules and can still apply when you are under $1M in federal spending.

2 CFR 200.501 says entities under the threshold are exempt from federal audit requirements "for that year." It doesn't override state law or private contracts.

Type of audit triggerWho sets itWhat it coversWhere to check
Federal single auditOMB, 2 CFR 200.501Financial statements plus compliance for federal programs2 CFR 200.501
Program-specific auditOMB, 2 CFR 200.507One federal program only, in limited cases2 CFR 200.501
State single auditEach state's lawState-funded programs; rules and dollar amounts varyYour state's compliance manual, e.g. Connecticut, North Carolina
State charity registration auditState attorney general or charity officeFinancial statements of registered charitiesYour state charity regulator
Award or funder termsFederal agency, pass-through entity, foundation, lenderWhatever the agreement saysYour award or loan agreement

Two mistakes to watch for:

  • A nonprofit spends $400,000 in federal funds and decides it needs no audit at all. Its state or its biggest foundation may still require audited financial statements. Check both.
  • A for-profit company assumes the federal rule covers it. Subpart F "does not apply to for-profit organizations." For for-profit subrecipients, "the pass-through entity is responsible for establishing requirements to ensure compliance" (2 CFR 200.501). That means your subaward or Notice of Award can contain its own audit clause. If you're a small business applying for federal money, the small business grants guide explains where those terms appear.

How to Run the 3-Step Single Audit Status Check

The check has three steps: total your federal awards expended for the fiscal year, compare the total to the right threshold, and confirm your entity type. If you're over, begin lining up a Yellow Book auditor. Plan on 30 to 60 minutes if your accounting system tags federal funds. Plan on more time if it doesn't.

Step 1: Total federal awards expended (not received)

  1. Pull your general ledger for the full fiscal year, using the fiscal period start and end dates exactly as they appear in your bylaws or charter.
  2. List every federal award, including subawards from a state, county, university or other nonprofit that are funded with federal money. Each one should come with an Assistance Listing number (formerly CFDA). If a subaward agreement doesn't show one, ask the pass-through entity.
  3. For each award, add up the expenses incurred in the year. Use the activity date, not the date the reimbursement arrived (2 CFR 200.502).
  4. Add federal loans: new loans made in the year, plus prior-year balances that still carry compliance requirements, plus any interest subsidy received (2 CFR 200.502).
  5. Add non-cash federal assistance, such as donated property, at fair market value.
  6. Leave out payments you received as a contractor (vendor). Under 2 CFR 200.501, payments for contractor services aren't subject to these audit requirements. If you can't tell whether an agreement is a subaward or a contract, the grant vs cooperative agreement guide covers how federal instruments are labeled.

Step 2: Compare to the correct threshold

  1. Look up when your fiscal year began. If it began on or after October 1, 2024, use $1,000,000. If it began earlier, use $750,000.
  2. If your total equals or exceeds the threshold, you're in. The rule says "$1,000,000 or more," so exactly $1,000,000 counts.
  3. If you're within roughly 10% of the line, have your accountant review the subaward-versus-contract calls and the loan figures, because those are the items that most often move the total.

Step 3: Confirm entity type and next action

  1. The FAC submission process is for "non-profits, state and local governments, institutions of higher education, and Indian tribes or Tribal organizations" (FAC eligibility). If you're one of those and over the threshold, you need a single audit. The alternative is a program-specific audit, but that's only available when you expend under a single federal program and no financial statement audit is required, or for R&D with prior agency approval (2 CFR 200.501).
  2. If you're a for-profit, go back to your award terms (see the section above).
  3. Contact auditors early. The audit must follow Government Auditing Standards, so ask each firm to confirm it performs single audits under GAGAS. The AICPA publishes its GAQC membership directory by state as one place to start.

Here's an example of all three steps. A tribal housing organization's fiscal year runs Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2026. It spends $720,000 under a HUD program and $310,000 under a USDA subaward from its state. It also receives $150,000 under a contract to provide services to a federal agency. The first two count: $1,030,000. The contract payment is vendor income, so it's excluded. The fiscal year began after October 1, 2024, so the threshold is $1,000,000. The organization is a tribal organization and has two programs, so it needs a single audit.

What Is the Single Audit Major Program Threshold?

The major program threshold, called the Type A threshold, decides which of your federal programs auditors test in depth. It isn't the same thing as the single audit trigger. For entities expending between $1,000,000 and $34 million, the Type A threshold is also $1,000,000, which is why people mix up the two numbers.

Once you're in a single audit, the auditor sorts your programs. Programs at or above the Type A threshold are Type A. Smaller ones are Type B. Type A programs are assessed for risk, and the auditor only has to risk-assess Type B programs that exceed 25% of the Type A threshold (2 CFR 200.518). Here is the full table from 2 CFR 200.518(b)(1):

Total federal awards expendedType A threshold
$1,000,000 to $34 million$1,000,000
Over $34 million to $100 millionTotal expended × 0.03
Over $100 million to $1 billion$3 million
Over $1 billion to $10 billionTotal expended × 0.003
Over $10 billion to $20 billion$30 million
Over $20 billionTotal expended × 0.0015

Coverage rules also apply. The major programs the auditor selects must together cover at least 40% of total federal awards expended, or 20% if you qualify as a low-risk auditee (2 CFR 200.518).

Back to the tribal housing example, with $1,030,000 expended. Its Type A threshold is $1,000,000, so neither the $720,000 HUD program nor the $310,000 USDA program is Type A. Both are Type B. Each is above $250,000 (25% of $1M), so both are candidates for risk assessment, and whatever the auditor picks has to reach the 40% coverage floor of $412,000. The auditor makes the final selection. The table shows you how the logic works, but it doesn't let you pick your own major programs.

Low-risk status reduces coverage to 20%. To qualify under 2 CFR 200.520, you need two consecutive years of timely single audits, unmodified opinions, no material weaknesses, no going-concern doubt, and no Type A program with material weaknesses, modified opinions or questioned costs over 5% of that program's expenditures. A first-time auditee can't qualify. Expect the 40% floor in your first year.

What Are Single Audit Standards?

A single audit is conducted under Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS, also called the Yellow Book) and the Uniform Guidance compliance rules. A standard financial statement audit done only under GAAS doesn't satisfy the requirement.

The standards stack in layers:

  • AICPA auditing standards (GAAS) for the financial statement opinion.
  • GAO's Government Auditing Standards. The 2024 revision is effective for financial audits of periods beginning on or after December 15, 2025, and it requires audit organizations to have a system of quality management in place by that date (GRF CPAs; Wolters Kluwer). If your fiscal year begins January 1, 2026, your audit falls under the 2024 Yellow Book.
  • 2 CFR 200 Subpart F, which defines the reports, major program selection and auditee duties.
  • The OMB Compliance Supplement, which tells auditors which compliance requirements to test for each program. The 2026 edition covers audits of fiscal years beginning after June 30, 2025 (Baker Tilly).

What this means if you're hiring:

  • A firm that only does GAAS audits may not meet the Yellow Book's independence and continuing-education requirements. Ask each firm directly whether it performs GAGAS single audits, and when its last peer review was. The AICPA Peer Review Public File shows peer review enrollment and whether a firm is a GAQC member.
  • If your bookkeeper or a consultant prepared your financial statements or SEFA, that can raise Yellow Book independence questions for the firm doing the audit. Tell candidate firms up front who is doing what.

What Are the Single Audit Requirements for 2026?

Crossing $1,000,000 means you have to hire a qualified auditor, prepare a reporting package and submit it with the data collection form to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. The deadline is 30 days after you receive the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end, whichever is earlier (2 CFR 200.512(a)).

The reporting package has four parts (2 CFR 200.512(c)):

  1. Financial statements and the schedule of expenditures of Federal awards (SEFA)
  2. Summary schedule of prior audit findings
  3. Auditor's report(s)
  4. Corrective action plan

The data collection form (SF-SAC) includes a statement signed by a senior-level representative confirming the information is accurate and authorizing public posting on the FAC (2 CFR 200.512(b)). Audits submitted to the FAC are posted publicly, so write findings responses as though anyone could read them.

Submitting on FAC.gov: exact screens

The FAC submission guide walks through these screens:

  1. Click Submit an audit and sign in with Login.gov. Old Census FAC credentials no longer work.
  2. On Auditee information, enter your UEI (the 12-character ID from SAM.gov) and your fiscal period start date and end date.
  3. On the FAC submission eligibility page, answer one multiple-choice question about entity type and three true/false questions. The screen states both thresholds: $750,000 and $1,000,000.
  4. On the Audit submission access page, add email addresses for the Auditee certifying official, Auditor certifying official, auditee contacts and auditor contacts. The emails must match each person's Login.gov email.
  5. Complete the SF-SAC workbooks from the FAC's audit resources page, upload the reporting package, and have both certifying officials certify before final submission.

Example deadline: if your fiscal year ends June 30, 2026, the outer limit is March 31, 2027. If your auditor delivers the report on November 15, 2026, the 30-day clock runs out first, on December 15, 2026.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeFix
UEI rejected or expiredRenew your SAM.gov registration first. See how to check SAM.gov registration status and the UEI lookup guide.
Certifying official can't log inTheir Login.gov email has to match exactly what's on the Audit submission access page. Correct it under User Access Management.
Only tracking the nine-month dateCalendar the 30-day-after-report date as soon as the auditor gives you a delivery date.
SEFA missing pass-through award numbersRequest the identifying number and Assistance Listing from each pass-through entity before fieldwork begins.
Charging audit fees to a grant while under $1MNot allowed. Audit costs of entities under the threshold aren't allowable direct charges (2 CFR 200.425).

Single audit costs are allowable for entities that are required to have one, as "a reasonably proportionate share" (2 CFR 200.425). How you recover them depends on your indirect cost setup. The de minimis 15% election guide covers that choice.

Single Audit Limit 2026 vs Prior Years: What Changed?

The limit went from $750,000 to $1,000,000, a 33% increase, for fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024, and it's still $1,000,000 in 2026. Other numbers changed in the same 2024 revision, and some of them affect your SEFA and budgets:

ItemBefore (fiscal years beginning before Oct 1, 2024)Now (incl. 2026)Source
Single audit threshold$750,000$1,000,000FAC; 2 CFR 200.501
Type A threshold, smallest tier$750,000$1,000,000 (up to $34M expended)2 CFR 200.518; Pease Bell
Subaward amount included in MTDCFirst $25,000First $50,000Pease Bell
Equipment capitalization floor$5,000$10,000Pease Bell
De minimis indirect rate10%15%Pease Bell

If you spend between $750,000 and $999,999, the raise may take you out of single audit territory starting with your first fiscal year that began on or after October 1, 2024. You still have to finish and file any audit owed for an earlier year. Keep in mind that the raise has a ceiling. If your federal portfolio is growing, a single new award can push you back over.

Next steps

Today, you can do the following yourself:

  1. Write down your fiscal year start date and identify which threshold applies, $750,000 or $1,000,000, using the table in the 2026 section.
  2. Export a list of every federal award and subaward with its Assistance Listing number and year-to-date expenses, then run Steps 1–3.
  3. If you're over the threshold or close to it, confirm your SAM.gov registration and UEI are active, since the FAC won't start a submission without a valid UEI (FAC).

If you'd rather not work through this yourself, the usual route is to hire a CPA firm that performs GAGAS single audits. The GAQC state-by-state directory and the AICPA Peer Review Public File are free ways to build a shortlist. There's no official price list. Fees are quoted per engagement and depend on how many programs you have and how clean your records are, so get written quotes from two or three firms (as of October 2026; check each firm's engagement letter). Hiring a firm makes sense if you're over the threshold, because the audit is required and the cost can be charged proportionately to your awards. It doesn't make sense if you're clearly under $1M and nothing else requires an audit: you'd be paying for something the rules don't ask for, and you couldn't charge it to your federal awards (2 CFR 200.425). One limitation to know about: a firm can't both keep your books and audit them without Yellow Book independence safeguards. If your outsourced bookkeeper also does audits, use a different firm for the audit.

FAQ

What is the single audit threshold?

It's the amount of federal awards a non-federal entity can expend in one fiscal year before a single audit is required. It is currently $1,000,000 under 2 CFR 200.501. The test is based on money spent, not money received or awarded.

What is the single audit limit 2026?

$1,000,000 for any fiscal year beginning on or after October 1, 2024, which includes all fiscal years beginning in 2026. OMB's May 2026 proposed rewrite of 2 CFR 200 is reported to leave the threshold unchanged (Pease Bell). Check eCFR in case a final rule changes the text.

What is the single audit major program threshold?

It's the Type A threshold, which decides which programs get tested in depth once a single audit is required. For entities expending $1M to $34M, it is $1,000,000, and it scales up from there under 2 CFR 200.518. Major programs together have to cover at least 40% of expenditures, or 20% for low-risk auditees.

What is the federal single audit threshold 2026 for for-profit companies?

Subpart F doesn't apply to for-profit organizations, so the $1,000,000 rule doesn't automatically cover them (2 CFR 200.501). Pass-through entities and award terms can still impose audit requirements on for-profit recipients. Check your Notice of Award or subaward agreement.
