item.title: Grants.gov Workspace: Create and Submit in 5 Steps (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Grants.gov Workspace in 5 steps: create it from Apply Now, add participants, assign an AOR, run Check Application, Sign and Submit before the deadline.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A Grants.gov Workspace is the shared online area where your team fills out a federal application package and submits it. To create one, you sign in, open the opportunity, click Apply (or use Apply Now in the Applicant Center), enter an Application Filing Name, and click Create Workspace. The person who builds the Workspace usually isn't the person allowed to submit it. Only a participant with the Standard AOR or Expanded AOR role can click Sign and Submit (Grants.gov Forms Tab help). Grants.gov's Participants help says at least one participant should hold one of these AOR roles "so that the workspace can be submitted" (Participants Tab help), so plan that handoff from the start.

Which option is right for you?

Your starting point depends on whether you're applying alone or with a team, and on whether your organization's Grants.gov roles are already set up. Use the row that matches your situation.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant with no Grants.gov account yetRegister with SAM.gov (UEI) and Login.gov before anything elseGrants.gov Quick Start for Applicants
Solo founder or 1–2 person nonprofitThe "Basic" Workspace approach, where one person is both Owner and AORWorkspace Basic
Team of 3–5 that applies regularlyThe "Intermediate" approach: a Workspace Owner builds the package and a separate AOR submitsWorkspace Overview
Working with an outside consultant or partner orgThe "Advanced" approach: add external participants and limit their form accessWorkspace Advanced
No budget for helpGrants.gov's free 24/7 support plus an SBA Small Business Development CenterGrants.gov support / SBA local assistance

Here's why each pick fits. Registration comes first because Workspace can't be used without a UEI-linked profile. In the Basic approach one person holds every role, so there is no handoff to get wrong. The Intermediate approach splits the work and needs a clear handoff, which the roles section covers. The Advanced approach lets you hide budget forms from outsiders. Grants.gov groups these three approaches by user count: 1–2 users for Basic and 3–5 for Intermediate, as of October 2026 (Workspace Overview).

How Does Grants.gov Work?

Grants.gov is the federal portal where you find opportunities and submit applications. You register, find an opportunity, complete its forms in a Workspace and submit, and then the agency retrieves your package. Grants.gov calls Workspace "the standard way for organizations or individuals to apply for federal grants" (What Is Workspace?). It replaced the old single-PDF package with separate forms that several people can work on at once.

The whole process looks like this:

  1. Register your organization in SAM.gov to get a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI). Grants.gov says this takes "up to 10 business days" if your documents are ready (Quick Start).
  2. Create a Login.gov account and a Grants.gov account, then add an applicant profile tied to your organization's UEI (Register).
  3. Find an opportunity and read its Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO).
  4. Create a Workspace, add your team and complete the forms.
  5. Submit and track your application until the agency retrieves it.

Grants.gov's own Workspace progress bar uses five stages, and this guide follows them: Created → Fill Out Forms → Complete and Notify AOR → Submit → Agency Received (Manage Workspace help).

A newer interface, Simpler.Grants.gov, has been piloting its own "Apply" workflow. Its roadmap describes two opportunities opened for application there in late 2025 and targets 2027 for Simpler becoming the default Grants.gov experience (Simpler.Grants.gov Roadmap). Grants.gov's help still describes the classic Workspace as the standard way to apply (What Is Workspace?). Follow whatever the "Apply" link on your specific opportunity points to.

If the order of the SAM.gov and Grants.gov registrations is confusing, see Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: Registration Order in 4 Steps.

How to Access Grants.gov Workspace

To use Workspace you need three things: a Grants.gov account linked to Login.gov, an applicant profile tied to your organization's UEI, and a role that can create workspaces. If any one of these is missing, the Apply button turns gray.

Steps to get in for the first time:

  1. Go to grants.gov, click Register, fill out the form and confirm your email (Register).
  2. Sign in with Login.gov, or create a Login.gov account first. Grants.gov says every user who downloads or edits forms online needs a Login.gov account (Quick Start).
  3. Add a profile. Choose an organization applicant profile and enter your organization's UEI, or choose an individual profile if you're applying for yourself.
  4. Ask your organization's E-Business Point of Contact (EBiz POC) to assign you a role. Any EBiz POC who existed on January 21, 2023 was automatically given the Expanded AOR role (Workspace Roles).
  5. When you sign in after that, open the Applicant Center. The Workspace tools are there: Apply Now under Grant Applications, and Manage Workspaces in the left navigation.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Different email addresses. Grants.gov tells you to "use the same email address to register your organization's electronic business point of contact at SAM.gov as the one you use to register at Grants.gov" (Quick Start). If the two don't match, the EBiz POC can't be recognized automatically.
  • A gray Apply button. Grants.gov lists four causes (Grants.gov blog, June 2023): no profile or role, a deadline that has passed, a forecast with no package yet, or an agency that didn't post a package on Grants.gov. The fix depends on which one applies. Either get a role assigned, check the Package tab for the closing date, wait for the posting, or read the Synopsis for the agency's own submission site.
  • An expired SAM.gov registration. Before you build anything, follow How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step). If you need your UEI, see UEI Number Lookup.

How to Create a Grants.gov Workspace

You create a Workspace by entering the opportunity's Funding Opportunity Number (or Package ID) plus an Application Filing Name, then clicking Create Workspace. Grants.gov loads that package's forms automatically.

Steps, using the exact labels from Grants.gov's Apply Now help:

  1. Sign in and go to the Applicant Center.
  2. Click Apply Now under the Grant Applications heading. You can also click Apply on the opportunity's listing page.
  3. Fill in either the Funding Opportunity Number field or the Opportunity Package ID field. If you don't know either one, find the opportunity under Search Grants.
  4. If more than one package matches, click Select next to the right one. Check the competition ID and the opening and closing dates.
  5. Type a descriptive name in Application Filing Name.
  6. Click Create Workspace. Grants.gov opens the Manage Workspace page, and the Activity tab logs the action as "Created."

For example, a nonprofit applying to a hypothetical opportunity numbered "ABC-2027-001" would enter that number, name the Workspace "ABC-2027-001 Youth Literacy – Riverside Nonprofit", and click Create Workspace.

Two limits apply. You can't create a Workspace for a multi-project package through this flow (Apply Now help). And Grants.gov recommends a separate Workspace for each opportunity (Quick Start).

If you applied for something similar before, you can Copy that Workspace instead of starting fresh. Go to Manage Workspaces, run a Search, click Copy in the Actions column, enter the new Funding Opportunity Number, name it and click Copy Workspace (Copy Workspace help). The Copy link only shows up if you have access to all forms or to all non-budget forms. Grants.gov also warns that form versions often change between packages, so recheck every field after copying.

How to Find My Workspace in Grants.gov

Your existing Workspaces are on the Manage Workspaces page in the Applicant Center's left navigation. Search there, then click Manage in the Actions column to open one.

Steps (Manage Workspaces help):

  1. Sign in and open the Applicant Center.
  2. Click Manage Workspaces.
  3. Enter search criteria and click Search. You can filter and sort the results.
  4. Click Manage next to the Workspace you want.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • "My colleague's Workspace isn't in my list." Grants.gov says the results depend on "the roles assigned to your profile and workspaces in which you are a participant" (Manage Workspaces help). Ask the Workspace Owner to add you on the Participants tab, or ask an Expanded AOR to do it.
  • Signed in under the wrong profile. If you belong to more than one organization, the list only covers the profile you're using right now. Switch profiles and search again.
  • Searching with filters you no longer need. Clear the status filter. Submitted and archived Workspaces drop out of view if you're only looking at in-progress ones.

Grants.gov Workspace Roles: Lead Applicant vs. Submitter

Grants.gov doesn't use the term "lead applicant." The person who builds and runs the application is the Workspace Owner, and only a participant with the Standard AOR or Expanded AOR role can submit. That separation is the most common reason a finished application never goes out.

Many guides use "lead applicant" loosely for whoever is driving the application. In Grants.gov terms that person is usually the Workspace Owner. Each Workspace has exactly one Owner, who needs either the Workspace Manager role or a custom role with the "Own Workspace" privilege (What Is Workspace?). The Owner can add people and fill in forms, but can't submit unless they also hold an AOR role.

Roles and what they allow, based on Grants.gov's Workspace Roles page and the Forms Tab help as of October 2026:

RoleCreate WorkspaceOwn/administer WorkspaceEdit formsClick Complete and Notify AORClick Sign and Submit
Expanded AORYesYes; can also manage participants in any org WorkspaceYesOnly if OwnerYes, for organization workspaces
Standard AORYesYesYesOnly if OwnerYes, for its own workspaces
Workspace ManagerYesYes (inherits Owner access)YesYes, as OwnerNo
Workspace Participant (no org role)NoNoYes, for the forms it can accessNoNo

The handoff runs like this:

  1. The Workspace Owner gets every included form to Passed status.
  2. The Owner clicks Complete and Notify AOR. That button only becomes active when there are no alerts, the selected forms show "Passed," and the Workspace has a participant with the AOR role (Forms Tab help). Clicking it unlocks any locked forms and notifies the AOR participants.
  3. The AOR opens the Workspace and clicks Sign and Submit.

Ways an application gets stuck:

  • Nobody in the Workspace holds an AOR role. Grants.gov's Participants help says that "at least one Participant should have one of the core AOR roles so that the workspace can be submitted" (Participants Tab help). Fix: add the AOR before the deadline week, not on the day it's due.
  • The Owner thinks "Passed" means sent. Grants.gov's help states that "Passed" means the form has no errors. It does not mean the form was submitted to the grantor (Forms Tab help).
  • The AOR is unavailable. Grants.gov's Quick Start tells organizations to designate at least one person with the Expanded or Standard AOR role (Quick Start). Two AORs is safer, so a vacation or sick day doesn't block a deadline.
  • Sign and Submit stays gray even for the AOR. According to Grants.gov's support team, the button also needs every required form to pass, no alerts, an active SAM registration, and an opportunity whose Open Date has passed (Grants.gov blog, Oct 2018).

In a one-person organization you can be both Owner and AOR. Standard and Expanded AORs can create and own Workspaces as well as submit (Workspace Roles), so that setup has no handoff at all.

How to Set Up a Workspace in Grants.gov (Team & Permissions)

Set up the Workspace before anyone types data: add participants on the Participants tab, limit form access where needed, and confirm an AOR is attached.

Steps, using the labels from the Participants Tab help:

  1. Open the Workspace (Manage Workspaces → Manage) and click the Participants tab.
  2. Click Add from Workspace Organization to add colleagues inside your organization, or Add by Username or Email Address to add someone inside or outside it, such as a consultant or a partner organization's staff.
  3. For each person, click Manage Access and choose their form access: all forms (the default), "only non-budget forms," or "Subform(s) only" when the package has subforms.
  4. Check that at least one participant has the Standard AOR or Expanded AOR role.
  5. If ownership needs to move, for example because the grant writer is leaving, click Make Owner next to the new owner. That person must have the Workspace Manager role or the "Own Workspace" privilege.
  6. Go to the Forms tab, click Download Instructions and read the grantor's guidance before you assign anyone a form.

Only the Workspace Owner can use Remove, Make Owner and Manage Access. For everyone else those links are inactive. An Expanded AOR can also add participants (Participants Tab help).

Filling out forms on the Forms tab (Forms Tab help):

  • Use Webform to complete a form in your browser, or Download and later Upload to work on a PDF offline. Changes sync between the two formats (Grants.gov blog, Oct 2018).
  • Click Lock to stop others from editing a form while you work on it. The form then shows as "[Locked]."
  • Use Reuse to pull in a form from an earlier Workspace.
  • Complete the SF-424 first. Grants.gov says to do this "before any other form in the application package" because it fills in fields on the other forms. Field-by-field help is in SF-424 Instructions: Field-by-Field Table and Steps (2026).
  • If the agency updates the package after you start, click Get Updated Grantor Package so your forms match the current version.

For example, a small business working with an outside grant writer might give the writer "only non-budget forms" and keep the SF-424A budget form internal. The Owner stays in-house and the CEO holds the Standard AOR role.

Pitfall: a participant who downloaded a PDF and never uploaded it can leave a form sitting in "In Progress." Look at the Activity tab to see who touched it last, then ask that person to upload or unlock it.

What Does Grants.gov Workspace Status "Archived" Mean?

An "Archived" Workspace is read-only history. You can't reopen it, run Check Application on it, or reuse forms from it. If the opportunity is offered again, copy it into a new Workspace.

Grants.gov's help documents what archived status blocks, though not every reason a Workspace lands there:

  • The Reopen button is hidden when a Workspace is New, In Progress or Archived (Reopen a Workspace help).
  • The Check Application button is inactive for New, Submitted or Archived applications (Check Application help).
  • The Reuse link isn't available when the Workspace is Ready for Submission, Submitted or Archived (Reuse Workspace Form help).
  • Separately from archiving, once a package passes its closing date Grants.gov stops accepting submissions. It also deactivates the form action links and the Submit, Complete and Reopen buttons (Resolving Problems and Errors).

What you can do:

  1. If the opportunity repeats next cycle, use Copy from Manage Workspaces with the new Funding Opportunity Number. Then recheck every form, because versions change.
  2. If you think a system problem stopped you from submitting on time, call Grants.gov support at 1-800-518-4726 or email support@grants.gov, and keep the case number (Quick Start). Whether a late application is accepted is up to the funding agency and its NOFO, not Grants.gov. Contact the agency's listed grants contact as well.
  3. If you only need the record, archived Workspaces still show up in Manage Workspaces search, so you can look up what you filed.

Don't confuse the two meanings of "Archived" on Grants.gov. Opportunity listings also have "Archived" status for past grants kept for reference. That label applies to the funding notice, not your Workspace.

How to Apply for Grants on Grants.gov (End-to-End Steps)

Once every form passes, run Check Application. The Owner then clicks Complete and Notify AOR, and the AOR clicks Sign and Submit. Grants.gov returns a tracking number and sends status emails until the agency retrieves the package.

The full process, following the five progress-bar stages (Manage Workspace help):

  1. Created. Build the Workspace (see the section above). Check the SAM status shown on the Workspace before you go further.
  2. Fill Out Forms / Forms Passed. Complete each included form until it shows "Passed." Make sure the Include in Application selections cover the optional forms your NOFO requires. For writing the narrative, see How to Write Grants for Nonprofits.
  3. Check Application. On the Forms tab, click Check Application. It only works while the Workspace is "In Progress" or "Ready for Submission," there are no alerts, and the selected forms have passed. A clean result says: "No errors found in Application Package. Additional validations may occur once you submit your application and it is retrieved by the Federal Agency" (Check Application help).
  4. Complete and Notify AOR. The Owner clicks it, which unlocks any locked forms and emails the AOR participants.
  5. Submit → Agency Received. The AOR clicks Sign and Submit. A confirmation with a tracking number appears in Grants.gov, followed by a submission receipt email and then either a validation email or a rejection email listing errors (Check Application Status help).

After you submit, the statuses run in this order (Check Application Status help):

StatusMeaning
ReceivedGrants.gov has the package and it is waiting for validation
ValidatedIt passed Grants.gov checks and the agency can download it
Received by AgencyThe agency has confirmed it retrieved the package
Agency Tracking Number AssignedThe agency assigned its own number. Grants.gov doesn't track anything after this

You can look up as many as five tracking numbers at once on Track My Application without signing in (Track My Application).

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • "Rejected" after submission. Read the rejection email, click Reopen (available to the Workspace Owner and AOR participants when the Workspace is Ready for Submission or Submitted and its forms are current), fix the errors and resubmit. Reopening sets the status back to "In Progress" (Reopen a Workspace help). This only works while the opportunity is still open.
  • "Action cannot be performed due to Workspace changes." Someone else changed the Workspace after your page loaded. Refresh and try again (Check Application help).
  • Submitting on deadline day. Grants.gov says to submit "well before the deadline, just in case a submission error occurs" (Quick Start). A rejection plus a fix needs hours, and sometimes days.

Small businesses should also read How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide) for opportunity-specific eligibility checks.

Grants.gov Workspace Application Filing Name: What to Enter

The Application Filing Name is a required label you choose for the Workspace. It's for your own use and isn't an official ID. It can be up to 240 characters, and you can change it later with Edit Name (Manage Workspace help).

Grants.gov only asks for "a descriptive application name" (Apply Now help). The agency identifies your application by the Grants.gov tracking number and its own number, so the filing name is mainly there to help your team find the right Workspace among many.

A naming pattern that sorts well (example only):

[Funding Opportunity Number] – [Short project name] – [Org or department] – [Cycle]

For example: "ABC-2027-001 – Youth Literacy – Riverside Nonprofit – FY27"

To rename:

  1. Open the Workspace.
  2. Click Edit Name next to the Application Filing Name field.
  3. Type the new name in the Edit Name pop-up and save (Manage Workspace help).

Pitfalls:

  • Copied Workspaces keep their old names. Rename the copy right away so nobody edits last year's version by mistake.
  • Names like "Grant app final v2." When an organization has several open Workspaces, an AOR searching Manage Workspaces can end up submitting the wrong one. Put the opportunity number in the name.
  • Mixing up the filing name with the SF-424 project title. They're separate fields. The SF-424 "Descriptive Title of Applicant's Project" goes to the agency, while the filing name stays in your Workspace list.

Next steps

You can finish the setup work today in under an hour, and if you get stuck, Grants.gov's Support Center is free (Quick Start).

Do it yourself today:

  1. Sign in, open Manage Workspaces, and check that every active Workspace has at least one participant with the Standard AOR or Expanded AOR role. If one doesn't, ask your EBiz POC to assign the role now.
  2. Check that your SAM.gov registration is active and won't expire before the deadline (SAM.gov status steps).
  3. Choose an internal deadline at least a few business days before the real one, and put a Check Application run and an AOR Sign and Submit session on the calendar.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • Grants.gov Support Center: free and available 24/7, except federal holidays, at 1-800-518-4726 or support@grants.gov (as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits anyone stuck on roles, buttons or errors. It won't help you write the proposal or judge eligibility.
  • SBA Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs): SBA describes free or low-cost counseling through a network of 63 lead centers with more than 800 locations (as of October 2026; check the official page). This is a good fit for small business owners who want one-on-one advice, and you can find a center with SBA's local assistance finder. It's less useful for university researchers, who should go to their institution's sponsored programs office, which often acts as the AOR anyway. Advisor availability and grant expertise vary by center.
  • A paid grant writer or consultant: they can be added as an external Workspace participant with "only non-budget forms" access. This makes sense if you have a large application and no staff time. If you just need to get through submission mechanics, the free support line covers that. Rates vary widely, so get a written scope and price. Even then, a consultant can't click Sign and Submit unless your organization gives them an AOR role, which most organizations shouldn't do.

FAQ

How do I log in to Grants.gov Workspace?

Sign in at grants.gov through Login.gov, which every Grants.gov user who works on forms online needs (Quick Start). Then open the Applicant Center and click Manage Workspaces. If the page is empty or Apply is gray, you probably don't have an applicant profile or role yet.

What is a Grants.gov Workspace Manager?

Workspace Manager is a basic organization role that can create and own Workspaces (Workspace Roles). A Workspace Manager can add participants and click Complete and Notify AOR. It can't click Sign and Submit, which requires the Standard AOR or Expanded AOR role.

What forms are in a Grants.gov Workspace?

Each Workspace loads the forms in the agency's package for that specific opportunity. That usually means the SF-424 plus agency forms, some mandatory and some optional. Grants.gov says to complete the SF-424 first because it fills in other forms (Forms Tab help). You can fill out each form as a Webform or as a downloaded PDF.

Where are the official Grants.gov Workspace instructions?

The main sources are the Workspace Overview, the Workspace Roles page, and the online help pages for Manage Workspace, the Forms tab and the Participants tab. Always read your opportunity's NOFO and the Download Instructions file on the Forms tab too, because agencies add their own rules.

item.title: Indirect Cost Rate De Minimis: 15% Election in 4 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: The indirect cost rate de minimis is now up to 15% of MTDC, not 10%. See who can elect it, how to calculate it, and how to document the election.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The de minimis indirect cost rate is now up to 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC). It used to be 10%. If your organization has no current federally negotiated indirect cost rate, 2 CFR 200.414(f) lets you elect it without negotiating with anyone (2 CFR 200.414, Cornell LII). The 15% figure applies to awards issued on or after October 1, 2024. You make the election by putting the rate, the MTDC base and a short statement in your budget, and then using the same rate on all of your federal awards (NSF; Clark Nuber).

Which option is right for you?

The table below shows the best first choice for each common situation.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner nonprofit or first-time applicant, never had a negotiated rateDe minimis, up to 15% of MTDC. You don't need a cost study.2 CFR 200.414(f), then your NOFO's budget section
Nonprofit with a current NICRAYour negotiated rate. You can't use de minimis while the NICRA is current.Your NICRA letter, plus the budget instructions in the NOFO
NICRA expired and you don't plan to renewDe minimis. The 2024 rule allows it once you have no current rate.Clark Nuber summary of the 2024 change
Your real overhead is well above 15% and you manage many awardsStart a negotiated rate proposal. De minimis leaves money on the table.DOL guide to indirect cost rate determination
For-profit small businessRead the NOFO first. Part 200 applies to for-profits only where the agency chooses to apply it.2 CFR 200.101
Tight budget with a fixed award ceilingDe minimis at a rate below 15% if you need more room for direct costs. The rule says "up to."Your NOFO's award ceiling and cost-share rules

What Is the De Minimis Indirect Cost Rate? (Meaning & Definition)

The de minimis indirect cost rate is a flat rate of up to 15% of MTDC. Organizations without a current negotiated rate can charge it in place of documented overhead. The regulation says recipients and subrecipients "that do not have a current Federal negotiated indirect cost rate (including provisional rate) may elect to charge a de minimis rate of up to 15 percent of modified total direct costs (MTDC)" (2 CFR 200.414(f)).

You need three terms to read that sentence.

Indirect costs are shared costs you can't tie to one project without a lot of effort. Examples include the executive director's time, accounting, rent for the main office, insurance and IT.

MTDC is the base you multiply the rate by. According to 2 CFR 200.1, it covers "all direct salaries and wages, applicable fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each subaward." It excludes "equipment, capital expenditures, charges for patient care, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, participant support costs, and the portion of each subaward in excess of $50,000."

Equipment is tangible property with a useful life of more than one year. Its per-unit cost must meet or exceed the lower of two amounts: your own capitalization threshold or $10,000 (2 CFR 200.1). A $1,400 laptop is a supply and stays in MTDC. A $12,000 instrument is equipment and comes out.

The words "up to" are easy to miss. You can choose 15%, or you can pick a lower number such as 12%. A federal agency can't force you below 15% unless a statute requires it (2 CFR 200.414(f)). The regulation also says you don't need documentation to justify using the rate, and you can use it indefinitely (Clark Nuber).

Pitfall: Many blog posts and older agency form instructions still describe the rate as "10% of MTDC" with a "$25,000" subaward limit. Those numbers come from the pre-October 2024 rule. If you copy them, you'll under-recover indirect costs on new awards.

Federal Indirect Cost Rate De Minimis: Who Can Elect It and When

Any recipient or subrecipient without a current federal negotiated rate, including a provisional rate, can elect the federal de minimis rate. You elect it when you build the application budget. Under the old rule only organizations that had never had a negotiated rate qualified. The 2024 revision changed that test to having no current rate, so an organization whose NICRA has expired can now use de minimis (NSF; Clark Nuber).

Who qualifies

  • Nonprofits, institutions of higher education, and state, local and tribal governments without a current NICRA. Part 200 applies to these "non-federal entities" by default.
  • Subrecipients. The text of 200.414(f) names subrecipients alongside recipients. A pass-through entity, such as a state agency passing federal money to you, follows the same rule.
  • For-profit organizations, only if the agency applies Part 200 to them. Section 200.101 says agencies "may apply subparts A through E of this part to... for-profit organizations... as permitted in agency regulations or program statutes" (2 CFR 200.101). For small businesses this means the NOFO is the deciding document. Our small business grant application guide explains how to find the cost principles that apply to your award.

Who does not qualify

You can't elect de minimis while you hold a current negotiated rate, provisional or final. In Clark Nuber's words, "A Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA) must expire before using the De Minimis rate" (Clark Nuber). Some programs also cap or ban indirect costs by statute. When that happens, the NOFO's "Funding Restrictions" or budget section will say so, and the statute overrides 15%.

When the 15% rate applies

According to NSF's guidance, new awards executed on or after October 1, 2024 may elect the 15% rate. Existing awards may apply it to costs incurred after October 1, 2024, but not retroactively (NSF). Clark Nuber points out that a pre-existing award moves to 15% only if it's formally amended after that date (Clark Nuber). If you hold a 2023 award at 10%, ask your grants officer about an amendment. Don't change the rate on your own.

How to Calculate the De Minimis Indirect Cost Rate

To calculate it, add up your MTDC (allowed direct costs plus the first $50,000 of each subaward) and multiply by your elected rate, up to 15%. All the work is in building the base correctly (2 CFR 200.1).

Steps

  1. List every direct cost line in your draft budget.
  2. Tag each line In MTDC or Excluded using the 200.1 definition.
  3. For each subaward, put the first $50,000 in MTDC and exclude the rest. The limit is per subaward, not per year.
  4. Add up the "In MTDC" lines. That total is your base.
  5. Multiply the base by your rate (0.15, or lower if you choose).
  6. Add the indirect amount to total direct costs to get the total request. Check it against the NOFO's award ceiling.

Worked example (sample numbers, for illustration only)

Here is a one-year budget for a hypothetical community health nonprofit:

Budget lineAmountIn MTDC?MTDC amount
Salaries and wages$120,000Yes$120,000
Fringe benefits$36,000Yes$36,000
Travel$8,000Yes$8,000
Supplies (incl. laptops under $10,000 each)$6,000Yes$6,000
Equipment (one $15,000 unit)$15,000No (equipment)$0
Participant support (stipends for trainees)$10,000No$0
Subaward to partner clinic$80,000First $50,000 only$50,000
Program space rental$12,000No (rental costs)$0
Total direct costs$287,000Sum of MTDC amountsMTDC = $220,000

At 15%, indirect costs are $220,000 × 0.15 = $33,000, so the total request is $320,000. If the NOFO ceiling were $310,000, one option is to elect a lower rate. At 10.5% the indirect amount is $23,100, which brings the total to $310,100, so you'd still need to trim $100 of direct costs. The other option is to cut direct costs and keep 15%. Either is allowed because the rule says "up to."

A common mistake is to apply 15% to total direct costs. In this example that gives $43,050, which is $10,050 more than allowed, and it's the most common reason indirect lines get cut in budget review. To fix it, keep the "In MTDC?" column in your budget spreadsheet and put the indirect formula on the MTDC subtotal cell, not the grand total.

How to Elect the De Minimis Rate: The 2 CFR 200.414(f) Process in 4 Steps

Electing the rate takes four actions: confirm you're eligible, state the election in your budget forms and narrative, use it consistently, and keep your MTDC workpapers. None of these involves filing a request with an agency. The election is the statement in your application.

Step 1: Confirm eligibility and check the NOFO

  1. Check whether your organization holds a current NICRA, including a provisional rate. Look in your finance files and ask your auditor. If you do, stop here and use that rate.
  2. Open the NOFO and search for "indirect," "de minimis," and "MTDC."
  3. Look for program-level caps. A statutory cap of, say, 8% overrides 15%.
  4. For for-profit applicants, confirm the NOFO applies 2 CFR 200 Subpart E (2 CFR 200.101).

If you're not sure whether an opportunity is a grant or a cooperative agreement, it makes no difference here. Both fall under Part 200 (our comparison).

Step 2: Enter the election in the budget forms

The labels depend on which budget form the NOFO requires.

SF-424A (Budget Information – Non-Construction Programs):

  1. Section B – Budget Categories, line 6j "Indirect Charges": enter the indirect dollar amount ($33,000 in the example).
  2. Section F – Other Budget Information, line 22 "Indirect Charges": the official instructions ask for "the type of indirect rate (provisional, predetermined, final or fixed) that will be in effect during the funding period, the estimated amount of the base to which the rate is applied, and the total indirect expense" (Grants.gov SF-424A instructions). For example: "De minimis rate, 15% of MTDC per 2 CFR 200.414(f); base $220,000; indirect $33,000."

R&R Budget (common for NSF, NIH and other research funders): the indirect cost section has fields for Indirect Cost Type (enter "Modified Total Direct Costs"), the rate, Indirect Cost Base, funds requested, and Cognizant Federal Agency (Grants.gov R&R Budget form). If you have no cognizant agency because you've never negotiated, write "None – de minimis rate elected," unless the NOFO tells you otherwise.

For the rest of the SF-424 package, see our field-by-field SF-424 instructions.

Step 3: Write the election statement in the budget narrative

Agencies expect a plain statement. NEH, for example, says your budget "must include the base, rate, and amount of indirect costs" (NEH). Agency instructions found in search results also ask applicants to state in the Budget Narrative that they don't have a NICRA and are electing the de minimis rate.

Sample wording (an example, not official language):

"[Organization] does not have a current federally negotiated indirect cost rate agreement and elects the de minimis rate of 15% of modified total direct costs under 2 CFR 200.414(f). The MTDC base of $220,000 excludes equipment ($15,000), participant support costs ($10,000), rental costs ($12,000), and the portion of the subaward to [Partner] in excess of $50,000 ($30,000). Indirect costs requested: $33,000."

Listing the exclusions takes a few extra lines. It also answers the reviewer's first question before they ask it. For help with the rest of the narrative, see how to write federal grant proposals for nonprofits.

Step 4: Apply it consistently and keep the file

  1. Use one rate on every federal award. NSF says the rate "must be applied consistently across all an organization's federal awards until the organization chooses to negotiate an indirect cost rate" (NSF).
  2. Don't double-charge. If rent sits in your indirect pool, you can't also charge rent directly to the grant. The regulation requires costs to be "consistently charged as direct and indirect costs and not double charged or inconsistently charged as both" (Clark Nuber quoting 200.414(f)).
  3. Keep these items in an "Indirect – De Minimis" folder: the budget spreadsheet with the MTDC column, the narrative statement, the award notice showing the approved rate, and a one-page written policy listing which cost types you treat as indirect.
  4. Recalculate when you draw funds. Indirect costs are claimed on actual MTDC spent, not the budgeted amount. If you spend only $180,000 of MTDC, you can claim $27,000 at 15%.

You don't have to justify the rate with documentation. You still have to show the base was calculated correctly, and auditors test that. It's a different question from whether you were entitled to 15%.

Indirect Cost Rate vs. De Minimis: What's the Difference?

A negotiated indirect cost rate (NICRA) is calculated from your actual costs and approved by your cognizant federal agency. The de minimis rate is a self-elected flat rate of up to 15% of MTDC with no negotiation. Section 200.414(c) requires federal agencies to accept negotiated rates unless a statute, regulation or documented agency approval allows a deviation (2 CFR 200.414).

FactorDe minimis (200.414(f))Negotiated rate (NICRA)
RateUp to 15% of MTDCWhatever your cost data supports. Often higher or lower than 15%.
ApprovalNone; you elect it in the budgetCognizant agency reviews an indirect cost proposal
Documentation to justify the rateNot requiredFull proposal under Appendices III–IX of Part 200
BaseMTDC as defined in 200.1Set by your agreement (MTDC, salaries and wages, etc.)
Who it suitsNew, small or lightly funded organizationsOrganizations with high shared costs and several awards
Time to set upMinutesMonths, with ongoing annual or multi-year proposals
Extension optionUsed indefinitelyOne-time extension of up to four years may be requested under 200.414(g)

How to decide

Work out your actual indirect costs divided by your MTDC from last year's audited financials. If the result is well above 15%, for example 24%, and you expect several federal awards, a negotiated rate is probably worth the effort. If it's near or below 15%, or you have one small award, de minimis is the simpler choice. The DOL guide to indirect cost rate determination shows how the calculation is set up.

Pitfall: Don't mix the two approaches. You can't use de minimis on one award and a negotiated rate on another during the same period (search summary of agency guidance).

De Minimis Indirect Cost Rate Under Uniform Guidance: Key Rules

Under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR Part 200, Subpart E), de minimis is a simpler alternative to negotiation with five firm rules. These are the ones most likely to come up in an audit.

  1. Ceiling of 15% of MTDC, with any lower rate allowed (200.414(f)).
  2. Agencies can't require a lower rate unless a statute says so (same section). If a program officer asks you to cut to 10% without citing a statute, ask which authority they're relying on.
  3. The MTDC exclusions are fixed. Other items may be excluded "only... when necessary to avoid a serious inequity... and with the approval of the cognizant agency for indirect costs" (200.1). You can't create your own exclusions.
  4. Classify costs consistently. The same type of cost can't be direct on one award and indirect on another.
  5. No end date. Once elected, you keep the rate until you negotiate one.

The rule applies to subrecipients as well. If you pass money to a partner without a NICRA, they can elect de minimis on their subaward. Your own MTDC still counts only the first $50,000 of that subaward.

Pitfall: inconsistent agency pages. NEH's guidance page lists the 15% rate but, as of October 2026, still describes MTDC with "up to the first $25,000 of each subaward" (NEH). Some agency SF-424A instructions also still mention 10% and $25,000 (Grants.gov search results for SF-424A instructions). The fix is to follow the current regulation ($50,000) for awards made on or after October 1, 2024. If your NOFO says something different, email the grants management contact named in the NOFO and keep the reply.

Is There a 15% De Minimis Indirect Cost Rate?

Yes. Under the current 2 CFR 200.414(f), the de minimis rate is up to 15% of MTDC. Confusion comes from a different "15%" policy at NIH that no longer applies.

On February 7, 2025, NIH issued NOT-OD-25-068. It tried to cap indirect cost rates at 15% on NIH research grants, including organizations that held negotiated rates (Clearinghouse case record). That was a cap on everyone's rate, not the de minimis election. A federal court blocked it. On January 5, 2026, the First Circuit affirmed that the cap violated the appropriations rider and HHS regulations (Higher Ed Dive; Forbes). According to the American Council on Education, the administration did not seek Supreme Court review and the litigation is over (ACE).

So when you see "15%":

Where you saw 15%What it meansApplies to you?
2 CFR 200.414(f)Voluntary de minimis ceiling for entities without a current NICRAYes, if eligible
NIH NOT-OD-25-068 (Feb 2025)Attempted mandatory cap on all NIH granteesNo. Struck down.
Blog posts about "10%"The pre-October 2024 de minimis rateOnly on older, unamended awards

De Minimis Indirect Cost Rate in 2024, 2025, and 2026: Has It Changed?

Yes, it changed once. The 2024 Uniform Guidance revision raised the rate from 10% to 15% and the MTDC subaward limit from $25,000 to $50,000, effective October 1, 2024. Nothing in 2025 or 2026 has changed it as of October 2026 (NSF; Clark Nuber).

YearDe minimis rateSubaward amount in MTDCEligibility test
2014 to Sept 30, 202410% of MTDCFirst $25,000Never had a negotiated rate
Oct 1, 2024 onwardUp to 15% of MTDCFirst $50,000No current negotiated rate
2025Unchanged at 15% (NIH cap litigation was separate)$50,000Same
2026 (proposed rewrite)Proposal leaves 15% unchanged$50,000Same

On May 29, 2026, OMB published a proposed rewrite of 2 CFR Part 200, Federal Register document 2026-10817 under docket OMB-2026-0034. Comments closed on July 13, 2026, and the target effective date was October 1, 2026 (CASRAI). Law-firm summaries report that the proposal leaves the 15% de minimis rate and the NICRA framework unchanged, even though Executive Order 14332 had directed OMB to address indirect costs (search summary of Venable/Jenner analyses; Jenner & Block). Commentary has also flagged a proposed "lower indirect rate preference" in § 200.205(b), which could affect how applications with lower rates are scored (NeedICR).

Before you submit in late 2026, open 2 CFR 200.414 on eCFR and check the "up to date as of" banner. Also check the Federal Register for a final rule. The most recent status reports found for this guide said no final rule had been published (CASRAI). Until one takes effect, the current text governs.

Next steps

You can finish most of this today with your draft budget open.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Add an "In MTDC?" column to your budget spreadsheet. Tag each line using the 200.1 exclusions and put the indirect formula on the MTDC subtotal.
  2. Paste the sample election statement from Step 3 into your budget narrative, replacing the example numbers with yours.
  3. Write a one-page indirect cost policy listing which cost types are indirect, and file it with your budget workpapers.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: a CPA firm that audits nonprofits under the Single Audit, or an indirect cost consultant, can build your MTDC base. They can also tell you whether a negotiated rate would recover more. This suits organizations with several federal awards or overhead well above 15%, because a negotiated rate may justify the fee. It's usually poor value for a single small award, where de minimis already works. These firms don't publish standard fees, so prices vary by firm and scope (as of October 2026; ask for a written quote). One limitation is that a consultant can't approve a rate. Only your cognizant federal agency can. The free option is the DOL indirect cost rate guide. It's useful for preparing a negotiated rate proposal, though it doesn't cover agency-specific NOFO rules.

Related guides on Outlay Grants:

FAQ

What is the current de minimis indirect cost rate?

As of October 2026 it's up to 15% of modified total direct costs under 2 CFR 200.414(f). It applies to awards made on or after October 1, 2024. OMB's 2026 proposed rewrite of Part 200 would leave it unchanged, but check eCFR for a final rule before you submit.

What is the 10% de minimis indirect cost rate?

It's the earlier version of the rule, in effect from 2014 until September 30, 2024. Only organizations that had never had a negotiated rate could use it, and MTDC included just the first $25,000 of each subaward. Older awards keep 10% unless they're amended.

What is the de minimis indirect cost rate under 2 CFR 200?

Section 200.414(f) lets recipients and subrecipients without a current negotiated rate charge up to 15% of MTDC, as defined in 200.1. You don't need documentation to justify the rate. You do have to use it consistently on all federal awards and never charge the same cost both directly and indirectly.

De minimis indirect rate: can I switch to a negotiated rate later?

Yes. The de minimis rate lasts until you choose to negotiate. To switch, you submit an indirect cost proposal to your cognizant federal agency, and once a rate is approved it replaces de minimis on your awards. Under the current rule you can also go back to de minimis after a NICRA expires.

item.title: UEI Number Lookup: Free SAM.gov Search in 3 Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: UEI number lookup made simple: search any organization's UEI free on SAM.gov with no login, find your own UEI, and know when you need to sign in.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To look up a UEI number for free, open SAM.gov, click Search, choose Entity Information, and type the organization's legal name, UEI or CAGE code. You don't need an account or a login. Anyone can look up a public SAM.gov record (SAM.gov Entity Information). You need a login only to register your own entity, renew it, or request a new UEI. Many guides blur the free search and the login-only steps together, so this guide treats them separately.

Which option is right for you?

Pick your row in the table below and start on the page it lists. Every option here is free, because SAM.gov doesn't charge to register or to keep your entity information up to date (SAM.gov entity registration).

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to openWhy
Beginner who needs a UEI for a grant form today and isn't sure one existsPublic Entity Information search by legal namesam.gov/searchNo login. It shows whether your organization already has a public record
Already registered and need the UEI or expiration date for daily workSign in, then open Entity Workspacesam.gov → Sign InYour workspace shows the record even if you opted out of public search
Never registered, and you'll apply for awards yourselfRegister Entity (the UEI is assigned along the way)sam.gov/entity-registrationYou can't apply directly for federal awards with only a UEI
Subrecipient or partner that only needs an ID on someone else's applicationGet a Unique Entity ID (UEI only)sam.gov/entity-registrationNeeds only your legal business name and physical address
Checking a vendor, partner or competitorPublic search by name, UEI or CAGE codesam.gov/searchPublic, view-only, no account
Veteran-owned business that needs to confirm its certified listingSBA Small Business Searchsearch.certifications.sba.govAccepts business name, UEI or CAGE code
On a tight budget and stuckFree counseling from a local APEX Acceleratorapexaccelerators.usNo fee for SAM.gov registration help

How to Look Up a UEI Number (Free, No Login Required)

You can look up a UEI number for free with SAM.gov's public Entity Information search. Anyone can use it, for any organization that keeps a public record, without an account. GSA's Entity Information page says the general public can search active entity registrations. Logins are only for federal users who need records that are hidden from the public.

Steps (UI labels as shown on SAM.gov at the time of writing)

  1. Go to sam.gov. Click Search in the top navigation.
  2. Under the domain selector, choose Entity Information. If you skip this step, your keyword runs against contract opportunities instead.
  3. Type one of these in the keyword box: the legal business name, the 12-character UEI, or the CAGE code. Then press Enter. GSA lists all three as searchable values (GSA bulletin, April 2022).
  4. Click the entity name in the results. The record shows the Unique Entity ID, CAGE code, registration status, expiration date and physical address (SellToState summary of SAM.gov fields).
  5. Before you copy the UEI into a form, check that the physical address matches the organization you mean.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • No results for a name you know is registered. Registrants can untick the option to include their non-sensitive information in public search. Those records then show up only for signed-in federal users (SAM.gov Entity Information). Fix: ask the organization for its UEI, or have its administrator sign in and read it from the workspace.
  • Searching a trade name. SAM.gov stores the legal business name that was validated at registration. If a search for "Main Street Bakery" (example) returns nothing, try the LLC or corporate name from the IRS paperwork.
  • Searching an old DUNS number. Since April 4, 2022, "You can no longer use the DUNS Number to search entities or exclusions" (GSA bulletin). Search by name instead.
  • Paying a third-party "lookup" site. You don't need to. The official search is free, and paid sites usually show the same public data, sometimes out of date.
  • Needing bulk or automated lookups. GSA publishes the Entity Management API and public data extracts at open.gsa.gov. They do require an API key, and records that opted out are left out of public keys and extracts.

How Do I Find My Own UEI Number?

If your organization is already registered, sign in to SAM.gov and open your Entity Workspace to see your UEI. You can also search your legal name in the public search without signing in. According to GSA, every entity registered in SAM.gov, active or not, already has a UEI that "is viewable at SAM.gov" (GSA bulletin).

Option A: no login (fastest)

Use the public search steps above with your legal business name. This works only if your record is set to appear in public search.

Option B: sign in (always works for your own record)

  1. On sam.gov, click Sign In at the top right. SAM.gov uses Login.gov for sign-in, so you'll need the email address and multi-factor method you set up there (SAM.gov entity registration).
  2. After sign-in you land in Workspace. Open the Entities widget, then your Entity Workspace.
  3. Your entity shows up in a status bubble such as Active, Work in Progress, or ID Assigned (UEI only). Click the bubble, then the entity name. The UEI appears next to the legal business name (FSD Quick Start Guide for Getting a Unique Entity ID).

For example, the finance manager at a small nonprofit who needs the UEI for an SF-424 can start with Option A. If the public search comes back empty, the person who manages the SAM.gov registration can sign in and use Option B. To find out where the UEI goes on the application, see our SF-424 field-by-field guide.

Common mistake

You can't sign in, or your login doesn't show the entity. Your Login.gov account may not have a role on the entity. Only the entity administrator can grant roles. Ask that person, or file a ticket at the Federal Service Desk (FSD.gov). If you just need the number, the public search doesn't care about roles.

Where Can I Find My UEI Number If I'm Not Registered Yet?

If you've never registered, you don't have a UEI yet. SAM.gov creates one for you during either Register Entity or Get a Unique Entity ID. There's no separate application. Since April 4, 2022, SAM.gov has generated the UEI itself, so you no longer have to get an identifier from a third-party website such as Dun & Bradstreet (GSA news release). Some older guides still say D&B issues the UEI. That's outdated.

Which path to choose

Register EntityGet a Unique Entity ID (UEI only)
UEI assigned?YesYes
Can apply directly for federal grants and contracts?YesNo: "You cannot apply directly for federal awards"
Information requiredFull set (see SAM.gov's Entity Registration Checklist)Legal business name and physical address
RenewalEvery 365 days to stay activeNot a registration, so there's no annual renewal
Typical userPrime applicants and contractorsSubrecipients, or anyone who needs an ID now and will register later

Source for the table: SAM.gov Get Started with Registration and the Unique Entity ID.

Steps

  1. Create or sign in to your SAM.gov account through Login.gov.
  2. In Workspace, find the Entity Management widget and select Get Started.
  3. Choose Get Unique Entity ID for a UEI only, or Register Entity for full registration (FSD Quick Start Guide).
  4. Enter the legal business name and physical address exactly as they appear on official documents. SAM.gov validates both.
  5. When validation passes, the UEI appears in your Entity Workspace. A UEI-only record shows the status ID Assigned.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Validation fails because of a mismatched name or address. SAM.gov may ask you to upload documents through an FSD ticket. You can track that ticket in your Workspace or at FSD.gov (FSD Quick Start Guide). Check spelling, suite numbers and abbreviations against your incorporation or IRS documents before you submit.
  • Choosing UEI only when you plan to apply as the prime. You'll need a full registration before you can apply. If you're also setting up Grants.gov, follow our Grants.gov vs SAM.gov registration order guide so you don't have to redo steps.

UEI Number Lookup vs. UEN Number Lookup: What's the Difference?

A UEI and a UEN are unrelated. The UEI is the U.S. federal identifier issued by SAM.gov. The UEN is Singapore's business registration number. If you typed "uen number lookup" while trying to apply for a U.S. grant, SAM.gov is the place you want.

UEI (Unique Entity ID)UEN (Unique Entity Number)
CountryUnited StatesSingapore
Issued bySAM.gov (GSA)ACRA and other Singapore agencies
Used forFederal grants, contracts, subawardsBusiness registration and dealings with Singapore government agencies
Format12 characters, alphanumeric (GSA)9-10 characters (Harvest Accounting)
Free lookupsam.gov/searchBizfile or uen.gov.sg

One edge case: a Singapore company that wants U.S. federal awards needs a UEI as well. Its UEN doesn't replace the UEI, and SAM.gov won't accept a UEN in the UEI field.

How to Check If a UEI Number Is Valid or Active

To check a UEI, paste the 12-character code into SAM.gov's public Entity Information search. Then confirm three things: the record exists, the name and address match, and the registration status is Active. An entity keeps its UEI whether its registration is active or not (GSA bulletin), but the registration itself must be renewed every 365 days to stay active (SAM.gov). Mixing up the two is the trap that catches many first-time applicants.

Steps

  1. Count the characters. A UEI has 12 alphanumeric characters (GSA). A 9-digit number is probably an old DUNS. A 5-character code is probably a CAGE code.
  2. Search the UEI at sam.gov/search with Entity Information selected.
  3. Open the record and compare the legal business name and physical address with what the organization gave you.
  4. Read the registration status and the expiration date. Registrations must be renewed every 365 days to stay active (SAM.gov).
  5. If you're vetting a partner or subrecipient, also search their name in SAM.gov's Exclusions records, which SAM.gov search covers alongside entity records (GSA bulletin).

What the result means

What you seeWhat it meansWhat to do
Active registration, details matchValid and ready for awardsUse it
Inactive or expired registrationThe UEI still exists (GSA bulletin), but the registration must be renewed to be active again (SAM.gov)The entity administrator renews in Workspace
No public recordOpted out, UEI only, or the code is wrongAsk the organization to confirm the UEI from its Workspace
Record found, but the name differsWrong UEI, or a parent or affiliate recordAsk for the UEI tied to the exact legal entity on the application

For a full walkthrough of renewal timing and status meanings, see How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status.

How to Find a Company's UEI Number (Looking Up Someone Else's Entity)

To find a company's UEI, search SAM.gov's public Entity Information by legal business name, address or CAGE code. You don't need an account, because you're searching public award and registration data, not private records. This also answers "federal uei number lookup." There's only one federal UEI system, and SAM.gov is where it lives.

Steps

  1. At sam.gov/search, select Entity Information.
  2. Search the legal name. If it's a common name, narrow the results with the location filters (state, ZIP) in the left panel.
  3. If you have a CAGE code from a past contract or a proposal, search that instead, since it leads to a single record.
  4. Open the record and copy the UEI.

Example

Say a university researcher is putting together a proposal with a small engineering subcontractor named "Example Fabrication LLC" (an illustrative name). They search that name, see two records in different states, and pick the one whose physical address matches the subcontractor's letterhead. Then they ask the subcontractor to confirm the UEI by email before it goes into the budget justification.

When SAM.gov comes up empty

  • USAspending.gov lists federal award recipients and can show the UEI attached to past awards. It's useful when you know a company has received federal money (USAspending recipient search). Keep in mind that it shows award history, not current registration status.
  • SBA Small Business Search (search.certifications.sba.gov) accepts business name, UEI and CAGE code. It pulls from SAM.gov, but only businesses with an active SAM registration appear there (SmallGovCon; Squared Compass).
  • If both come up empty, ask the company. An organization that opted out of public search still knows its own UEI.

DUNS Number vs. UEI: How to Find Your UEI If You Only Have a DUNS

You can't turn a DUNS into a UEI with a lookup, because SAM.gov stopped accepting DUNS searches on April 4, 2022. Search your legal business name instead, or sign in to your existing account. Entities that were registered at the transition were assigned a UEI, and GSA states that every registered entity, active or not, has a UEI viewable at SAM.gov (GSA bulletin).

Official facts (as of October 2026)

  • On April 4, 2022, SAM.gov and all other GSA award systems switched to the Unique Entity ID (SAM) as the authoritative identifier (GSA news release).
  • "You will no longer find the DUNS number in any SAM.gov searches, views, or extracts" (GSA bulletin).
  • SAM.gov, eSRS, FSRS, FPDS, FAPIIS and CPARS identify entities by UEI only (GSA bulletin).

Steps

  1. Find the legal business name and physical address you used back when you had a DUNS.
  2. Search that name at sam.gov/search under Entity Information.
  3. If nothing appears, sign in with the Login.gov account tied to your old registration and open Entity Workspace.
  4. If you can't get into the old account at all, open a ticket at FSD.gov. Don't start a new registration. That can create a duplicate entity that you'd have to untangle later.

Pitfalls

  • Old grant forms or templates still ask for a DUNS. Put the UEI in the identifier field. Federal systems no longer use DUNS.
  • Dun & Bradstreet still exists, and DUNS numbers are still used commercially. But a D&B profile is not a SAM.gov registration, and paying D&B won't get you a UEI.

How to Look Up a VA (Veteran-Owned Business) UEI Number

A veteran-owned business has the same SAM.gov UEI as every other entity, so look it up in SAM.gov's public search first. To confirm the certified VOSB or SDVOSB listing, use SBA's Small Business Search. VetBiz no longer does this job. The plan many older guides follow points to VA's VetBiz/VIP database, but SBA took over veteran certification under the FY2021 NDAA and opened its VetCert application portal on January 9, 2023 (Federal News Network).

Steps

  1. UEI: search the business name at sam.gov/search under Entity Information. Or, if it's your business, sign in and read it from Entity Workspace.
  2. Certification status: VA's small business office tells contracting officers and firms to use SBA's small business search database as the official place to verify certification (VA OSDBU). On July 9, 2025, that database moved from DSBS to the new Small Business Search at search.certifications.sba.gov (SmallGovCon).
  3. Search by business name, UEI or CAGE code, and check that the SDVOSB or VOSB designation appears on the profile.

Pitfalls

  • The certified profile disappeared from SBS. SBS shows only businesses with an active SAM registration (Squared Compass). Renew in SAM.gov first.
  • Joint ventures. As of August 1, 2025, VOSB and SDVOSB joint venture designations no longer show in SBS (Squared Compass). Confirm JV status directly with SBA.
  • For VA-specific questions, VA's OSDBU line is 1-866-584-2344, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern (VA OSDBU).

Next steps

Today, do the search that matches your situation, then fix whatever it shows.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Search your legal business name at sam.gov/search under Entity Information, and write down the UEI and expiration date.
  2. If the expiration date is within 60 days, or the status isn't Active, sign in and start the renewal. Registrations lapse after 365 days (SAM.gov). To read each status label (Active, Submitted, Work in Progress), use our SAM.gov registration status guide.
  3. If you have no record at all, choose Register Entity if you'll apply yourself, or Get Unique Entity ID if you'll only be a subrecipient. Have the legal name and physical address ready.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) give free, one-on-one help with SAM.gov registration through local offices funded by the Department of Defense. Cost: $0 (as of October 2026; check the official page). This suits small businesses and nonprofits that want a person to walk them through validation problems. It's less useful if you need help the same day, because appointment availability depends on your local office. Their main focus is government contracting, so for grant-writing help you may need to look elsewhere.
  • Paid registration services charge for something SAM.gov does for free. Federal sources warn that these companies solicit registrants and that the fee is unnecessary (summary of APEX guidance). They might be worth it for a busy firm that would pay to save time, but they can't get you validated any faster, and they still need you to grant access to your Login.gov-linked account. That's a real security trade-off.
  • Federal Service Desk at FSD.gov is free and the right place for account access problems or validation tickets.

Related guides on this site:

  • Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: Registration Order in 4 Steps (2026)

FAQ

How do I find my UEI number?

Search your legal business name at sam.gov/search with Entity Information selected. If your record doesn't appear, sign in and open Entity Workspace. Every entity that has registered in SAM.gov, active or not, has a UEI visible there. If you've never registered, you don't have one yet.

Where can I find my UEI number?

You'll find it on your public SAM.gov entity record and in your signed-in Entity Workspace. It also appears on federal award documents and past applications such as the SF-424. If you've never registered, SAM.gov issues one through Register Entity or Get Unique Entity ID.

Is UEI number lookup free?

Yes. The SAM.gov public search costs nothing, and so do getting a UEI and registering. Paid lookup or registration sites charge for data and services the government provides at no cost.

Does a UEI number lookup require a SAM.gov login?

No, as long as the record is public. Anyone can search by name, UEI or CAGE code without signing in. A login is needed only to manage your own entity, and federal users need one to see records that opted out of public search.

How is a UEI different from a DUNS number?

A DUNS was a 9-digit number from Dun & Bradstreet. A UEI is a 12-character alphanumeric ID that SAM.gov generates. The federal government switched to the UEI on April 4, 2022, and you can no longer search SAM.gov by DUNS.
