item.title: Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: Registration Order in 4 Steps (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: see the correct registration order—SAM.gov issues your UEI and active status first, then Grants.gov unlocks applications. Follow the 4 steps, timing, and common fixes.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

SAM.gov and Grants.gov are two separate federal systems. Organizations have to use them in a set order. SAM.gov confirms your organization's identity, gives it a Unique Entity ID (UEI) and makes it eligible to receive federal money. Grants.gov is where you find and submit grant applications, and an organization can't finish registering there until its SAM.gov registration is active. If you apply as an individual for yourself, Grants.gov says you do not need to register with SAM.gov.

Which option is right for you?

Start with SAM.gov if you apply for a business, nonprofit, university or government. Start with Grants.gov only if you apply as a private individual.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner applying for a small business or nonprofitSAM.gov entity registration ("Financial Assistance Awards Only" if you only want grants)sam.gov/content/entity-registration
Individual applying in your own name (not for an organization)Grants.gov account with an Individual Applicant profile. No SAM.gov neededgrants.gov/help/register/individual-applicant
Staff member joining an organization already registered in SAM.govGrants.gov account and an Organization Applicant profile using the existing UEIgrants.gov/applicants/applicant-registration
Grants office handling applications every dayCheck SAM.gov expiration dates and Grants.gov AOR roles before each cycleHow to Check SAM.gov Registration Status
You only want to browse opportunities for nowSearch on Simpler.Grants.gov or Grants.gov. Searching needs no registrationsimpler.grants.gov
Tight budgetDo it yourself. Both systems are freegrants.gov/applicants/applicant-registration

Here's why each pick fits. Beginners at an organization can't get past Grants.gov profile setup without a UEI. Individuals skip the organization requirements completely. Staff at a registered organization only need a role. Daily users mostly run into expiration problems, not first-time setup. Browsing is open to anyone, and paying a third party for a free registration rarely saves money.

What Is Grants.gov?

Grants.gov is the federal government's shared website for finding and applying to discretionary federal grants. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services manages it. According to its About page, the Grants.gov program management office was set up in 2002 under the President's Management Agenda. It runs under Office of Management and Budget governance and covers "over 1,000 grant programs" that distribute "more than $500 billion annually" (as of October 2026).

In practice, Grants.gov does three jobs:

  • Search. Anyone can browse open funding opportunities without an account. Each listing links to its Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO).
  • Apply. Registered users fill out forms such as the SF-424 in an online "Workspace" and submit the package to the agency.
  • Track. After you submit, you get a tracking number. Submitted applications are kept for 5 years and can be followed on the Track My Application page, per the Grants.gov applicant FAQs.

Grants.gov does not award money or score applications. The agency that posted the opportunity does that, often in its own system after the application leaves Grants.gov. For example, a Department of Justice applicant may submit the SF-424 through Grants.gov and then finish the rest in JustGrants, which is why OJP publishes its own Grants.gov guidance.

A newer interface is also being built. Simpler.Grants.gov describes itself as the place for "building new features for the next generation of Grants.gov." You can already search real Grants.gov data there. The site also says "You may need to visit Grants.gov to apply for most opportunities" (as of October 2026). It uses Login.gov for sign-in. Treat it as a search tool, and plan to submit through whichever system the NOFO names.

If you're deciding which kind of award to go after first, see Federal Grant vs Cooperative Agreement: Table + NOFO Steps.

What Is SAM.gov and Why Is It Required First?

SAM.gov is the System for Award Management. There, organizations get a Unique Entity ID (UEI) and register so they can receive federal funds. Organizations need an active SAM.gov registration before they can finish Grants.gov setup and submit. The General Services Administration (GSA) runs SAM.gov, not HHS. That's one reason the two sites have separate help desks.

SAM.gov offers two options, and picking the wrong one is a common first mistake. According to SAM.gov's entity registration page:

SAM.gov optionWhat you provideWhat it allowsWho it fits
Unique Entity ID onlyLegal business name and physical addressGetting a UEI, for example to report as a sub-awardeeSubrecipients that never apply directly
Full entity registrationMuch more detail (see the official checklist)Bidding on contracts and applying for federal assistanceAnyone applying directly for a grant

SAM.gov states it plainly: "If you choose to only get a Unique Entity ID, you cannot apply directly for federal awards." For grant applicants, the UEI-only path leads nowhere.

Within full registration, you choose a purpose. The FSD Quick Start Guide for Financial Assistance Registrations and widely used state guides such as Cal OES's Entity Registration Checklist describe them:

  • Financial Assistance Awards Only. For grants and other assistance, and it asks for less information. You can't bid on federal contracts with this type.
  • All Awards. For contracts and assistance. Pick this if you also plan to sell to the government.

So why does SAM.gov come first? When you create an organization profile in Grants.gov, you type in your UEI. Grants.gov then checks SAM.gov for an active registration and for the E-Business Point of Contact (EBiz POC) listed there, as Grants.gov describes. Without an active record, there's nothing for Grants.gov to link to.

Before you open SAM.gov, gather what the FSD quick start guide lists: your Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), bank account details for payments, and the name and email of the person who will be EBiz POC. Your legal name and address have to match your IRS records exactly. Mismatches are a frequent cause of delays (more in the timing section). Download SAM.gov's own Entity Registration Checklist and complete it offline first.

Grants.gov vs SAM.gov: What's the Difference?

SAM.gov confirms who you are and that the government can pay you. Grants.gov is where you search for and submit grant applications. They are separate systems with separate accounts that you link using your UEI and the EBiz POC email.

SAM.govGrants.gov
Main jobEntity registration, UEI, eligibility to receive federal fundsSearching for and submitting federal grant applications
Run byGSAHHS, with OMB governance (About Grants.gov)
Who registersThe organization, as an "entity"Each person, then linked to the organization through a profile
Sign-inLogin.govGrants.gov account linked to Login.gov (Grants.gov blog)
Key identifierUEI, a 12-character alphanumeric ID (GSA fact sheet)Your username, plus the UEI on your organization profile
RenewalEvery 365 days (SAM.gov)No annual renewal for the account. It depends on SAM.gov staying active
CostFreeFree (Grants.gov)
Help deskFederal Service Desk (fsd.gov)Grants.gov Support Center, 1-800-518-4726, 24/7 except federal holidays (OJP)
Needed by individuals?NoYes, with an Individual Applicant profile

Here's an example. Riverbend Food Pantry, a nonprofit, wants a USDA grant. Its executive director registers the nonprofit in SAM.gov with "Financial Assistance Awards Only" and lists herself as EBiz POC. Once the registration is active, she creates a Grants.gov account using the same email and adds an organization profile with the pantry's UEI. Then she gives her grant writer the AOR role. The grant writer never touches SAM.gov. The director never has to write the proposal. Each system does one job.

How to Register for Grants.gov (Step-by-Step)

Registration has to go in order. First get a UEI and complete SAM.gov entity registration. Then create a Grants.gov account. Last, link it to your organization with a role such as AOR. The steps below use the button labels found on the official pages (Grants.gov registration, FSD quick start guide).

Step 1: Register your entity in SAM.gov

  1. Go to SAM.gov and click Sign In. If you don't have a Login.gov account, create one. SAM.gov and Grants.gov both use Login.gov.
  2. Open your Workspace.
  3. Under Entities, click Get Started, then Register Entity. Don't choose the UEI-only option.
  4. Choose your purpose: Financial Assistance Awards Only if you only want grants, or All Awards if you'll also bid on contracts.
  5. Enter your legal name, physical address, TIN, banking details and points of contact. Write down the EBiz POC email, because you'll need it in Step 2.
  6. Submit. A UEI is assigned as part of the process, and SAM.gov reviews the registration. Grants.gov says to allow up to 10 business days for it to become active.

Step 2: The EBiz POC creates a Grants.gov account

  1. On Grants.gov, click Register.
  2. At the bottom of the page, click Get Registered Now. Fill in the form and click Continue.
  3. Click Send Temporary Code, copy the code from your email into the Temporary Code box, then click Continue (Grants.gov Register help).
  4. Link the account to Login.gov when prompted.

The EBiz POC has to use the same email that's listed in SAM.gov, per Grants.gov. If the emails don't match, Grants.gov won't recognize this person as the POC.

Step 3: Add the organization applicant profile

  1. When you're offered profile options, pick Add Organization Applicant Profile. Don't pick Add an Individual Applicant Profile if you're applying for an organization (Grants.gov Add Profile).
  2. Enter the organization's UEI, a profile name and your job title, then save.
  3. Grants.gov notes that the EBiz POC automatically gets the Expanded AOR role after adding the profile. In a one-person organization, you can now submit.

Step 4: Give roles to everyone else

  1. Each team member creates their own Grants.gov account (Step 2) and adds an Organization Applicant Profile with the same UEI (Step 3). Their request goes to the EBiz POC.
  2. The EBiz POC signs in, clicks Manage Applicants, finds the person and assigns a role (Grants.gov).
  3. Grants.gov emails the person when they've been approved. Grants.gov says this can happen the same day, depending on when the EBiz POC logs in.

Which role should you give? Per the applicant FAQs, a Standard AOR can submit only from workspaces where they are a participant. An Expanded AOR can submit from any of the organization's workspaces. A Workspace Manager can build and manage workspaces but can't submit. A careful setup gives submit rights to one or two people, plus a backup.

If you manage several organizations, keep one Grants.gov account and add each organization's UEI from the Manage Profiles tab, per Grants.gov.

Once you're registered, the application itself comes next. Two guides cover that: SF-424 Instructions: Field-by-Field Table and Steps (2026) and How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide.

How Long Does SAM.gov → Grants.gov Registration Take?

Grants.gov says to allow up to 10 business days for SAM.gov registration to become active. Grants.gov setup can follow the same day. First-timers should still plan on several weeks before any deadline.

Here's how the timeline breaks down:

StageOfficial figureWhat can stretch it
Login.gov accountMinutesIdentity verification problems
SAM.gov entity registration becomes activeUp to 10 business days (Grants.gov)IRS name or TIN mismatches, entity validation reviews, corrections
Grants.gov account and profileSame sessionEBiz POC email doesn't match SAM.gov
AOR role approvalCan be same day (Grants.gov)EBiz POC unavailable
Writing and submittingDepends on the NOFORejections that arrive after the deadline

The 10-business-day figure counts from when the registration is complete and correct. Federal contracting guides such as UseGrants and Federal Processing Registry say first-time registrations often take 2 to 8 weeks from start to active. They also note that the clock effectively starts over when a validation step fails. These are third-party estimates, not official limits, but they're a sensible planning buffer.

Some registrations also involve a notarized letter. The FSD quick start guide refers to one, and some third-party guides say the original must be mailed within 60 days of submitting. Check the current Federal Service Desk knowledge base for whether this applies to you before you rely on any timeline.

Remember that a registration can also run out. SAM.gov registrations must be renewed every 365 days. Third-party guides report reminder emails at 60, 30 and 15 days before expiration, sent to the registrant's email (SLED AI). If that person has left your organization, the reminders go to an inbox nobody reads.

Here's an example timeline. Say a NOFO closes on December 15. To be safe, start SAM.gov registration in October, aim to be active by mid-November, set up Grants.gov roles that same week, and submit at least several days before December 15.

Is Grants.gov Legit?

Yes. Grants.gov is an official U.S. government website on a .gov domain, managed by HHS (About Grants.gov). Paid "grant registration" sites that look like it are not affiliated with the government.

Neither system charges anything. Grants.gov says registration is free (Grants.gov). The UEI is issued at no cost. The Better Business Bureau has warned about third parties claiming to help with government grant registration. Third-party guides report fees of roughly $300 to $3,000 for registrations you can do yourself for free (GovCon Giants, as of October 2026; check the official pages).

Watch for these red flags:

  • An email saying your "SAM registration is expiring" with a payment link. The government never charges for registration, updates or renewals.
  • A website ending in .com or .org that copies the Grants.gov or SAM.gov look.
  • Someone offering a "guaranteed grant" for a processing fee. Federal grants are competitive, and the posting agency decides who gets them.
  • A request for your Login.gov password or one-time code.

For example, if you get a message warning that your SAM.gov registration will lapse, don't click it. Type sam.gov into your browser yourself and check the status. Our guide How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status walks through it.

Grants.gov Reviews: What Do Applicants Say?

Opinions are mixed. People value Grants.gov as a free, central and authoritative source. The common complaints are about the submission process, and official guidance confirms those trouble spots. This guide doesn't quote individual user reviews. The documented pain points below come from official sources.

What works. You get one free place to search the 1,000+ programs, one set of standard forms, a tracking number for every submission and 24/7 phone support at 1-800-518-4726 (OJP).

What frustrates applicants, according to official guidance:

  • Strict file-name rules. Attachment names must be 50 characters or fewer and use only allowed characters (Grants.gov FAQs). OJP's example: Police^FirePlan.doc gets the whole application rejected, while Police$FirePlan.doc is fine (OJP).
  • Rejection notices that come late. OJP warns that applicants "may not receive rejection notices until after the deadline has passed."
  • Two systems, two help desks. SAM.gov problems go to the Federal Service Desk, and Grants.gov problems go to the Grants.gov Support Center. You can lose a day just figuring out which one to call.
  • A dated interface. HHS is rebuilding the experience at Simpler.Grants.gov, which lists "transparency and usability" as its goals. That points to the legacy Workspace being the weak spot.

Here's an example of how these problems stack up. An applicant names a budget file FY27 Budget Justification – Final (v3) revised by finance.pdf. That's over 50 characters, and the long dash isn't on the allowed list. If they submit an hour before the deadline, the rejection could arrive too late to fix anything.

Common Registration Pitfalls That Delay or Block Submission

Most failed submissions come from three causes: an expired SAM.gov registration, a UEI not yet linked to the Grants.gov account, or a missing AOR role. You can prevent all three by checking status before you apply.

PitfallSymptomFix
Chose "Unique Entity ID only" in SAM.govYou have a UEI but can't applyGo back and complete full Register Entity (SAM.gov)
SAM.gov registration expiredGrants.gov blocks submission for your organizationRenew in SAM.gov. Start 60+ days early next time
EBiz POC used a different email in Grants.govPOC can't approve rolesSign in with the email listed in SAM.gov, or update the POC in SAM.gov
Added an Individual profile instead of OrganizationApplication isn't linked to your UEIAdd an Organization Applicant Profile with the UEI
Standard AOR isn't a workspace participantNo submit optionAdd them as a participant, or assign Expanded AOR (FAQs)
"Email Already Exists in System"Can't create an accountSign in to the existing account or use another email (FAQs)
Bad attachment file namesWhole package rejectedRename to ≤50 allowed characters
Legal name doesn't match IRS recordsSAM.gov stalls in validationUse your exact IRS name and address, then resubmit

Run this check about 30 days before any deadline:

  1. In SAM.gov, confirm the entity status is Active and the expiration date falls after the award date, not just after the deadline.
  2. Confirm the EBiz POC is still with your organization and their email works.
  3. In Grants.gov, sign in as the submitter and confirm your profile shows the right UEI and an AOR role.
  4. Open the Workspace for the opportunity and make sure the submitter is a participant.
  5. After you submit, save the tracking number and download the submitted package. Grants.gov recommends downloading a copy to verify the contents of the submission zip file.

Small businesses chasing their first grant can pair this checklist with How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide).

Next steps

You can finish most of the setup today, and it's all free.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open SAM.gov's Entity Registration Checklist and gather your TIN, exact IRS legal name, bank details and EBiz POC email.
  2. Create or check your Login.gov account, then start Register Entity in SAM.gov. If you already have a registration, check its expiration date.
  3. If you're an individual applying for yourself, skip SAM.gov. Register on Grants.gov and add an Individual Applicant profile.

If you'd rather not do it yourself:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) are federally funded offices that give small businesses free help with SAM.gov registration (as of October 2026; check the official page). They're a good fit for small businesses, especially ones that may also bid on contracts. Their focus is government contracting, so nonprofits that want help writing grant narratives may get less out of them.
  • Grants.gov Support Center (free, 1-800-518-4726, 24/7 except federal holidays, OJP) is for registration and submission problems. It won't review your proposal.
  • Paid grant consultants can help with writing and strategy. Fees vary, so ask for a written quote. This option suits teams without writing capacity. It's a poor fit if all you need is SAM.gov registration, since that's free and paying for it is what the BBB warns about. No consultant can guarantee an award.

FAQ

Do I need a DUNS number or just a UEI now?

You only need a UEI. On April 4, 2022, the federal government stopped using DUNS numbers in SAM.gov and switched to the Unique Entity ID (SAM), a 12-character ID issued free in SAM.gov (GSA fact sheet). Organizations that already had registrations were given UEIs automatically.

Can I use Grants.gov without registering on SAM.gov?

Yes, in two cases. Anyone can search opportunities without registering. Individuals applying for themselves don't need SAM.gov or a UEI. Organizations do need an active SAM.gov registration before they can set up a profile and submit.

How often do I need to renew my SAM.gov registration?

Every 365 days, per SAM.gov. Renewal is free. Start at least 60 days early, because validation problems can push activation past your deadline.

Is there a fee to register on Grants.gov or SAM.gov?

No. Grants.gov says registration is free, and the UEI costs nothing. Anyone asking you to pay for registration or renewal is not the federal government.

What is an AOR on Grants.gov?

An Authorized Organization Representative is a person the EBiz POC has allowed to submit applications for the organization. A Standard AOR can submit only from workspaces they participate in. An Expanded AOR can submit from any of the organization's workspaces (Grants.gov FAQs). The EBiz POC gets Expanded AOR automatically.

item.title: Federal Grant vs Cooperative Agreement: Table + NOFO Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Federal grant vs cooperative agreement compared side by side: funding control, reporting burden and eligibility, plus steps to spot the type in any NOFO.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A federal grant and a cooperative agreement both give you federal money for a public purpose. The legal difference is how involved the agency will be. Under a grant, the agency is not expected to be substantially involved in the work (31 U.S.C. 6304). Under a cooperative agreement, it is expected to take part in carrying it out (31 U.S.C. 6305). You don't choose the instrument. The agency picks it before it publishes the NOFO, so what you're really deciding is whether to apply to that NOFO, given how much control you'll share.

Which option is right for you?

Choose by how much outside direction you can work with and how much staff time you have for coordination.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant, small team, no grants staffGrant NOFOs: you set the direction and coordinate lessSimpler.Grants.gov search, with Funding Instrument → Grant checked
Researcher who wants access to agency scientists, data or a multi-site networkCooperative agreement (for example, NIH "U" activity codes)The NOFO section titled "Cooperative Agreement Terms and Conditions of Award" (example: NIH PAR-26-116)
Nonprofit with a program manager who can attend regular agency callsEither. Cooperative agreements can bring technical helpThe NOFO's program description, where the agency must describe its planned involvement (2 CFR 200 Appendix I)
Tight budget for admin timeGrant: about the same compliance load, fewer meetings2 CFR 200.329 (reporting intervals)
Small business that sells to the governmentNeither. If the government is buying your product or service, it's a procurement contractThe Procurement Contract filter on Simpler.Grants.gov

Federal grant vs cooperative agreement: side-by-side table

Funding control is the only one of the three areas that really changes. Reporting and eligibility are mostly the same under both.

FactorFederal grantCooperative agreement
Legal testNo substantial agency involvement expected (31 U.S.C. 6304)Substantial agency involvement expected (31 U.S.C. 6305)
Who steers the workYou, subject to normal monitoringMostly you, but some tasks, approvals or decisions are shared with agency staff
Agency role (NIH wording)"Patron""Partner" (NIH OIR)
Performance reporting floorQuarterly to annual, set by award (2 CFR 200.329)Same rule, plus coordination such as joint input on progress reports in some NOFOs
Single AuditRequired if you spend $1,000,000+ in federal awards in a fiscal year (2 CFR 200.501)Same threshold
Who can applyWhoever the NOFO's eligibility section listsWhoever the NOFO's eligibility section lists
Where it's spelled outAward termsAward terms, plus a required description of agency involvement in the NOFO (Appendix I)

Both instruments are common. With the default filters on Simpler.Grants.gov on October 19, 2026, the Funding Instrument filter showed 969 Grant listings, 546 Cooperative Agreement listings, 26 Procurement Contract listings and 52 Other. These counts change every day.

Difference 1: Funding control and "substantial involvement"

In a cooperative agreement you still run the project, but agency staff take an active part in specific pieces of it. The Uniform Guidance definitions in 2 CFR 200.1 say a cooperative agreement "provides for substantial involvement" of the agency, and a grant agreement "does not."

What counts as substantial involvement

The DOE Office of Science describes it as a federal employee "actively assisting, guiding, coordinating, or participating in the project." Its examples include managing how resources are split across sites and taking part in the research itself. It also notes that "normal oversight and stewardship are not substantial involvement" (DOE Office of Science). NIH's examples include an NIH scientist having primary responsibility for one specific aim, building a major database for the extramural team, or joining a multi-institution collaboration. Occasional advice or occasional sample analyses don't count (NIH OIR). NOAA puts it more simply: in a cooperative agreement the agency "supports the recipient's work to achieve the award's purpose" (NOAA).

What it looks like in a real NOFO

Take NIH's PAR-26-116 (a U01, clinical trial optional) as an example. It lists the instrument as "Cooperative Agreement" in Section II, Award Information. Section VI.2 then gives the PD/PI "primary responsibility to define objectives and approaches, and to plan, conduct, analyze, and publish results." An NIH intramural scientist has primary responsibility for "a substantial portion of the proposed research." Annual progress reports are prepared with that scientist's input, and disagreements go to a three-member Dispute Resolution Panel (PAR-26-116). That's the trade-off. You gain a federal collaborator, and some of your decisions become joint ones.

Difference 2: Reporting burden

The formal reporting rules are mostly the same. The extra burden in a cooperative agreement is coordination time, which doesn't show up as extra forms. Under 2 CFR 200.329, performance reports are due no more often than quarterly and no less often than annually. Annual reports are due within 90 calendar days after the reporting period, quarterly or semiannual reports within 30 days, and the final report within 120 days after the period of performance ends. Those deadlines apply to both instruments.

An agency can require more frequent or more detailed reports only by adding a "specific condition." Before doing so, it has to tell you the reason and what you must do to get the condition removed (2 CFR 200.208). That depends on your risk profile, not on whether you hold a grant or a cooperative agreement.

When you plan staff time, budget for:

  • Steering committee or check-in meetings named in the cooperative agreement terms
  • Agency review or approval steps written into the terms, such as work plans or protocols
  • Drafting progress reports together with agency staff (as in PAR-26-116)

In practice, if a NOFO lists monthly steering committee calls, put those hours into your personnel budget. Don't assume they fit inside your normal admin time.

Difference 3: Eligibility (mostly not a difference)

Who can apply is set by the program and the NOFO, not by the instrument type. Both statutes use the same recipient language, "a State, a local government, or other recipient" (6304, 6305). Simpler.Grants.gov handles Eligibility as its own filter, separate from Funding Instrument. It has 13 options covering governments, tribes, schools, nonprofits, businesses and individuals (Simpler.Grants.gov).

The registration steps are also the same for both. If you haven't confirmed your SAM.gov registration yet, do that first using our guide on how to check SAM.gov registration status.

One real eligibility-type boundary does exist. If the government's main purpose is to buy something for its own use, the law requires a procurement contract, not either kind of assistance award (31 U.S.C. 6305).

How to check the instrument type on any NOFO (step by step)

This takes about five minutes per opportunity, and it's the quickest way to decide whether a NOFO fits your capacity.

  1. Open simpler.grants.gov/search.
  2. Under Opportunity Status, check Open (and Forecasted if you want to plan ahead).
  3. Under Funding Instrument, check Grant, Cooperative Agreement or both.
  4. Under Eligibility, check your entity type. If you can put up a match, look at Cost Sharing too.
  5. Open a listing and read the full announcement. Look for "Funding Instrument" in the Award Information section (Section II in NIH NOFOs).
  6. If it says Cooperative Agreement, find the description of agency involvement. Federal rules require it in the program description or a reference to where it lives (2 CFR 200 Appendix I). In NIH NOFOs it's Section VI.2.
  7. Write down every meeting, approval and shared task, and estimate the hours.
  8. If a role is unclear, email the program officer named in the NOFO's agency contacts section before you start writing.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Treating a cooperative agreement as "harder to win." Nothing in the statutes says that. Fix: judge each NOFO on fit and capacity.
  • Skipping the involvement section. Then your narrative ignores the agency's planned role. Fix: describe in the application how you'll work with agency staff. Our federal proposal guide for nonprofits covers how to structure the narrative.
  • Assuming lighter compliance under a grant. Cost rules, audits and reporting intervals come from the same 2 CFR 200 sections. Fix: plan the same compliance work either way.
  • Applying to a procurement contract by mistake. Fix: check that the Funding Instrument field doesn't say Procurement Contract.

Next steps

Pick one live NOFO today and run the eight steps above. That will tell you more than reading definitions.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Run the Simpler.Grants.gov search with your Eligibility box checked and save the links to two or three matching NOFOs.
  2. For any cooperative agreement on that list, copy the agency-involvement text into a document and add up the meeting hours.
  3. Start your SF-424 early with our field-by-field SF-424 instructions.

If you'd rather have help: Small businesses can use a local Small Business Development Center. There are about 1,000 SBDCs, offering no-cost consulting and low-cost training (as of October 2026; check the official SBA page). An SBDC is a good fit for business owners who need help with funding strategy. It isn't the right choice if you need someone to write your science or program narrative, because SBDC advisors are business generalists and availability varies by center. Researchers at universities can usually go to their sponsored programs office, which is often free to faculty. Independent grant writers charge fees that vary widely, so ask for a written scope and quote before you sign.

Related guides on this site:

  • How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)
  • Small Business Grants for Women: Federal Options (2026)
  • How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide

FAQ

Is a cooperative agreement a grant?

It's a separate legal instrument, but both are federal financial assistance and both fall under 2 CFR 200. The difference is whether the agency is substantially involved in the work (2 CFR 200.1). Many people informally call both "grants."

Can I ask the agency to switch a cooperative agreement to a grant?

Not when you apply. The agency picks the instrument when it designs the program and publishes it in the NOFO. If the involvement terms don't work for you, the realistic choice is to skip that NOFO and look for a different one.

What does a "U" code mean in NIH funding?

NIH "U" activity codes such as U01 are cooperative agreements. "R" codes such as R01 are grants. NIH describes its role in a U award as "partner" and its role in an R award as "patron" (NIH OIR).

How is a cooperative agreement different from a contract?

A contract is used when the government is acquiring property or services for its own direct benefit. A cooperative agreement supports a public purpose with the agency taking part (31 U.S.C. 6305). On Simpler.Grants.gov, contracts appear under the Procurement Contract filter.

item.title: SF-424 Instructions: Field-by-Field Table and Steps (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SF-424 instructions in plain English: what to type in all 21 fields from your SAM.gov profile, the district format, field 19-21 picks, and common fixes.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The SF-424 (Application for Federal Assistance) is the cover form for most federal grant packages on Grants.gov. It has 21 numbered fields, and you fill nearly all of them with three things: your SAM.gov entity record (legal name, UEI, EIN, address), the funding notice (agency, Assistance Listing number, opportunity number) and your own project budget. The current version 4.0 has OMB number 4040-0004 and an expiration date of 03/31/2029 (Grants.gov SF-424 4.0 form). Below, each field gets a plain-English line telling you what to type.

Which option is right for you?

The right starting point depends on whether your SAM.gov registration is already active and on how often you apply.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never applied, not sure SAM.gov is activeConfirm an active SAM.gov registration before you touch the SF-424SAM.gov entity record (see our guide /how-to-check-sam-gov-registration-status-step-by-step/)
First application, SAM.gov already activeFill the SF-424 as a webform in Grants.gov WorkspaceGrants.gov Workspace overview
Daily or repeat work (grants office, several applications a year)Set up Workspace roles so someone with the AOR role can submitWorkspace roles
No budget, need helpFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator, plus the free Grants.gov Contact CenterSAM.gov external resources
Applying through an agency portal (e.g., DOJ JustGrants)Read that agency's SF-424 notes as well; some fields carry agency-specific meaningOJP Grant Application Resource Guide

If you're a beginner, start with SAM.gov. Grants.gov won't let you submit without an active SAM registration (Grants.gov: Submit a Workspace Application), so a polished SF-424 can't get past a lapsed record.

Before you start: gather these five items

You need about five pieces of information, and most of them come straight from your SAM.gov record.

  1. Legal business name and physical address, exactly as SAM.gov shows them. SAM.gov requires these to match your IRS/TIN records (SAM.gov Entity Registration Checklist).
  2. UEI. This is the 12-character Unique Entity ID that SAM.gov assigns (SF-424 instructions).
  3. EIN/TIN from the IRS.
  4. From the funding notice (NOFO): agency name, Assistance Listing number, funding opportunity number, competition ID if there is one, and the deadline.
  5. Your budget totals, split into federal request and any match.

Registration in SAM.gov is free and has to be renewed every 365 days (SAM.gov checklist). Anyone charging a fee to "register" you is a third-party service, not the government.

SF-424 field-by-field: what to type

Each row below gives the field as it appears on the form and what to enter. Field numbers follow the official version 4.0 form (SF-424 4.0; instructions).

Fields 1–7: submission type and identifiers

FieldWhat to typeWhere it comes from
1. Type of Submission"Application" for a normal submission. Use "Preapplication" only if the NOFO asks for one, and "Changed/Corrected Application" only when you're resubmitting before the deadline to replace an earlier oneNOFO
2. Type of Application"New" for a first-time award. "Continuation" or "Revision" only for an existing award, and Revision asks you to pick a revision typeYour award history
3. Date ReceivedLeave it alone; Grants.gov fills it in when you submitSystem
4. Applicant IdentifierOptional internal tracking number (for example, your own file code)You
5a/5b. Federal Entity / Award IdentifierUsually blank for new applicants. For continuations or revisions, enter the existing federal award numberPrior award
6–7. State Use OnlyBlank unless your state's review process gives you an identifierState SPOC

Field 8: applicant information (copy from SAM.gov)

This is where most rejections and mismatches start. The Office of Justice Programs tells applicants to enter the UEI, legal name and EIN "exactly as it appears on the matching SAM.gov record". It also warns that if the SF-424 and SAM.gov disagree, OJP "will default to the SAM.gov record" (OJP guide).

  • 8a. Legal Name: The legal business name from SAM.gov. Don't use a DBA or a shortened name. For example, if SAM shows "Riverbend Community Health Inc.", don't type "Riverbend Health".
  • 8b. EIN/TIN: Your IRS Employer Identification Number.
  • 8c. UEI: The 12-character UEI from SAM.gov. In Workspace this often comes over automatically from the organization tied to your workspace. Check it anyway.
  • 8d. Address: Street, city, county/parish, state, country and ZIP, matching the physical address in SAM.gov.
  • 8e. Organizational Unit: Department and division name if you have them, such as "School of Engineering". Small businesses can usually leave this blank.
  • 8f. Contact person: The person who can answer questions about this application. In JustGrants, DOJ uses this email address to assign the application to a user (OJP guide), so use a real inbox that someone watches.

Fields 9–15: applicant type, program and project

FieldWhat to type
9. Type of ApplicantChoose at least one type and no more than three. The form may already show these if the agency set them (instructions). Small businesses typically choose "Small Business". Nonprofits choose the option for organizations with or without 501(c)(3) status that fits them
10. Name of Federal AgencyUsually pre-filled from the opportunity
11. Assistance Listing NumberPre-filled or copied from the NOFO (format like 10.xxx)
12. Funding Opportunity Number and TitlePre-filled from the package
13. Competition IdentificationPre-filled if the agency uses competitions; otherwise blank
14. Areas Affected by ProjectCities, counties or states where the work happens. Attach a list if it's long
15. Descriptive Title of Applicant's ProjectA short, specific title. For example: "Mobile Dental Screening for Rural Pike County Schools" rather than "Health Project"

Field 16: congressional districts

Enter the districts in a fixed format: a two-letter state code, a hyphen, then a three-digit district number. CA-005 means California's 5th district, MD-all covers every district in Maryland, and US-all is for nationwide projects (SF-424 instructions). 16a is your organization's own district. 16b is the main district your project affects. You can attach a list for additional districts. A common mistake is typing "CA-5" or "5". Pad the number to three digits.

Fields 17–18: dates and money

  • 17. Proposed Project start and end dates: Use the period of performance the NOFO describes. If the notice says awards begin around a certain date, don't pick a start date earlier than that.
  • 18. Estimated Funding: Lines for Federal, Applicant, State, Local, Other and Program Income, plus a Total. These figures need to match your detailed budget form (such as the SF-424A) and your budget narrative. Reviewers compare them.

For example, if you're asking for $250,000 with a $50,000 cash match, Federal is 250,000, Applicant is 50,000 and Total is 300,000. The 50,000 then needs to show up the same way in the budget narrative.

Fields 19–21: review, debt and signature

  • 19. Is Application Subject to Review by State Under E.O. 12372? Choose (a) only if your state reviews this program and you've sent the application to the state SPOC; enter that date. Choose (b) if the program is covered but your state hasn't selected it. Choose (c) if the program isn't covered. Check the NOFO and the official SPOC list. States that aren't on the list don't take part (OJP guide).
  • 20. Is the Applicant Delinquent on Any Federal Debt? Answer Yes or No for the organization. If Yes, explain and attach the explanation. Don't leave a Yes without one.
  • 21. Certification: Check "I Agree". In Workspace, the authorized representative fields are tied to the person who submits, and signing happens when that person submits.

How to submit the SF-424 in Grants.gov Workspace (steps)

You don't sign the SF-424 by hand. A user with the right role signs it electronically when they submit the whole Workspace package.

  1. Find the opportunity on Grants.gov, click Apply and create a workspace. You need at least the Workspace Manager role to do this (Workspace roles).
  2. On the Forms tab, open the SF-424 as a webform. You can fill forms in the browser rather than download PDFs (Grants.gov).
  3. Do the SF-424 first. The forms share common fields such as name, address and UEI, and that information carries over to the other forms only after the SF-424 is filled in (instructions).
  4. Finish the other forms and attachments until every required form shows Passed.
  5. The participant with the Standard AOR role (or a user with the Expanded AOR role) goes to Manage Workspace → Forms and clicks Sign and Submit in the Workspace Actions box (Grants.gov).
  6. When the pop-up asks whether this is a changed/corrected application, answer Yes or No. Then click Sign and Submit again.
  7. Save the Grants.gov tracking number from the confirmation screen; it's also emailed to you (Grants.gov).

Common SF-424 mistakes and how to fix them

Most SF-424 problems are data mismatches, not writing problems.

MistakeFix
Legal name or address differs from SAM.govCopy straight from your SAM.gov entity record. If SAM itself is wrong, update SAM first, which takes time (checklist)
SAM registration lapsed during the applicationSAM registration has to be renewed every 365 days. Check the expiration date weeks before the deadline
Sign and Submit is grayed outPrerequisites include: forms show Passed, package still open, active SAM, and you hold an AOR role (Grants.gov). Ask your Expanded AOR to assign you the Standard AOR role
District typed as "TX-7"Use three digits: TX-007
Field 18 total doesn't match the budget formFix the budget form first, then copy its totals into field 18
Field 19 set to (a) with no SPOC contactChoose (a) only after you've actually submitted to your state's SPOC

Limitation: Grants.gov's check for Passed status confirms that the format is correct. It can't tell whether your numbers or your district are right, so a "Passed" form can still be wrong.

Next steps

You can fill out a correct SF-424 today if your SAM.gov record is active. The free help covers most of the rest.

DIY today:

  1. Open your SAM.gov entity record. Write down the exact legal name, UEI, EIN and physical address, plus the registration expiration date (step-by-step: /how-to-check-sam-gov-registration-status-step-by-step/).
  2. Ask whoever manages your organization's Grants.gov account to confirm you have the Standard AOR role, or name the person who does.
  3. Fill in fields 10–13 and 16–18 from the NOFO and your budget, then compare field 18 with the budget form.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators give free counseling with SAM.gov registration, paid for by the Department of Defense and local host organizations (SAM.gov external resources). This suits small businesses. It's less suited to university research offices, which usually have their own sponsored-programs staff. Their main focus is contracting, so they may not review the substance of a grant narrative.
  • The Grants.gov Contact Center at 1-800-518-4726 is free. It's open 24/7 except federal holidays (Grants.gov Support). Call it for technical errors, but don't expect advice on budgets or project design.
  • Paid grant consultants charge different fees depending on scope (as of October 2026; ask for a written quote). They make sense for a large, complex application. They don't make sense if your only problem is an SF-424 field, because the free options above already cover that.

Related guides on this site:

  • /how-to-apply-for-grants-for-small-business-2026-guide/
  • /how-to-write-grants-for-nonprofits-federal-proposal-guide/
  • /small-business-grants-for-women-federal-options-2026/

FAQ

Where do I find my UEI for the SF-424?

Look in your entity record on SAM.gov. The UEI is a 12-character ID that SAM.gov assigns (instructions). Copy it exactly as shown; don't type it from memory.

What do I put for congressional district on the SF-424?

Write a two-letter state code, a hyphen and a three-digit district, such as CA-005. If the project covers a whole state, use the "all" form (MD-all), and for a nationwide project use US-all (instructions).

Which box do I check in SF-424 field 19?

Check the NOFO and the SPOC list. Choose (a) only if your state reviews the program and you've already sent it to the state, (b) if the program is covered but your state hasn't selected it, and (c) if E.O. 12372 doesn't apply.

Who signs the SF-424?

The authorized organization representative signs it electronically by clicking Sign and Submit in Workspace. That person needs the Standard AOR role as a workspace participant, or the Expanded AOR role (Workspace roles).

Is the SF-424 the same as the SF-424 (R&R)?

No. The SF-424 (R&R) is a separate research-and-related version that some research agencies use. Use the form that's in your opportunity's package, because it's the one Grants.gov will check.

item.title: How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Learn how to write grants for nonprofits the way federal reviewers score them: needs statement, goals, budget narrative, and Grants.gov submission steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To write a federal grant for a nonprofit, start with the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), not with a template. Find its "Application Review Information" section and write one narrative section for each scored criterion, using the NOFO's own headings. Give each section space in proportion to its points, and make the budget narrative explain every cost. Federal rules require agencies to publish their review criteria and, when the criteria differ in importance, to publish their relative weights. That means the scoring rubric is usually printed in the NOFO you're answering (2 CFR Part 200, Appendix I).

Which option is right for you?

Choose where to start based on how much federal experience you have and how much time or money you can spend. Every path below starts with free official tools.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never applied federallyGet registered first, then read one NOFO's review criteriaSAM.gov (see our SAM.gov status guide)
Small business owner, not a nonprofitCheck eligibility before writing anything, because many NOFOs exclude for-profitsOur small business grant guide
Grant writing is part of your regular jobBuild a reusable outline that matches the eight Appendix I sections2 CFR Appendix I
Researcher applying to NSFWrite to Intellectual Merit and Broader ImpactsNSF merit review
Zero budget, need human helpFree advising from a Small Business Development CenterSBA local assistance
Some budget, want structured trainingA paid proposal-writing courseCandid Learning

What federal reviewers actually score

Reviewers score the criteria printed in the NOFO's "Application Review Information" section, and nothing else. Generic fundraising polish doesn't earn points.

Under the Uniform Guidance, every federal NOFO must use the same or similar section headings, plus a table of contents. The required sections are Basic Information, Eligibility, Program Description, Application Contents and Format, Submission Requirements and Deadlines, Application Review Information, Award Notices, and Post-Award Requirements and Administration (Appendix I). The same appendix says that "if criteria vary in importance, the relative percentages, weights, or other means used to distinguish between them" must be disclosed.

Agencies are also told to make opportunities available "for at least 60 calendar days" and to write them in plain language (2 CFR 200.204). Their Program Description must cover "performance goals, indicators, targets, baseline data, data collection" (Appendix I). This is useful: the NOFO tells you which measures the agency wants you to report.

What scoring looks like in real NOFOs

AgencyScored criteriaNotes
HRSA (HHS)Need, Response, Evaluative Measures, Impact, Resources/Capabilities, Support RequestedIn one HRSA NOFO the weights were 10 / 35 / 15 / 10 / 25 / 5, out of 100 (HRSA-21-066). Weights vary by NOFO.
DOJ / OJPDescription of the need, goals and objectives, project design and implementation, capabilities and competencies, plus the budget"Each section of the proposal narrative and the budget are given a numeric score" (OJP guide)
NSFIntellectual Merit and Broader ImpactsReviewers ask whether the plan is "well-reasoned," whether the team is qualified, and whether resources are adequate (NSF)

The HRSA example shows a common pattern. The needs statement carried only 10 points, while the work plan ("Response") carried 35 and organizational capacity 25. Many first-time applicants spend half their pages on the problem and leave little room for the plan. Size each section to its points.

Since August 2025, Executive Order 14332 has also required senior agency appointees to review new NOFOs, so they line up with agency priorities (EO 14332, govinfo; Ballotpedia summary)). In practice, read the current NOFO's Program Description closely. Don't reuse priority language from an older version of the same program.

How to write each scored section

Write each section as a direct answer to its criterion. Use the NOFO's exact heading and echo its wording so a reviewer can find what they're scoring.

Needs statement (often "Need" or "Statement of the Problem")

The needs statement shows that a specific, measurable problem exists in your service area and that your project addresses it.

  • Open with one local data point and its source, for example a county rate compared with the state rate.
  • Name the population you'll serve and how many people that is.
  • Connect the gap directly to the NOFO's purpose statement, and stop there. You don't get extra points for a long history of the issue.

Example (illustrative): "In [County], [X]% of adults report [condition], compared with [Y]% statewide ([source]). This project will serve [N] residents in [ZIP codes]."

Goals, objectives, and project design (often "Response" or "Project Design and Implementation")

This section usually carries the most points, so it should take up the most space.

  • Write 2–4 objectives that are specific and measurable: who, what, how much, and by when.
  • For each objective, list the activities, the responsible staff role, and the timeline (a table works well).
  • Reuse the NOFO's performance measures word for word as your targets. Appendix I requires agencies to state the indicators and targets they expect (Appendix I).

Capacity (often "Resources/Capabilities" or "Capabilities and Competencies")

Prove that your organization can run this project and manage federal money.

  • Name the key staff, their qualifications, and their percentage of time (it must match the budget).
  • Mention partners and attach signed letters if the NOFO asks for them.
  • Briefly describe your financial controls. NOFOs must describe the agency's risk review factors, so look for them (Appendix I).

Evaluation (often "Evaluative Measures" or "Plan for Collecting Data")

Explain how you'll know the objectives were met: data source, frequency, who collects it, and how results feed back into the program.

Budget narrative (often "Budget Justification" or "Support Requested")

The budget narrative explains how each line item was calculated and why it's needed. OJP, for example, says the budget detail "should provide detailed computation for each budget line item" and "a thorough and clear description of every cost listed." It also says budgets must be "allowable (e.g., reasonable, allocable, and necessary for project activities)" (OJP guide).

Example format (illustrative): "Program Coordinator: $52,000 salary × 50% effort × 12 months = $26,000. Coordinates intake and data collection for Objectives 1–2."

Every person, activity, and number in the narrative should appear in the budget, and every budget line should trace back to an activity in the narrative.

Step-by-step: from NOFO to Grants.gov submission

Register early, build the outline from the NOFO, and submit days before the deadline, not hours.

  1. Register your organization in SAM.gov to get a Unique Entity ID (UEI). Grants.gov says this can take "up to 10 business days" once your documents are ready. Use the same email you'll use at Grants.gov, because that match gives you the expanded AOR role (Grants.gov Quick Start). To check progress, follow our SAM.gov registration status guide.
  2. Create your Grants.gov account. Click Register on the home page, then Get Registered Now. Someone in your organization needs the expanded AOR, standard AOR, or workspace manager role to create a workspace. Only AOR roles can submit (Grants.gov Quick Start).
  3. Download the NOFO and build your outline. Copy the headings from the "Application Contents and Format" and "Application Review Information" sections into a document. Note each criterion's points, the page limit, and the font and format rules.
  4. Create a workspace. Open the opportunity, click Apply, enter an application name, and create the workspace. You need a separate workspace for each application (Grants.gov Quick Start). FEMA's tutorial describes entering the Funding Opportunity number and clicking Create Workspace, then using the Webform link in the Actions column to fill in forms (FEMA Workspace tutorial).
  5. Complete the forms, starting with the SF-424. Attach the project narrative and budget justification as PDFs.
  6. Submit. Click Sign and Submit (FEMA tutorial). Grants.gov says to submit "well before the deadline," and DOJ urges submitting the SF-424 "at least 48 hours prior to the Grants.gov deadline" (Grants.gov; OJP). Some agencies, including DOJ, use a second system after Grants.gov (JustGrants), with its own deadline.
  7. Track the status. Go to Applicants → Check Application Status, then click Search and Details. The statuses move from Received to Validated to Received by Agency to Agency Tracking Number Assigned. "Rejected with Errors" means you have to fix the problem and resubmit (Grants.gov status help).

Common mistakes and fixes

Most problems come from not following the NOFO or from starting registration too late.

MistakeFix
Spending the most pages on the need, even though it carries few pointsSize each section to its points in the NOFO's review criteria
Using your own headingsUse the NOFO's headings word for word so reviewers can find each criterion
Starting SAM.gov registration the week of the deadlineStart now. Registration can take up to 10 business days (Grants.gov)
Different email addresses in SAM.gov and Grants.govUse the same email so expanded AOR is assigned automatically
Budget lines with no mathShow quantity × rate × time for every line (OJP)
Status shows "Rejected with Errors"Read the error email, correct the problem, and resubmit before the deadline (Grants.gov)
Small business applying to a nonprofit-only NOFOCheck the Eligibility section first. See our small business guide

Next steps

You can make real progress today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Look up your SAM.gov status, or start registering, using our step-by-step SAM.gov guide.
  2. Pick one open NOFO on Grants.gov and copy its review criteria and point values into a blank outline.
  3. Draft your needs statement in one paragraph with one sourced local statistic, then move on to objectives.

If you'd rather get help:

  • SBDC advising (free): SBA-funded Small Business Development Centers offer "free business consulting and low-cost training" (SBA). This suits small businesses and startups. It isn't a grant-writing service, and how much grant expertise you get varies by center.
  • Candid Learning: a free Introduction to Proposal Writing course, plus a three-week Proposal Writing Boot Camp listed at $650 early-bird or $800 regular (as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits nonprofit staff who will write proposals repeatedly. One limitation: it covers proposal writing in general, including foundation proposals, so you still have to apply it to each NOFO's federal rules. If you only need one application, it's probably more than you need.
  • Grants.gov support (free): 1-800-518-4726 or support@grants.gov, available 24/7, for technical submission problems only. They don't help with writing (Grants.gov).

Related guides on Grant Radar:

  • How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)
  • How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)

FAQ

What are the main parts of a federal grant proposal?

Most federal proposals include an SF-424 cover form, a project narrative, a budget and budget justification, and attachments. The narrative's sections come from the NOFO, and they usually include need, goals and objectives, project design, capacity, and evaluation (OJP). Always follow the "Application Contents and Format" section of your specific NOFO.

How long does it take to be ready to apply for a federal grant?

Plan for registration before any writing. Grants.gov says SAM.gov registration can take up to 10 business days once your documents are ready (Grants.gov). NOFOs are generally open for at least 60 days (2 CFR 200.204), so starting registration as soon as you spot an opportunity leaves time to write.

How are federal grant applications scored?

Reviewers score each criterion listed in the NOFO's "Application Review Information" section. When the criteria differ in importance, their weights must be disclosed (Appendix I). HRSA, for example, has used a 100-point scale, while NSF uses Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.

What is a budget narrative in a grant?

A budget narrative (or budget justification) explains how each line item was calculated and why it's necessary for the project. DOJ asks for the calculation and a clear description for every cost (OJP).

Can small businesses apply for the same grants as nonprofits?

Only if the NOFO's Eligibility section lists for-profit organizations. Many federal grants are limited to nonprofits, governments, or institutions. Check eligibility before you write anything.

item.title: Small Business Grants for Women: Federal Options (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Small business grants for women from the federal government are limited. Learn which SBA programs, SBIR/STTR awards, and WOSB certification apply to you.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The federal government has no general grant program that gives women money just to start or grow a small business. The SBA says directly: "SBA does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business." The federal options that do exist for women-owned businesses are research grants (SBIR/STTR), set-aside contracts under the Women-Owned Small Business (WOSB) Federal Contract Program, SBA microloans, and free or low-cost help from Women's Business Centers.

Which option is right for you?

Choose based on what your business does today, not on which program sounds most generous.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner or pre-launch, with no funding plan yetA Women's Business Center (free or low-cost counseling)SBA local assistance finder
Tech or science startup with an R&D ideaSBIR/STTR (grants and contracts that don't take equity)SBIR.gov
Business that already sells, or wants to sell, to government agenciesWOSB or EDWOSB certificationSBA Certifications
Small budget and needs under $50,000 for equipment or inventorySBA Microloan (a loan, not a grant)SBA Microloans
Nonprofit that serves women entrepreneursSearch Grants.gov with an eligibility filterGrants.gov Search Grants
Exporter or planning to exportState Trade Expansion Program (STEP) through your stateSBA Grants page

Why each pick:

  • Women's Business Center: the counseling is "free, to low-cost," so you can start without spending anything.
  • SBIR/STTR: this is the largest real federal grant source open to for-profit small businesses. It is only for R&D work.
  • WOSB: it limits competition for some federal contracts, which turns into revenue rather than a one-time grant.
  • Microloan: it is fast, small, and meant for early-stage needs. You have to repay it.

What federal funding actually exists for women-owned businesses

Federal money for women business owners comes through four channels, and only one of them is a true business grant.

SBIR and STTR research grants

SBIR and STTR fund research and development at small businesses. They pay "equity free funding through federal agencies" across 11 participating agencies. As of October 2026, SBIR.gov lists Phase I awards of up to $335,937 and Phase II awards of up to $2,239,578 (SBIR.gov). Each agency sets its own amounts and topics, so check every solicitation.

Status matters here. Both programs lapsed on September 30, 2025, and new awards paused. They were reauthorized on April 13, 2026, under the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act of 2026 (S. 3971), which runs through September 30, 2031 (Crowell & Moring; IEDC). Starting in fiscal year 2027, agencies will set their own caps on how many proposals one company can submit (Crowell & Moring).

Not for: service, retail, or restaurant businesses with no research component. Limitation: competition is strong, and the work has to match a topic an agency has published.

WOSB Federal Contract Program (contracts, not grants)

The WOSB program limits competition for certain federal contracts to certified women-owned firms. The government's goal is to award 5% of federal contracting dollars to these businesses (SBA).

Eligibility (SBA; 13 CFR Part 127):

  • The business is small under SBA size standards.
  • It is at least 51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizens.
  • Women manage day-to-day operations and make long-term decisions.
  • EDWOSB (economically disadvantaged) has extra limits for each qualifying owner: personal net worth under $850,000, adjusted gross income of $400,000 or less averaged over three years, and personal assets of $6.5 million or less.

Not for: businesses that don't want to sell to government agencies. Limitation: certification doesn't guarantee any contract. You still have to find and win bids.

SBA Microloans (loan, not grant)

Microloans go up to $50,000 and average about $13,000. Terms run up to seven years, and interest rates are generally 8% to 13%, depending on the intermediary lender (as of October 2026; check the official page) (SBA). You can use the money for working capital, inventory, supplies, and equipment. You can't use it to pay existing debts or buy real estate.

Not for: anyone who needs money they don't have to repay.

Women's Business Centers and other SBA-funded help

SBA grants go to organizations that train entrepreneurs, and those organizations pass the help on to you. Women's Business Centers offer free or low-cost counseling and training. The SBA also funds the Women Veteran Entrepreneurship Training Program for women veterans, service members, and spouses (SBA Grants).

How to find and apply for a federal grant, step by step

You'll register once and then search on Grants.gov or SBIR.gov. Most federal awards require an active SAM.gov registration.

Step 1: Register your entity in SAM.gov

  1. Go to SAM.gov, sign in through Login.gov, and start the entity registration.
  2. Use your legal business name and address exactly as they appear in IRS records.
  3. Renew every 365 days. SAM.gov states: "You must renew your registration every 365 days to keep it active."

If you're already registered, confirm you're active with our guide to checking your SAM.gov registration status.

Step 2: Search Grants.gov with the right filters

  1. Open Grants.gov → Search Grants.
  2. Under Opportunity Status, check Posted, and also Forecasted if you want to see upcoming programs.
  3. Under Eligibility, change All Eligibilities to the category that fits you, such as small businesses or nonprofits.
  4. In Keyword(s), try "women," "entrepreneur," or your industry.
  5. Set the sort to Close Date (Ascending) so the nearest deadlines show first.

Step 3: For R&D, check SBIR.gov solicitations

Open SBIR.gov, filter open topics by agency, and read the agency's own solicitation for page limits and amounts. Rules for FY2027 may change because of the new submission caps (Crowell & Moring).

Step 4: For WOSB, apply through SBA Certifications

  1. Confirm your primary NAICS code and your size standard.
  2. Make sure your SAM.gov profile is active.
  3. Go to SBA Certifications, use the pre-application checklists, and upload your documents, including proof of citizenship (SBA).
  4. Update your SAM.gov profile every year. SBA does a program examination every three years.

You can also get certified through an SBA-approved third-party certifier: the El Paso Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, the National Women Business Owners Corporation, the U.S. Women's Chamber of Commerce, or the Women's Business Enterprise National Council. These certifiers may charge fees (SBA).

For a fuller walkthrough of application packages, see How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide).

Common mistakes and how to fix them

Most rejections and delays come from eligibility mismatches and paperwork problems, not from weak ideas.

MistakeFix
Applying to "grant" sites that ask for a feeFederal grants are listed on Grants.gov and SBIR.gov. Start your search there.
Assuming SBA gives grants to start a businessIt doesn't (SBA). Look at microloans, SBIR, or WOSB instead.
Letting SAM.gov expire mid-applicationRenew before the 365-day mark (SAM.gov).
Claiming WOSB when a man controls key decisionsWomen must control both daily operations and long-term decisions (13 CFR 127).
Filtering Grants.gov only by keywordAdd the Eligibility filter. Many results only accept states, universities, or nonprofits.
Pitching a product with no R&D to SBIRSBIR funds research that meets an agency's goals, not general growth (SBA).

What nonprofits and researchers should know

For nonprofits, the federal money aimed at women entrepreneurs usually goes to organizations that serve them, not to the business owners themselves. The SBA funds counseling and training organizations rather than individual businesses. That includes Women's Business Centers, PRIME (Program for Investors in Microentrepreneurs), SCORE, and SBDCs (SBA Grants). If your nonprofit runs or wants to run this kind of program, use the Eligibility filter on Grants.gov to find nonprofit opportunities and watch for SBA notices of funding opportunity. Our federal proposal guide for nonprofits covers narratives, budgets, and evaluation sections.

Researchers at universities usually take part in STTR by partnering with a small business. In STTR, the small business is the applicant (SBIR.gov).

Next steps

You can make real progress today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Check or start your SAM.gov registration (SAM.gov).
  2. Run one Grants.gov search with Posted and Forecasted checked and the Eligibility filter set to your category.
  3. If you sell to government agencies, open SBA Certifications and read the WOSB checklist to see whether you qualify.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • Women's Business Center (free to low-cost): good for first-time applicants who want help with a business plan or loan package. It's less useful if you need deep technical help writing an SBIR proposal. Counseling availability depends on the local center (SBA).
  • SBA-approved third-party WOSB certifiers (fees vary; as of October 2026, check each certifier's official page): good if you also want a private-sector women-owned certification. It's not needed if you only want federal WOSB status, because you can apply directly through SBA Certifications (SBA).
  • SBDCs and SCORE (SBA resource partners): good for general business and finance mentoring. They're less specialized than a paid proposal consultant for complex R&D bids (SBA Grants).

Related guides on Grant Radar:

  • How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)
  • How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)
  • How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide

FAQ

Does the federal government give free grants to women to start a business?

No, not as a general program. The SBA states that it does not give grants to start or expand a business (SBA). Federal options include SBIR/STTR for R&D, WOSB contracting, and microloans.

Are SBIR grants available again in 2026?

Yes. SBIR and STTR were reauthorized on April 13, 2026, through September 30, 2031, after a six-month lapse (Crowell & Moring). Check each agency's solicitation for its current open topics.

What is the difference between WOSB and EDWOSB?

Both require at least 51% ownership and control by women who are U.S. citizens. EDWOSB adds economic limits for each owner: net worth under $850,000, average AGI of $400,000 or less, and personal assets of $6.5 million or less (SBA).

How much can I borrow with an SBA microloan?

Up to $50,000, with an average of about $13,000 and terms of up to seven years (SBA). Rates generally run 8% to 13%, depending on the lender.

Is it safe to pay a website to find women's business grants?

You don't need to. Federal grant listings are public on Grants.gov and SBIR.gov. Be careful with any service that promises a guaranteed grant.

Sources

  • SBA – Microloans
  • SBA Certifications portal

  • Grants.gov – Search Grants
